PREFACE 

The proper function of the professional historian, wrote Carl Becker, “is not to repeat the past but to make use of it, to correct and rationalize for common use Mr. Everyman's mythological adaptation of what actually happened." The editors of this volume would go Mr. Becker one better and endeavor, in his celebrated phrase, to make “Everyman his own historian." We would teach Everyman to set his own mythologies aright and to adapt the past, if adapt it he must, from a deeper knowledge of what actually happened. 

For the historical method is not necessarily the preserve of the professional. 

More than two centuries ago White Kennet observed that "the laws of history are all but the dictates of good sense, drawn out and methodized in rules,” and the subsequent development of fancy techniques and terminology has done nothing to destroy the basic accuracy of that definition. Still, we may too easily assume that obstreperously individualistic Everyman will submit readily to the dictatorship of good sense. It is a self-imposed tyranny which demands habits of mental discipline and rigorous objectivity that do not dwell naturally with our cherished emotions and preconceptions. These habits must be acquired. The primary purpose of this volume is to train the student to follow "the dictates of good sense" in his study of the past-to read diverse materials in an intelligent yet critical fashion, to evaluate these materials judiciously, to distinguish fact from opinion and prejudice, to suppress his own predilections, and to formulate objective judg ments of historical events. 

Yet these Problems are more than mere exercises in the application of the historical method. In his study of them the student will also gain an insight into the complexity of history, the tangle of instincts and forces that lies behind any historical event. It is true, of course, that the real significance of history's complexity will not become apparent without a sound knowledge of the narrative of history, and for this we count upon the lecture and textbook. While they provide the conventional summary of broad trends and outstanding events, the Problems permit the student to burrow beneath the surface for a deeper comprehension of the underlying factors and their interaction. Thus, where the text or lecturer is obliged by considerations of time and space to dismiss in a few sentences an event such as the Petition of Right, the Problem leads the student into the maze of fear and hope, interest and altruism, experiment and compromise, from which emerged that famous document. A genuine awareness of both the sweep and complexity of history will enable the student to partake of the philosophical insight, the detachment which comes with broad perspective and deep comprehension, and the moral and intellectual inspiration which are the richest rewards of historical study.

Each of these Problems in historical interpretation deals with an important crisis, or some vital aspect of an important crisis, in England's history from 1066 to 1945. The "crisis approach" serves our purpose in a dual fashion. On the one hand, it calls for a wide variety of historical materials, as the crises occur in such different fields as the political and the intellectual, the economic and the diplomatic. The student's experience is thus broadened by an acquaintance with many types of historical sources. The search for the best materials in each field, moreover, has impelled the editors to unearth hitherto unpublished documents. The reader of this volume will encounter in print for the first time, for example, some valuable accounts of parliamentary proceedings in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, Captain Jenkins' own version of the incident which caused the war of [v]

vi. 

Preface 

1739 to be named after his ear, and some revealing records of electioneering in the heyday of Sir Robert Walpole. On the other hand, the "crisis approach" prevents wasteful dispersion of effort by providing an excellent series of focal points. for an analysis of English history. The ramifications of each crisis extend so far into many aspects of British culture that the student is not narrowly restricted in the scope of his inquiry, but the grouping of each set of documents about a central issue permits fruitful concentration with a reasonable degree of completeness upon a clearly defined historical problem. 

At first glance the reader will find that numerous memorable crises have been omitted while others seemingly less prominent have been included. In the period of liberal reform, for example, there is a Problem on factory legislation but none on the Great Reform Act of 1832. The reasons for discrimination of this sort are in general two. A crisis such as the Great Reform Act does not lend itself to profitable analysis within brief compass; actual experiment in the classroom has proved this to be true. Moreover, the editors recognized that "real crises are often concealed in occurrences so trivial in appearance that they pass unnoticed." We have therefore occasionally excluded a spectacular crisis for the sake of one less obvious but of equal or greater significance. 

To facilitate the study of these Problems the editors have provided a certain amount of consistency in their arrangement. Each is preceded by an introduction which sets the scene by furnishing necessary background and indicating the reason for studying the specific issue at hand. Most problems also contain a set of "questions for study," designed to guide the student in handling and evaluating the disparate materials that he is called upon to read. The materials in each Problem are then grouped into parts, each of which is designed as a single assignment. 

Most Problems are divided into two parts to constitute a single week's work, but a few have three parts. This type of arrangement offers considerable flexibility, permitting the teacher to deal with the materials in the manner which best commends itself to him. He will probably find also that there are more Problems in this volume than he may wish to use in a year, so that he will have sufficient latitude to vary his assignments from one year to another. 

The editors have kept the text as free from footnotes as possible. Only those which provide information indispensable to a study of the documents are placed at the bottom of the pages. All references to the sources from which the materials have been drawn are grouped at the back of the book, where they constitute a convenient bibliography of each Problem. 

In teaching these Problems at Yale University for the last three years, the editors have found that college students take genuine pleasure in working at the stuff of history for themselves. Indeed, somewhat to our surprise we have found that those Problems that require the student to approximate the most difficult work of the professional historian, such as Problems I and XIV, have proved the most popular. We believe that this work in original materials, if properly organized, may profitably be made the central rather than a supplementary part of the course, and that the techniques of the historian, taught in this fashion, will contribute much to the intellectual powers of every undergraduate. 

In a volume of this sort the editors' debt to others has of course been very great. 

Thomas C. Mendenhall II, trailblazer for the problem method, labored unselfishly to produce Problem XIX. Lewis P. Curtis suggested the approach and much of the material for Problem XIV. To Miss Mildred Campbell and Douglas M.

Knight we are grateful for laying aside their own research to procure us photographs of manuscripts in the British Museum and Public Record Office. To 

Hartley Simpson we are indebted for providing us with transcripts of the unpublished documents used in Problem X and for his uncanny deciphering of wellnigh illegible manuscripts. Clarence W. Mendell and George E. Woodbine lent

Preface vii us their skill in translating medieval Latin for Problems IV and V. Anyone who is familiar with earlier collections of sources and readings will immediately recognize how much we owe to our many predecessors in this field. They have all been an inspiration and an example in our common task of teaching the student to learn his history at first hand. 

For aid and encouragement in making this project possible we owe much to Leonard W. Labaree, chairman of the History Department at Yale when the problem method was first introduced. James L. Mathias shared with us the teaching of these materials in the experimental stage, and we are truly grateful to the students in History 21 at Yale, past, present, and future, who are ultimately responsible for the writing of this book. Though we sometimes forget it, a college education is not complete without somebody on the other end of Mark Hopkins' log.

We owe a special debt of gratitude to Rena A. Wilmot and Roger W. Nelson, whose painstaking and conscientious work on the preparation of the manuscript went far beyond the typing of it.

Select Problems in Historical Interpretation

I 

William's Claim to the English Throne HAVE done what I could to throw light on the most perplexing question in my history [William's claim], one of the most perplexing questions in all history. I shall not be surprised if I am thought to have only made what was before dark darker still. But no one can conceive how thick the darkness really is except by groping in it, as I have done, in his own person.

E. A. FREEMAN CONTENTS

Questions for Study  The Problem:

QUESTIONS FOR STUDY 

1. Which of the sources are pro-Harold and which are pro-William? 

2. Between what dates was the Life of King Edward written? 

3. Do you think William of Malmesbury had read the Life of William by William of Poitiers? 

4. Did William have any claim to the English throne by hereditary right? 

5. "The account of William of Poitiers regarding Edward's bequest to William can be proven false by a close study of chronology." Explain. 

6. Evaluate the account given by William of Poitiers of the circumstances surrounding Edward's accession to the throne. 

7. "Eadmer's account of Edward's bequest can also be proven false by a study of chronology." Explain. 

8. Is the account of Edward's bequest to William as given by Eadmer pro-English or pro-Norman? 

9. If Edward ever chose William as his successor, when did he do it? 

10. Three chroniclers mention hostages sent by Edward to William. Which story do you believe? 

11. What different reasons are given for Harold's visit to Normandy? Which seems to you to be the correct reason? 

12. Compare and contrast the different versions of Harold's oath given by the chroniclers. What significant differences are there? 

13. Where did Harold take the oath to William? 

14. When, in relation to other events, did Harold take the oath to William? 

15. None of the contemporary English chroniclers nor any of the subsequent ones make any mention of Edward's bequest to William or of Harold's oath. How can the historian use this silence? 

16. Did Harold have any claim to the throne of England? 

17. Did the Normans believe that Harold was King of England or a usurper? 

18. Explain the order of episodes 26 through 30 in the Bayeux Tapestry. 

19. What is the significance of William's dealings with the Pope? What interest did the Pope have in English affairs? [2]

For the student of English history who begins his study with the Conquest, the first historiographical problem is the nature of William's claim to the English throne. The fact of the military conquest is indisputable, but it was asserted then and later that William was King of England by right as well as by might. 

This assertion hinged mainly on two points: (1) that Edward the Confessor, who reigned from 1042 until 1066, had bequeathed the kingdom to William, and (2) that Harold, son of the great Earl Godwin and brother-in-law of King Edward, had sworn an oath that he would support William's claim to the throne. The historical evidence supporting these assertions is, however, conflicting and confused, and the purpose of this Problem is to give the student an opportunity to arrive at his own conclusions after studying the evidence for himself. 

Our only available evidence is found in contemporary or near-contemporary chronicles. These narratives were usually planned on ambitious lines; and the chronicler sought to produce a general history beginning either at the creation or at the birth of Christ rather than to write the history of his own time. Thus only small portions of any chronicle may be regarded as a strictly contemporary record, although in cases where a chronicler utilized earlier works which have since been lost those sections of his chronicle may be regarded as having independent authority. In this Problem all the relevant evidence has been reprinted. There are, of course, more chronicles than are reproduced, but they neither add to nor modify the evidence appreciably.

In working out the Problem the following procedure is suggested: 

1. With particular attention to the brief note preceding each document (in which information is printed concerning its date and the character of its writer), the student should read each document through. 

2. He should then reread the documents and attempt to answer the Questions for Study. 

3. While answering these specific questions, the student should remember that his primary task is to answer the fundamental question: "What constituted William's claim to the throne of England?"

THE PROBLEM 

A. 

"THE ANGLO-SAXON CHRONICLE" 

The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle is the fundamental authority for English history before the Conquest. The Chronicle, in reality, consists of four separate chronicles, written in Anglo- 

Saxon in various religious houses by we know not whom. While they contain accounts of the events in England from the invasion of Julius Caesar, they all derive from a set of annals begun in the reign of King Alfred (871-899). Each chronicle consists of entries under each year, but the entries vary in size, and the chroniclers often differ among themselves as to the content of each entry. For the period under discussion they may be regarded as contemporary accounts. The selections printed below are from the Worcester version of the Chronicle. (1) 

[1052] Then soon came Count William from beyond sea, with a great body of Frenchmen, and the King received him and as many of his companions as it pleased him, and let him go again. ... [1066] In this year the monastery at Westminster was hallowed on Childermas day [Dec. 28].

And King Edward died on Twelfth-mass eve [Jan. 5]; and he was buried on Twelfth-mass day, within the newly hallowed church at Westminster. And Earl Harold succeeded to the kingdom of England, as the King had granted it to him, and men had also chosen him thereto; and he was blessed as King on Twelfth-mass day. And in the same year that he was King, he went out with a naval force against William; and the while came Earl Tostig into the Humber, with sixty ships. Earl Edwin came with a land force and drove him out, and the butse-carls [shipmen] forsook him. And he went to Scotland with twelve B. smacks; and Harold the Norwegian King met him with three hundred ships, and Tostig submitted to him; and they both went into the 

Humber, until they came to York. And Earl

Morcar and Earl Edwin fought against them, and the Norwegian King had the victory. And it was made known to King Harold how it was there done and had happened; and he came with a great army of Englishmen, and met him at 

Stamford Bridge, and slew him and the Earl 

Tostig, and bravely overcame all the army. And the while Count William landed at Hastings, on 

St. Michael's mass day [Sept. 29]; and Harold came from the north and fought against him before his army had all come; and there he fell, and his two brothers, Gyrth and Leofwin; and 

William subdued this land, and came to Westminster, and Archbishop Eldred hallowed him king; and men paid him tribute and gave him hostages, and afterward bought their land.

FLORENCE OF WORCESTER 

Florence of Worcester was a monk of that place, who died in 1118. His chronicle is a compilation from many sources; he preserves what seems to be a genuine west-midland tradition of events in the eleventh century which he may well have derived from English landowners in the country around Worcester. His story approaches most closely to that told in the Worcester version of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, but it is not a mere transcript of that work, and he apparently employed a manuscript of the Chronicle which is now lost. (2) 

A.D. 1066. On Thursday, the vigil of our Lord's 

Epiphany [Jan. 5], . . . the pride of the English, the pacific King Edward, son of King Ethelred, died at London, having reigned over the 

Anglo-Saxons twenty-three years, six months, and twenty-seven days. The next day he was buried in kingly style, amid the bitter lamentations of all present. After his interment, the subregulus 

Harold, son of Earl Godwin, whom the King had nominated as his successor, was elected King by the chief nobles of all England, and on the same day was crowned with great ceremony, by Eldred, Archbishop of York. On taking the helm of the kingdom, he immediately began to abolish unjust laws and make good ones; to patronize churches and monasteries; to pay particular attention and yield reverence to bishops, abbots, monks, and clerks; to show himself pious, humble, and affable to all good men: but he treated malefactors with the utmost severity, and gave general orders to his earls, ealdermen, sheriffs, and thanes to imprison all thieves, robbers, and disturbers of the kingdom; and he himself labored by sea and by land for the protection of his country. [5]

6.

On the 8th of the kalends of May [April 24] in this year, a comet was seen not only in England but, it is said, all over the world, and shone for seven days with exceeding brightness. Shortly afterward Earl Tostig returned from Flanders and landed at the Isle of Wight. After making the islanders pay tribute and stipend, he departed and went pillaging along the seacoast until he arrived at the port of Sandwich. As soon as King

Harold, who was then at London, heard this, he assembled a large fleet and an army of cavalry, and he prepared to go in person to the port of Sandwich. When Tostig was informed of this he took some of the shipmen of the place, willing and unwilling, and bent his course toward Lindsey, where he burned many vills and put many men to death. Thereupon Edwin, Earl of the 

Mercians, and Morcar, Earl of the Northumbrians, hastened up with an army and expelled him from that part of the country. Departing thence he went to Malcolm, King of the Scots, and remained with him during the whole of the summer. Meanwhile King Harold arrived at the port of Sandwich, and waited there for his fleet. When it was assembled, he crossed over with it to the 

Isle of Wight, and inasmuch as King Edward's cousin William, Earl of the Normans, was preparing to invade England with an army, he watched all the summer and autumn for his coming; and in addition distributed a land force at suitable points along the seacoast. But about the feast day of the Nativity of St. Mary [Sept. 8] provisions fell short, so the naval and land forces returned home.

After this Harold Hardrada, King of the Norwegians, and brother of St. Olaf the King, arrived on a sudden at the mouth of the River Tyne, with a powerful fleet, consisting of more than five hundred large ships. Earl Tostig, according to previous arrangement, joined him with his fleet. They hastened their course and entered the River Humber, and then sailing up the River Ouse against the stream, landed at a place called Richale. King Harold, on hearing this, marched in haste toward Northumbria; but before his arrival the two brothers, Earls Edwin and Morcar, at the head of a large army, fought a battle with the Norwegians on the northern bank of the River Ouse near York, on Wednesday, being the vigil of the feast day of St. Matthew the Apostle [Sept. 20], and they fought so bravely at the onset that many of the enemy were overthrown. But after a long contest the English were unable to withstand the attacks of the Norwegians, and fled with great loss; and more were drowned in the river than slain in the field. The 

Norwegians remained masters of the field of carnage, and having taken one hundred and fifty hostages from York, and leaving there one hundred and fifty of their own men as hostages, they went to their ships. Five days afterward, that is, on Monday the 7th of the kalends of October [Sept. 25], as Harold, King of the English, was coming to York with many thousand well-armed fighting men, he fell in with the Norwegians at a place called Stamford Bridge, slew King Harold [of Norway] and Earl Tostig, with the greater part of their army, and gained a complete victory; nevertheless, the battle was stoutly contested. He, however, permitted Olaf, the son of the Norwegian King, and Paul, Earl of Orkney, who had been sent off with a portion of the army to guard the fleet, to return home without molestation, with twenty ships and the remains of the army; first, however, taking hostages and oaths [of submission] from them.

In the midst of these things, and when the King might have considered that all his enemies were subdued, it was told to him that William, Earl of the Normans, had arrived with a countless host of horsemen, slingers, archers, and foot soldiers, having brought with him powerful auxiliaries from all parts of Gaul, and that he had landed at a place called Pefnesea [Pevensey]. 

Thereat, the King at once, and in great haste, marched his army toward London; and though he well knew that some of the bravest Englishmen had fallen in his two [former] battles, and that one half of his army had not yet arrived, he did not hesitate to advance with all speed into South Saxony against his enemies; and on Saturday the 11th of the kalends of September [Oct. 14], before a third of his army was in order for fighting, he joined battle with them nine miles from Hastings, where they had fortified a castle. But inasmuch as the English were drawn up in a narrow place, many retired from the ranks, and very few remained true to him; nevertheless from the third hour of the day until dusk he bravely withstood the enemy, and fought so valiantly and stubbornly in his own defense, that the enemy's forces could hardly make any impression. At last, after great slaughter on both sides, about twilight the King, alas! fell. There were slain also Earl Gyrth, and his brother Earl Leofwin, and nearly all the nobility of England. Then 

Earl William returned with his men to Hastings. 

Harold reigned nine months and as many days.

On hearing of his death, the Earls Edwin and Morcar, who had withdrawn themselves and their men from the conflict, went to London and sent their sister, Queen Algitha, to Chester; but Eldred, Archbishop of York, and the said earls, with the citizens of London and the shipmen, were desirous of elevating to the throne Edgar the 

Atheling, nephew of King Edmund Ironside, and promised that they would renew the contest under his command. But while numbers were pre-

paring to go out to fight, the earls withdrew their assistance and returned home with their army. 

Meanwhile Earl William was laying waste 

South Saxony, Kent, South Hamptonshire, Surrey, Middle Saxony, and Hertfordshire, and kept on burning the vills and slaying the natives until he came to a vill called Beorcham. There Archbishop Aldred, Wulstan, Bishop of Worcester, Walter, Bishop of Hereford, Edgar the Atheling, Earls Edwin and Morcar, the chief men of London, and many more came to him, and, giving hostages, surrendered and swore fealty to him. 

So he entered into a treaty with them; yet, nevertheless, he permitted his army to burn the vills and keep on pillaging. But when the feast of our Lord's Nativity [Dec. 25] drew nigh, he went to London with his whole army in order that he might be made king. And because Stigand, the

Primate of all England, was accused by the Pope of having obtained the pall in an uncanonical manner, he was anointed king at Westminster with great ceremony on Christmas day (which in that year fell on a Monday) by Aldred, Archbishop of York, having previously (for the Archbishop had made it a condition) sworn at the altar of St. Peter the Apostle, in the presence of the clergy and people, that he would defend the holy churches of God and their ministers, and would also rule justly and with royal care the people who were placed under him, and would ordain and maintain right law, and utterly prohibit all spoliation and unrighteous judgments. C. 

"THE LIFE OF KING EDWARD" 

The author of the Latin Life of King Edward [the Confessor] cannot be identified by name. 

He was almost certainly not an Englishman, and modern scholars believe that he was probably from Flanders. The work was dedicated to Queen Edith (d. 1075), the wife of King 

Edward, and it seems probable that the author was in her service. He also had some connection with Godwin and Harold, for he speaks of them as his "lords" (domini). The 

Life, which is a mixture of Latin verse and prose, begins with the birth of King Edward and ends with his death, with a few scant allusions to subsequent events. The Battle of 

Stamford Bridge (September 1066) is alluded to, but no mention is made of the Norman conquest. (3)

We shall describe how this jewel of God put off the dunghill of the earthly body and obtained an eternal place of splendor in the diadem of the Heavenly King. While his men stood and wept with love for him at the point of death, he said: "Do not weep, but pray to God for my soul and give me leave to go to God. . . ." To the Queen sitting at his feet he addressed his last words in this order: "May God give grace to this my bride for the diligent readiness of her service [to me]. 

For she has submitted to me devotedly and she has always remained close at my side like a most beloved daughter, wherefore may she receive from a Gracious God the recompense of eternal felicity."

With his hand stretched out toward her beforementioned guardian, her brother Harold, he said: "I commend her safekeeping with all the realm [to you], that you may protect and honor her as lady and sister (as she is) with faithful service, in order that she may not be deprived of the due honor received from me as long as she shall live.

Also, I commend likewise those who for love of me have left their native land and have hitherto served me faithfully, [so] that you, having received from them fidelity (if they so wish) may protect and retain them, or that you may let them, with all they have acquired from me, cross the sea safely under your protection to their own [lands]. 

Let a grave be prepared in the monastery for my sepulcher in the place which will be designated to you. I ask you not to conceal my death, but to announce it everywhere quickly so that my faithful men may beg for the clemency of omnipotent 

God for me a sinner."

D. 

WILLIAM OF POITIERS 

William of Poitiers was born about 1020. Of a prominent Norman family, he served for a time as a soldier and later became a student at Poitiers. On his return to Normandy, he entered the Church and became a chaplain to Duke William. His life of William (Gesta 

Willelmi Ducis Normannorum et Regis Anglorum) was written between 1071 and 1077.

The beginning and end of the work have been lost; the extant portion covers the period 

1047-68. (4)

It was by William's strength and advice that at the death of Hardicanute, Edward [the Confessor] finally came to his father's throne; a glory which he deserved because of his wisdom, his outstanding honesty, and his ancient lineage. In reality, the English, in making their choice, based their decision on William's opinion of the most advantageous course of action, and preferred to consent to the just demands of his envoys rather than to test the strength of the Normans. They hurried to ask Edward to return with a small suite of Norman knights, fearing that if the Count of Normandy came with him they would be overthrown by his powerful army, for he was renowned for his bravery in combat. Edward, in affectionate recognition, reflecting on the sumptuous liberality, the signal honors, and the intimate friendship which he had received in Normandy from William, to whom he was more united by the benefits he had received than by family connection, considering too that he owed to his [William's] generous help the end of his exile and his reinstatement on the throne, wished, as a man of good will, to recompense him [William] by the best and most agreeable gift possible, and resolved, by a firm donation, to make him the heir to the throne which he owed to William's help. With the consent of his nobles he sent to him [William], with Robert, Archbishop of Canterbury, as chief of the delegation, hostages from a very powerful family, to wit, the son and nephew of Earl Godwin. . . .

At about the same time [1064] Edward, King of England, by a stronger guaranty than before, insured the succession to the throne to William, whom he had already established as his successor, and whom he loved like a brother or son. He wished to anticipate the inevitable power of death, which he, a man who by his saintly life aspired to the heavenly kingdom, thought he felt approaching. He sent to William, to confirm his faith by oath, Harold, the most noble and powerful of all those who had submitted to his rule, and whose brother and cousin had previously been given as hostages as a guaranty of this same succession. This was a very wise choice, as William's wealth and power would constrain the English to submit to him in case, with their usual perfidy and fickleness, they should wish to oppose 

Edward's decision. Hurrying to get there, after having escaped the dangers of the crossing, Harold landed on the banks of the Ponthieu, where he fell into the hands of Count Guy. He and his suite were captured and thrown into prison, which seemed worse to him than a shipwreck would have. Ingenious greed has resulted, in some Gallic nations, in an execrable custom, bar- Daric and contrary to all Christian justice. They lay traps for rich and powerful people, shut them up in prisons, and overwhelm them with outrages and torments. After having been brought close to death by bad treatment, they are often removed from some dungeon to be sold to a noble.

Having learned what had happened to Harold, Duke William promptly sent envoys, who got

Harold out of prison by means of petitions and threats. When Harold came before him he was received with honor. William gave worthy thank offerings, considerable lands, plenty of goods, and large sums of money to Guy who had merited them, since, without being either bribed or forced he had himself brought Harold to the Chateau d'Eu, when he could have tortured, killed, or sold him. He received Harold with the greatest honor at Rouen, his capital city, where the many pleasures of an obliging hospitality very agreeably revived the travel-weary voyagers. 

The Duke was overjoyed to have such an illustrious guest, sent to him by his nearest and dearest friend, and one in whom he hoped to find a faithful advocate with the English, among whom 

Harold was second only to the King. 

Before an assembly gathered at Bonneville, Harold swore fidelity to the Duke according to

Christian custom; and, according to the reports of the worthy, illustrious men who were there as witnesses, he added to the articles of the oath that as long as King Edward lived he [Harold] would be William's delegate [vicarius] at the court; that after Edward's death he would make every effort, by his advice and help, to confirm William as King of England; that until then, he would leave the castle of Dover to be held by the Duke's knights, to be fortified by him and at his expense; that in the same way he would turn over to the Duke other castles in other parts of England, when the Duke wished them, and that he would furnish abundant provisions to the troops. 

The Duke, after having received him as a vassal, gave him back, when he asked for them before the oath, all the lands belonging to him. No one expected Edward to live much longer, as he was already ill. 

Knowing that Harold and his men were brave and looking for more chances to become renowned, the Duke gave them very valuable arms and mounts, and took them with him to fight in Brittany. He treated his guest like a brother-inarms in order by this honor to make him more faithful and devoted. . . ...

All at once there came certain news that England had lost King Edward, and that Harold had been adorned with his crown. This cruel Englishman would not wait for the people to decide by an election; but on the same day on which

Problem 1: William's Claim to the English Throne 

9 that excellent King was buried, when the whole people wept, this perjured one seized the royal throne with the applause of certain iniquitous partisans. He obtained unholy consecration from 

Stigand, who had been deprived of his holy ministry by the just zeal and anathemas of the 

Pope. Duke William, having taken counsel with his own men, resolved to revenge this injury by force of arms, and by war to recover possession of the heritage which had been ravished from him, although many of his nobles tried to dissuade him from it by specious reasons, as a thing too difficult and beyond the strength of Normandy. . . . ...

At this time [1066] the throne of St. Peter's in 

Rome was occupied by Pope Alexander, who was most worthy of being obeyed and consulted by the Universal Church, for he gave both just and useful advice. Once Bishop of Lucca, he had not desired a higher rank; but the ardent wishes of great numbers of people who held high powers among the Romans, and the assent of a great council, raised him to a rank where he became chief and master of all the bishops in the world, which he deserved because of his saintliness and his learning, which shone around the world. The sun in its course is no more immutable than Alexander's undeviating adherence to the paths of truth; whenever he could he punished the evil in this world, never ceding a point. Since the 

Duke asked for the protection of the Pope, and had offered him a part in the expedition which he was preparing, he received the banner and the approval of St. Peter, which enabled him to attack his enemy with more confidence and assurance. . . . [William of Poitiers then tells of William's preparations, the crossing of the channel, and the landing. In his account of the landing, however, he does not mention the episode, described by William of Malmesbury, in which William falls on the beach. William of Poitiers goes on to recount that as Duke William is inspecting his ships, a monk, sent by Harold, is brought before him. William pretends to be his own seneschal, gets the message from the monk, and promises him an interview with the Duke on the next day.] 

The next day, seated among his nobles, he had the monk brought before him, and said to him: "I am William, Prince of the Normans, by the Grace of God. Tell these people now that which you told me yesterday." The messenger spoke as follows: "This is what King Harold wants you to know. You have come into his country, with unbelievable courage and daring. He remembers well that King Edward established you as heir to the kingdom of England, and that he himself brought to you in Normandy the guaranty of your succession. But he knows too, that, according to his right, that same King, his lord, on his deathbed gave him the kingdom; and since the time when the blessed Augustine came to this country, it has been the custom of this nation to count deathbed gifts as valid. This is why he asks you justly to return with your men to your own country. Otherwise he will break off your friendship and all the treaties which he himself concluded with you in Normandy. He leaves the choice entirely up to you."

After having heard Harold's message, the Duke asked the monk if he would conduct an envoy safely to the prince. The monk promised him that he would be as careful with the envoy as if he were his own. Then the Duke told a monk from Fecamp to take this message promptly to Harold. "It was not with daring and injustice, but deliberately and justly, that I came to this country, to whose throne King Edward, my lord and cousin, because of the dazzling honors and many benefits which I and my nobles heaped on both him, his brother, and his people, had made me heir as is admitted by Harold himself. Edward thought that I of all those who were allied to him by birth, was the best and most capable, both to come to his aid while he lived and to rule his kingdom after his death; and his choice of me was made not only with the consent of his nobles, but also the advice of Archbishop Stigand, Earl Godwin, Earl Leofric, and Earl Siward, who gave me their oath to acknowledge me as their lord upon Edward's death, swearing that they would not attempt during his lifetime to remove me from the succession. He gave me as hostages Godwin's son and nephew. Finally, he sent Harold himself to Normandy, for him to give before me the oath in my favor which, in my absence, had been made by his father and the above-mentioned lords. On his way to me Harold was captured and released only by my wisdom and power. He gave me his homage on his own account, and, his hands within mine, assured me also of the kingdom of England. I am prepared to bring suit against him, either according to 

Norman or English law, whichever he prefers.

If either the Normans or English decide, according to justice and truth, that this kingdom legitimately belongs to him, he may have it peacefully; but if they decide, in duty and justice, that it belongs to me he must let me have it. If he should refuse this suggestion, I believe it would be wrong for his men and mine, who have no part in our quarrel, to perish in combat. I am thus prepared to uphold, by risking my life. against his, my belief that the kingdom of England belongs to me rather than to Harold."

E.

EADMER 

Eadmer (c.1064-c.1144), a monk of Canterbury, was of English or, possibly, mixed Anglo- 

Norman descent. His Historia Novorum, written in 1112, was concerned chiefly with the events of his own lifetime and dealt with the career of his friend and patron Anselm, the great Archbishop of Canterbury. He began his History, however, with the events immediately preceding the conquest. Eadmer was regarded by his contemporaries as a very competent historian, a judgment endorsed in the main by modern scholars. (5) 

Now in the reign of Edward, whom Ethelred the aforementioned King of the English had begotten by Emma, sister of Richard, Count of the Normans, there occurred the greatest destruction of the monasteries which had up to that time escaped destruction. At this time, Godwin of Kent was considered the great earl throughout England on land and sea. When a deep-seated disagreement arose between him and the King, he was sentenced to exile from England with all his family. As a result, he went to Count Baldwin in 

Flanders, and his son, Harold, went to Ireland. 

From here Godwin and Harold went back to England after the death of the queen mother, Emma, and each one was protected by many ships and a sturdy band of soldiers. Upon learning this, several of the King's magnates feared that a war would result from this, and urged that both sides make peace. But the King stood firm through fear of Godwin's treacheries and was unwilling to agree to peace unless he should first obtain hostages as guarantees of his safety. Consequently,

Walfroth son of Godwin, and Hakon son of 

Suanus [and grandson of Godwin] were handed over as hostages and were sent for custody to 

Duke William in Normandy, . . . When these things had been done Godwin died shortly after; .. Godwin's son Harold gained his earldom of 

Kent in succession to his father. Harold, after a short time had passed, begged leave of the King to go to Normandy to set free and bring back his brother and nephew who were being held as hostages.

The King said to him, "This will not be done through my agency. However, lest I seem desirous of hindering you, I grant you permission to go where you will and to do what you can. I foresee, however, that you will become involved in [something which will bring about only] harm for the entire kingdom of England and disgrace for you personally. For I have never known him [William] to be so guileless that he would be willing to give them up to you unless he foresaw, in some way, a considerable advantage accruing to himself thereby."

So Harold took ship, trusting in his own counsel rather than that of the King, in company with the richer and more highborn of his followers.... 

The stormy sea frightened the voyagers and a mass of waves tossed the boat violently about. 

The boat was thrown up, with all its passengers, into the river of Ponthieu which is called Maia and was captured by the lord of that land according to the custom of the place. The men on board ship were bound into close custody. Then 

Harold, while under guard, enticed someone from the crowd with promise of reward and sent him secretly to the Duke of Normandy to explain to William what had befallen him. 

Straightway the Duke sent messengers ordering the Lord of Ponthieu to send him Harold and his company unharmed; the sooner the better if the lord wished to enjoy William's customary friendship. But since the former was unwilling to set Harold free, he received a second message that he had better free the Earl; otherwise, he should certainly realize that William, Duke of 

Normandy, would go, under arms, to Ponthieu. ... Consequently, the lord sent Harold with his companions after having first removed the fine things the Englishmen had brought with them. 

When Harold reached William from Ponthieu he was received with due honor. When William had heard the reason why Harold had left England, he answered that the affair would succeed were certain circumstances to be altered. 

He kept Harold with him for several days and, while he delayed, revealed to Harold what he intended. He said that when, as a youth, King Edward was sojourning in Normandy when William was young, he [Edward] had promised the Duke on his solemn oath, that if he should become King of England, he would bequeath the right to the kingdom to William. Then, of a sudden, William said to Harold, "If you too will pledge yourself to be an aid to me in this affair, and if, in addition, you will promise to assign the castle of Dover with its spring to me for my use; and if you will promise to hand over your sister for me to give as wife to one of my chief nobles at some time convenient for us, and if you will also promise to take my daughter as your wife, at such a time you shall have your nephew back, and you shall receive your brother safe at such time as I come to reign in England. If at some time I shall be confirmed in this realm by your favor, I promise you shall have from me whatever can reasonably be granted."

Harold felt the danger everywhere in this; yet he knew not how to escape unless he acquiesced to William's pleasure in all these matters. So he yielded. But William brought out relics of the saints and, so that all might remain settled, induced Harold to swear on the relics that he would strive to perform all that which had been agreed between them unless he be snatched from this present life by the fate common to all mortals. 

When this had been accomplished, Harold took his nephew and returned to England. 

When, at the King's request, he had told him what had happened and what he had done, Edward answered, "Did I not tell you I knew William, and that, because of your journey, a multitude of sorrows would befall this realm?" Shortly afterward, Edward died and in accordance with the decree which he had made before his death, Harold succeeded him in the kingdom. Then a messenger came to England sent from William demanding Harold's sister in accordance with the covenant made between them, and he regretted the other agreement which had not been kept when the oath was broken. To this, Harold is said to have answered thus: "My sister, whom you demand according to the agreement, is dead. 

However, if the Duke wishes to have the body in its present condition, I shall send it, lest I be adjudged a violator of an oath I have made. The castle of Dover and its spring I have given over to someone as our right. By what right could I F. assign or promise a kingdom not yet mine? If he is concerned about his daughter whom, as he has said, I ought to have taken to wife, let him know that I ought not, nor indeed cannot without great harm, place a foreign woman over the realm of England when my chief men have not been consulted."

The messenger returned, bearing the answer to his master. When he had heard this, William ordered Harold at least to take his daughter to wife, although the other matters had been left out, in order to keep the guaranty of the bargain. Otherwise he should know without doubt that the Duke would make good, by force of arms, his promised succession to the crown. But 

Harold answered that he was not willing to do even that nor did he fear this threat. At this William grew angry and was stirred by great hope of winning the war because of Harold's injustice.

A fleet was assembled and he made for England. 

A fierce battle ensued; Harold fell in the front rank and William as victor gained the kingdom.

Concerning this battle the Franks who were present still bear witness that, although a different outcome resulted from it, there was, nevertheless, such great slaughter and flight of the Normans that the victory they won is to be ascribed truly and without doubt to a miracle from God alone who, in punishing through this victory the wicked sin of forsworn Harold, showed that it was he and not God who willed the evil deed. 

WILLIAM OF MALMESBURY 

William of Malmesbury, apparently of mixed Norman and English descent, was born about 1095 and died soon after 1142. In the preface of the Third Book of his History of the Kings of England he writes, "Incited by different motives, both Normans and English have written of King William: the former have praised him to excess . . . while the latter, out of national hatred, have laden their conqueror with undeserved reproach. For my part, as the blood of each people flows in my veins, I shall steer a middle course." 

William was a monk in the abbeys of Malmesbury and Glastonbury, two institutions possessing excellent libraries. It was at Malmesbury that he wrote his History, a work which he completed about the year 1125. Bishop Stubbs, in the preface of his edition of William's History, wrote of him as follows: "He deliberately set himself forward as the successor of the Venerable Bede; and it is seldom that an aspirant of the sort comes as near as he did to the realization of his pretensions. . . . We may fairly claim for him the credit of being the first writer after Bede who attempted to give to his details of dates and events such a systematic connection, in the way of cause and consequence, as entitles them to the name of history." (6)

King Edward declining into years, as he had no children himself, and saw the sons of Godwin growing in power, despatched messengers to the King of Hungary, to send over Edward, the son of his brother Edmund, with all his family; intending, as he declared, that either he or his sons should succeed to the hereditary kingdom of England, and that his own want of issue should be supplied by that of his kindred. Edward came in consequence [1057], but died almost immediately. . . . He left three surviving children; that is to say, Edgar, who, after the death of Harold, was by some elected king and who, after many revolutions of fortune, is now living wholly retired in the country, in extreme old age; Christina, who grew old at Romsey in the habit of a

nun; and Margaret, whom Malcolm, King of the 

Scots, espoused.

The King, in consequence of the death of his relation, losing his first hope of support, gave the succession of England to William, Earl of Normandy. He was well worthy of such a gift, being a young man of superior mind, who had raised himself to the highest eminence by his unwearied exertion; moreover, he was his nearest relation by consanguinity, as he was the son of Robert, the son of Richard the second, whom we have repeatedly mentioned as the brother of Emma, Edward's mother. Some affirm that Harold himself was sent into Normandy by the King for this purpose; others, who knew Harold's more secret intentions, say, that being driven thither against his will by the violence of the wind, he imagined this device in order to extricate himself. This, as it appears nearest the truth, I shall relate. 

Harold being at his country seat at Bosham, went for recreation on board a fishing boat, and, for the purpose of prolonging his sport, put out to sea; when a sudden tempest arising, he was driven with his companions on the coast of Ponthieu. The people of that district, as was their native custom, immediately assembled from all quarters; and those who were unarmed and few in number, were, as it easily might be, quickly overpowered by an armed multitude and bound hand and foot. Harold, craftily meditating a remedy for this mischance, sent a person, whom he had allured by very great promises, to William, to say that he had been sent into Normandy by the King, for the purpose of expressly confirming in person, the message which had been imperfectly delivered by people of less authority; but that he was detained in fetters by Guy, Earl of Ponthieu, and could not execute his embassy.... 

By this means, Harold was liberated at William's command, and conducted to Normandy by Guy in person. The Earl entertained him with much respect, both in banqueting and in vesture, according to the custom of his country; and the better to learn his disposition, and at the same time to try his courage, he took him with himself in an expedition which he at that time led against Brittany. There, Harold well approved both in ability and courage, won the heart of the Norman; and, still more to ingratiate himself, he of his own accord, confirmed to him by oath the castle of Dover, which was under his jurisdiction, and the kingdom of England, after the death of Edward. Wherefore, honored both by having his daughter, then a child, betrothed to him, and by the confirmation of his ample patrimony, he was received into the strictest intimacy.

Not long after his return home, the King wore his crown at London on Christmas day, and being there seized with the disorder of which he was sensible that he should die, he commanded the church of Westminster to be dedicated on Innocents day [Dec. 28]. Thus, full of years and of glory, he surrendered his pure spirit to heaven, and was buried on the day of the Epiphany [Jan. 6], in the said church. . . . While the grief for the King's death was yet fresh, Harold, on the very day of the Epiphany, seized the diadem, extorting their consent from the nobles; though the English say, that it was granted him by the King; but I conceive it alleged, more through regard to Harold than through sound judgment, that Edward should transfer his inheritance to a man of whose power he had himself always been jealous; although, not to conceal the truth, Harold would have governed the kingdom with prudence and with courage, in the character he had assumed, had he assumed it lawfully. Indeed, during Edward's lifetime, he had quelled, by his valor, whatever wars were excited against him; wishing to signalize himself with his countrymen, and looking forward with anxious hope to the crown. ...

When King Edward died, England, fluctuating with doubtful favor, was uncertain to which ruler she should commit herself: to Harold, William, or Edgar; for the King had recommended him also to the nobility, as nearest to the sov ereignty in point of birth; concealing his better judgment from the tenderness of his disposition. 

Wherefore, as I have said above, the English were distracted in their choice, although all of them openly wished well to Harold. He, indeed, when once dignified with the diadem, thought nothing of the covenant betwixt himself and William; but he said that he was absolved from his oath, because his daughter, to whom he had been betrothed, had died ere she was marriageable. 

For this man, though possessing numberless good qualities, is reported to have been careless about abstaining from breach of trust, if he might, by any device whatever, elude the reasonings of men on this matter. Moreover, he supposed that the threats of William would never be put into execution, because the latter was occupied in wars with neighboring princes, and so he and his subjects gave full indulgence to their fancied security; and indeed, had he not heard that the 

King of Norway was approaching, he would neither have condescended to collect troops, nor to array them.

William, in the meantime, began mildly to address him by messengers, to expostulate on the broken covenant, to mingle threats with entreaties, and to warn him, that ere a year expired, he would claim his due by the sword, and that he would come to that very place where Harold supposed he had firmer footing than himself. 

Harold again rejoined what I have related concerning the nuptials of his daughter, and added

. that he had been presumptuous on the subject of the kingdom, in having confirmed to him by oath another's right, without the universal consent and edict of the council, and of the people; again, that a rash oath ought to be broken; for if the oath, or vow, which a maiden, under her father's roof, made concerning her person, without the knowledge of her parents, were adjudged invalid, how much more invalid must that oath be, which he had made concerning the whole kingdom, when he was himself only a subject under the King's authority, and compelled by the necessity of the time, and without the knowledge of all England; besides it was an unjust request to ask him to resign a government which he had assumed by the universal kindness of his fellow subjects, a thing which would neither be agreeable to the people nor safe for the military. In this way, confounded either by true or plausible arguments, the messengers returned without success. The Earl, however, made every necessary preparation for war during the whole of that year; and that no rashness might stain his just cause, he sent to the Pope, formerly Anselm, Bishop of Lucca, but who had assumed the name of Alexander, alleging the justice of the war he meditated with all the eloquence of which he was master. Harold omitted to do this, either because he was proud by nature, or else distrusted his cause, or because he feared that his messengers would be obstructed by William and his partisans, who beset every port. The 

Pope duly examining the pretensions of both parties, delivered a standard to William, as an auspicious presage of the kingdom, on receiving which he summoned an assembly of his nobles at Lillebon, for the purpose of ascertaining their sentiments on this attempt. And when he had encouraged, by splendid promises, all who approved his design, he ordered them to prepare shipping, in proportion to the extent of their possessions.

All then assembled round the crimson sail of the admiral's ship, and, having first dined, they arrived, after a favorable passage, at Hastings.

As he disembarked he slipped down, but turned the accident to his advantage, a soldier who stood near calling out to him, "You hold England, my lord, its future King." He then restrained his whole army from plundering, warning them that they should now abstain from what must hereafter be their own; and for fifteen successive days he remained so perfectly quiet that he seemed to think of nothing less than of war. 

In the meantime Harold returned from the battle which he had waged against the Norwegians, happy in his own estimation, at having conquered; but not so in mine, as he had secured the victory by fratricide. When the news of the 

Norman's arrival reached him, reeking as he was from battle, he proceeded to Hastings, though accompanied by very few forces. No doubt the fates urged him on, as he neither summoned his troops, nor had he been willing to do so would he have found many ready to obey his call, so hostile were all to him, as I have before observed, from his having appropriated the northern spoils entirely to himself. He sent out some persons, however, to reconnoiter the number and strength of the enemy; these, being taken within the camp, William ordered to be led amongst the tents, and after feasting them plentifully, to be sent back uninjured to their lord. On their return, Harold inquired what news they brought; when, after relating at full the noble confidence of the general, they gravely added, that almost all his army had the appearance of priests; as they had the whole face with both lips shaven; for the English leave the upper lip unshorn, suffering the hair continually to increase, which Julius Caesar, in his treatise on the Gallic War, affirms to have been a national custom with the ancient inhabitants of Britain. The King smiled at the simplicity of the relators, observing, with a pleasant laugh, that they were not priests, but soldiers, strong in arms and invincible in spirit. 

His brother Gyrth, a youth on the verge of manhood, and of knowledge and valor surpassing his years, caught up his words: "Since," said he, "you extol so much the valor of the Norman, I think it ill-advised for you, who are his inferior in strength and desert, to contend with him.

Nor can you deny that you are bound to him by oath, either willingly or by compulsion; wherefore you will act wisely, if, yourself withdrawing from this pressing emergency, you allow us to try the issue of a battle; we, who are free from all obligation, shall justly draw the sword in defense of our country. It is to be apprehended if you engage, that you will be either subjected to flight or to death; whereas, if we only fight, your cause will be safe at all events; for you will be able to rally the fugitives and to avenge the dead."

His unbridled rashness yielded no placid ear to the words of his adviser, thinking it base and a reproach to his past life, to turn his back on danger of any kind; and, with similar impudence, or to speak more favorably, imprudence, he drove away a monk, the messenger of William, not deigning him even a complacent look, imprecating only, that God would decide between him and the Earl. He [the monk] was the bearer of three propositions: either that Harold would relinquish the kingdom, according to his agreement; or hold it of William; or decide the matter by single combat, in the sight of either army. 

For William claimed the kingdom on the ground that King Edward, by the advice of Stigand the Archbishop, and of the Earls Godwin and Siward,

had granted it to him, and had sent the son and nephew of Godwin to Normandy, as sureties of the grant. If Harold should deny this, he would abide by the judgment of the Pope, or by battle; G. on all which propositions, the messenger being frustrated by the single answer I have related, returned, and communicated to his party fresh spirit for the conflict.

The Agreement between the Earls of Chester and Leicester c. 1150

WHEN the traitors perceived that he [Stephen] was a mild man, and soft, and good, and did no justice, then did they all wonder. They had done homage to him, and sworn oaths, but had held no faith; they were all forsworn, and forfeited their troth; for every powerful man made his castles, and held them against him; and they filled the land full of castles. . . . However a man tilled, the earth bare no corn; for the land was all fordone by such deeds; and they said openly that Christ and His saints slept.
