Problem IX: The Establishment of the East India Company abundance, and good cheap. On the island of Goa and there about are sparrows and some other small birds, yet not many; but, on the coast of 

Cochin and Malabar, there are very few sparrows, nor any such like small birds. There are in India many bats, and some of them so great that it is incredible to tell. They do great mischief to trees, fruits, and herbs, whereby the Canariins are constrained to set men to watch in their trees, and yet they can hardly rid them away. The Indians eat them and say they are as good meat as a partridge. There is a most wonderful number of black crows which do much hurt and are so bold that oftentimes they come flying in at their windows and take the meat out of the dish as it standeth upon the table before them that are set down to eat; and as I myself sat writing above in a chamber of the house, the windows being open, one of those crows flew in at the window and picked the cotton out of my ink horn and blotted all the paper that lay on my table, do what I could to let him. They sit commonly upon the buffaloes' backs and peck off their hair, so that you shall find very few buffaloes that have any hair upon their backs, and therefore to avoid the crows they get themselves into marshes and watery places, where they stand in the water up to the necks, otherwise they could never be rid of them.

There are likewise great numbers of rats, and some as big as young pigs, so that the cats dare not touch them. Sometimes they dig down the houses, for that they undermine the walls and foundations through and through, whereby many times the houses fall down and are spoiled. There is another sort of rats that are little and reddish of hair. They are called sweet smelling rats, for they have a smell as if they were full of musk. ...

Within the land there are also tigers; other cruel beasts, as lions, bears, and such like there are few or none. But venomous beasts, as snakes, lizards, and such like, there are many, for the lizards will climb and creep upon the walls in their houses and oftentimes fall upon men as they lie in their beds and sleep, and therefor many men that are of ability do hang testers and curtains over and about their beds. There are likewise many chameleons, which are said to live by the air, but they are not hurtful. Pepper is of divers sorts, that is to say, black, white, and long pepper is called canariin. The black is the commonest and is most brought hither and throughout all places of the world. The white and long are likewise carried into other places, though very little of it; but the pepper called canariin is never carried forth of India, for it is not much esteemed. The black pepper which is the commonest and the best, groweth most on the coast within the country of Malabar, which coast beginneth twelve miles southwards from Goa and reacheth to the Cape de Comorin and is the land lying on the seacoast, between the high land of Ballagate and the sea; further within the land there groweth none. And there is the place where all the pepper is yearly laden, which is carried in to Portugal and from thence spread abroad throughout all Christendom. From thence also it is much shipped by the Mohammedans to the Red Sea, and upon the land inwards beyond Ballagate, as also to Persia, Arabia, and all the countries bordering upon the same. And although it be expressly forbidden by the Portuguese and great care taken, and for the same cause coast and seas along the shore are watched, that it be not shipped or sent out without their license; yet there is great quantities carried forth, and sometimes with the salvo-conducto or passport from the Portuguese themselves. There groweth likewise much black pepper by Malacca and in the islands of Sumatra, Java, Sunda, and other places, as in the description of the coast and islands I have already declared, where also groweth white pepper, which is like the black, saving the first outermost husk is white and smooth, without any wrinkle, but hath the very self-same virtue and taste that black pepper hath. It cometh oftentimes mingled with the Malacca pepper. The pepper that groweth in the countries about Malacca is many times also brought in to Portugal, but very little, for that it is two years between every ship that saileth out of Portugal thither, which being there, taketh in some pepper, but mostly cloves and nutmegs with their flowers and other merchandises of China. But the most part of that pepper is used in the same countries, as in Pegu, Siam, and especially in China, and other countries bordering on the same, which deal continually one with another. . .

Pepper is used in the kitchen and in apothecaries' shops, although in both places not as a meat or food, but for a physic. It warmeth the maw and consumeth the cold sliminess thereof. 

To ease the pain in the maw which proceedeth of rawness and wind it is good to eat fine pepper corns every morning. He that hath a bad or thick sight, let him use pepper corns, with anise, fennel seed, and cloves, for thereby the mistiness of the eyes, which darken the sight, is cleared and driven away. The apothecaries make a confection of three sorts of pepper, in this sort: of white, black, and long pepper, of each 25 drams; wild thyme, ginger, anise seed, of each an ounce, with honey as much as needeth to make a confection, which is good for such as have a cold maw, the nucken [freakishness], the pain in the liver, and the dropsy.

Now to know the right manner of farming of the pepper, you must understand that the farmers

take the same to farm for five years and bind themselves every year to send their stock of ready money, for thirty thousand quintals of pepper, so that the King [of Portugal] will send ships to lade it in. The King, on the other side, bindeth himself to perform and to send every year five ships, the farmers bearing the adventure of the sea both of their money sending thither and of the pepper brought from thence, and must lade it in India into the ships at their own cost and charges; which being brought in to Portugal, they deliver all the pepper to the King at the price of twelve ducats the quintal. And if any be cast away or taken upon the sea, it is at the farmers' charge, for the King dealeth not but only with that which is delivered him in Portugal, being dry and fairly laid up in the King's storehouse in Lisbon, for the which he payeth not any money unto the farmers, until the said pepper be sold with the money whereof he payeth them; so that the King without any hazard or disbursing anything of his own, hath always his money for his pepper, without the loss of any one penny. And in that respect the farmers have great and strong privileges: first, that no man of what estate or condition so ever he be, either Portugal or of any place in India, may deal or trade in pepper, but they, upon pain of death, which is very sharply looked unto. Likewise they may not for any occasion or necessity whatsoever diminish or lessen the ordinary stock of money for the pepper, neither hinder or let them in any sort concerning the lading thereof, which is also very strictly observed. For although the pepper were for the 

King's own person, yet must the farmers' pepper be first laden, to whom the viceroy and other officers and captains of India must give all assistance, help and favor, with watching the same and all other things whatsoever shall by the said farmers be required for the safety and benefit of the said pepper. For the lading and providing whereof, the said farmers are to send their factors, servants, and assistants, of what nation so ever they be (except Englishmen, Frenchmen, and Spaniards), unto every place, to see it laden and dispatched away, for other strangers may not go into India without the special license of the King or his council of India. . . . The ships and their freighting, with condition to build them and the provision of all necessaries for them, are also farmed by themselves, and all at the adventure of the farmers. And if the ship come safe home, they give the King a certain sum of money for every ship, and every year furnish five ships, likewise at their own charge. But such soldiers as are appointed to go in them are bound to sail for the King and have but only meat and drink at the farmers' charge; the officers and sailors being placed therein by the King's admiralty, which the farmers may not once deny or refuse; so that the King adventureth nothing, neither in pepper nor in ships, but only if the ships be cast away, he loseth the money that he should have had for the farm of every ship if it had returned safe and the gain of the pepper that should have been delivered him at a certain price. Whereupon the admiralty of Portugal are now waxen very careless to see them well conveyed, as they used to be during the times of the Kings of Portugal, when all the pepper came for the King's own accounts. And although the King hath promised continually to send his navy by sea as far as the 

Flemish Islands, there to stay for the coming of the Indian ships, and from thence to convey them unto Lisbon, yet since they were farmed out, there are few fleets sent forth, so that they are but little thought upon, but howsoever it is in the payment of the fee farm for pepper, the King will not lose a penny of his due nor once abate them anything. B.

INITIAL ATTEMPTS TO ESTABLISH TRADE WITH THE INDIES 

The "Court Books," as the minutes of the meetings of the subscribers in the company were called, are a valuable source of information on the early history of the East India Company. The character of the minutes shows clearly that the company was aware of the value of a detailed record of proceedings and indicates that the men who were administering affairs had had considerable experience in business matters. This was true, for a number of the founders of the East India Company were members of an earlier company called the Levant Company. This had been founded in 1581 to establish trade with Turkey via the Mediterranean, but attacks from Barbary corsairs and the Spanish navy hindered the company from being entirely successful. Evidence of the connection between the personnel of the two companies is shown by the fact that some letters of the Levant Company are found at the beginning of the first volume of the Court Books. In the excerpts of the minutes here printed, lists of those present at the meeting have been omitted and paragraphing has been rearranged for purposes of clarification.

Problem IX: The Establishment of the East India Company 1. The Minutes of the Meeting of Septem ber 24, 1599. (2) 

Whereas the several persons above named, together with divers others whose names are registered in the beginning of this book, by the sufferance of Almighty God after royal assent of our sovereign lady the Queen's most excellent Majesty first thereunto had and obtained, do intend for the honor of our native country and for the advancement of trade of merchandise within this realm of England upon their several adventures according to the several proportions of the sums of money by them severally set down and registered under their own hands, to set forth a voyage this present year to the East Indies and the other islands and countries thereabouts; and there to make trade by the sale of such commodities as upon further deliberation shall be resolved to be provided for these parts, or otherwise by buying or bartering of such goods, wares, jewels, or merchandise as those islands or countries may yield or afford. And for the better ordering and disposing of the said voyage intended, and for the encouragement of all such as have already determined to adventure in the same, or shall before the voyage set forth determine to adventure therein, they have thought it meet to direct themselves by certain rules and orders to be held and observed as well in the preparing of such shipping as shall be thought fit for this enterprise as of all other provision of wares, merchandise, bullion and such other things as are to be provided and adventured in the same. And therefore at this assembly it is agreed, ordained, and resolved as follows: 

First that no ship shall be received to be brought in by any adventurer in this voyage to be employed in the same as his stock or portion of adventure at any rate whatsoever [i.e., a ship was not to count as payment for stock].

Also that all shipping to be employed in this voyage shall be brought and provided by such as shall be thereto appointed for ready money only. 

That no commodity shall be accepted in the said voyage to be brought in as any man's portion of adventure, but that all goods, wares, and other things shall be bought and prepared by such as shall be thereunto appointed as committees and directors of the said voyage for the buying and providing of shipping and merchandise. 

And this assembly do elect, nominate, and appoint these fifteen persons here undernamed committees of directors of this voyage to manage, order, and direct the affairs belonging to the same, as well concerning suit to be made to her Majesty for sole privilege to be granted to these adventurers for so many years as can be obtained, and for such immunities and freedoms of custom and other tolerations and favors as may be gotten, as also for the providing for shipping, wares, and merchandise to be adventured in the said voyage ratifying and allowing whatsoever the said committees or directors of the said voyage or the greater number of them shall do or agree upon in the premises provided; nevertheless that no factor [trader] or other officer to be employed in the voyage shall be admitted or appointed thereto but by a general assembly of the adventurers, and and there elected by the consent of the greater number of them assembled. . . .

It is resolved at this assembly that from henceforth no adventurer in this voyage shall be received to adventure in the same for a less sum than 200 pounds.

And it is generally agreed that there shall be brought into the hands of the treasurers with all expedition for the defraying some present petty charges that shall be expended in the affairs of the said voyage, 12d. upon every £100 set down and to be set down upon every man's portion of adventure. 

2. The Minutes of the Meeting of Septem ber 25, 1599. (3)

And it is resolved that a petition shall be exhibited to the lords of her Majesty's most honorable Privy Council in the name of the adventurers showing their honors that divers merchants, induced by the success of the voyage performed by the Dutch nation, and being informed that the Dutchmen prepare for a new voyage and to that end have bought divers ships here in England, were stirred with no less affection to advance the trade of their native country than the Dutch merchants were to benefit their commonwealth, and upon that affection have resolved to make a voyage to the East Indies if her Majesty will be pleased to add to their intention, the better to perform the enterprise, these several petitions or requests following, viz.

To grant to the adventurers a privilege in succession and to incorporate them in a company, for that the trade of the Indies being so far remote from hence cannot be traded but in a joint and a united stock. 

That the shipping of the adventurers being prepared for their voyages be not stayed upon any pretense of [naval] service, for that the stay of one month loses the opportunity of a whole year's voyage.

That it may be lawful for the adventurers, any state notwithstanding, to send out foreign coin, and if there shall be a want of foreign coin to furnish this present voyage, that there may be coined in her Majesty's mint so much foreign coin as shall supply the want, out of such bullion or

plate as shall be brought in by the adventurers or by their means. 

That freedom of custom be humbly required for all such goods as are carried out in six voyages, the rather for that many experiments are to be made before the country shall be fitted with merchandise vendable there, and for that also the Dutch merchants for their better encouragement are freed for diverse years both of custom outward and inward. 

3. The Minutes of the Meeting of October 

4, 1599. (4)

A petition having been delivered to the lords of her Majesty's most honorable Privy Council according to the agreement of the committees in the last conference, and the lords having received the same and favoring the enterprise, promised their furtherance to her Majesty for the obtaining of the things set down in articles mentioned in the said petition, this assembly do resolve that a present course is to be taken to solicit their honors again for her Majesty's answer to the said petition and articles, and to that end the persons hereunder named are appointed to go to the lord treasurer and Mr. Secretary if they be in town, and if not to go to the court to solicit their honors and the residue of lords at the council board. 

4. The Minutes of the Meeting of October 

16, 1599. (5) 

Upon the report of divers committees who have been at the court, of her Majesty's gracious acceptance of the voyage, and upon like report that the lords do require that some of the principal of the adventurers should resort to the court tomorrow to receive their honors' order for our further proceeding, it is ordered that the persons hereafter named shall repair to the court to attend their honors' direction at the council board, and as they shall find fit opportunity, to tender a petition to their honors containing these several requests following, viz. 

That the lords would by their honorable order of their assembly at the council board give the company a warrant to proceed in the voyage assuring them that they shall not be impeached in the same.

That they may have warrant to carry out in this first voyage without charge five thousand pound weight of bullion at the least.

That they may proceed with the drawing and preparing in a readiness of a grant of privilege upon such points as shall be reasonable and fit for such a trade. 

Moved that by reason of a treaty of peace in hand between the Queen's Majesty and the King of Spain, the company soliciting a warrant from the lords that they might proceed in their voyage without any impeachment; notwithstanding the said treaty and by reason thereof they should not be stayed when their shipping was prepared, the lords denied to give them such a warrant as thinking it more beneficial for the general state of merchandise to entertain a peace than that the same should be hindered by the standing with the Spanish commissioners for the maintaining of this trade to forego the opportunity of the concluding of the peace. Whereupon the adventurers, fearing lest after they were driven into a charge they should be required to desist their voyage, did proceed no further in the matter for this year, but did enter into the preparation of a voyage the next year following as hereafter may appear. 

5. The Merchants' Memorial to the Queen, 

1600. As a preliminary to the reopening of the question of East Indian trade, the merchants further investigated the state of affairs in the East Indies and early in 1600 presented a memorial on the subject to the Queen. The memorial, selections from which follow, was entitled “Certain reasons why the 

English merchants may trade into the East 

Indies, especially to such rich kingdoms and dominions as are not subject to the Kings of Spain and Portugal; together with the true limits of the Portuguese conquest and jurisdiction in those oriental parts." (6) 

Whereas, right honorable, upon a treaty of peace between the crowns of England and Spain like to ensue, it is not to be doubted, but that great exception will be taken against the intended voyage of her Majesty's subjects into the 

East Indies by the Cape of Buena Speranza [Good Hope]; therefore the adventurers in the said intended voyage most humbly crave, at your honor's hands, to take perfect knowledge of these few considerations underwritten. 

First, they desire that it would please your honors to urge the commissioners of the Spanish peace to put down, under their hands, the names of all such islands, cities, towns, places, castles, and fortresses, as they are actually at this present, possessed of, from the said Cape of Buena Speranza, along the coast of Africa, on the coast of Arabia, in the East Indies, the Moluccas, and other oriental parts of the world; which, if they may be drawn truly and faithfully to put down, so that we cannot be able, manifestly, to prove the contrary, then will we be content in no sort to disturb nor molest them wheresoever they are already commanders and in actual authority. 

Secondly, if they will not by any means be drawn to this themselves, then we, for your lordships' perfect instruction in this behalf, will take the pains to do it for them. It may please your

Problem IX: The Establishment of the East India Company honors, therefore, to understand that these be all the islands, cities, towns, places, castles, and fortresses, whereof they be, at this present, actual commanders beyond the Cape of Buena Speranza, eastward.

On the coast of Africa: Sofala or Zefala, Mozambique, Sena. 

In the mouth of the Persian Gulf: Ormuz.

From the Persian Gulf along the coast of India, southward: Diu, Damaon, Bacaim, Chaul, Goa, the seat of the viceroy, Onor, Barcelor, Mangalor, Cananor, Cranganor, Cochin, Coulaom, St. 

Thomé or Malipur, Negapatam, Manar, Columbo in Ceylon, Malacca, Molucca or Tidor, Amboyna, Macao, Manila in the island of Luzon, one of the Philippines, and certain other forts upon that island.

Thirdly, all the places which are under their government and command, being thus exactly and truly put down, and we being able to avouch it to be so, by many evident and invincible proofs and some eyewitnesses, if need require, it then remaineth that all the rest [of the] rich kingdoms and islands of the East, which are in number very many, are out of their power and jurisdiction and free for any other princes or people of the world to repair unto, whom the sovereign lords and governors of those territories will be willing to admit into their dominions, a chief part whereof are these here ensuing.

The names of the chief known islands and kingdoms, beyond the Cape of Buena Speranza, wholly out of the dominion of the Portuguese and Spaniards in the east, southeast, and northeast parts of the world: the Isle of Madagascar, or 

San Lorenzo, upon the backside of Africa; the kingdoms of Orissa, Bengal, and Aracan, in the

Borneo, Celebes, Jailolo, and Os Papuas; the long tract of New Guinea and the Isles of Solomon; the rich and innumerable islands of Moluccas and the Spicerie, except the two small isles of Tidor and Amboyna, where the Portuguese have only two small forts; the large islands of Mindanao and Calamines; the golden islands of the great and small Lequeos; the manifold and populous silver islands of the Japanese; the country of 

Korea, newly discovered to the northeast.

In all these, and infinite places more, abounding with great wealth and riches, the Portuguese and Spaniards have not any castle, fort, blockhouse, or commandment, as we are able to prove by these authors or witnesses following:-

Indies this year. 

Fourthly, let them show any just and lawful reasons, void of affection and partiality, why they should bar her Majesty and all other Christian princes and states of the use of the vast, wide, and infinitely open ocean sea, and of access to the territories and dominions of so many free princes, kings, and potentates in the East, in whose dominions they have no more sovereign command or authority than we or any Christians whosoever. 

6. The Minutes of the Meeting of Septem ber 23, 1600. (7)

Whereas divers merchants whose names are registered in the beginning of this book for the honor of their native country and for the advancement of the trade of merchandise within this realm of England, upon their several adventurers apportioned and set down of their voluntary assent, have undertaken to set forth a voyage for the discovery of the trade of the East Indies, and to that end have solicited the lords of her Majesty's most honorable Privy Council to move her most excellent Majesty for her gracious and royal assent to the said enterprise, and for to further the same with a grant of privilege and other tolerations and favors for the advancement of the said trade. And whereas the said lords, favoring

so honorable an attempt, have accordingly moved her most excellent Majesty for her gracious assent in this behalf, and having found her Majesty graciously inclined to the furthering of the same voyage and ready to grant unto the petition of the said adventurers touching the particular demands by them exhibited, did direct their letters to the said adventurers signifying thereby that it was her Majesty's pleasure that they should proceed in their purpose; assuring them that they should not be stayed or prohibited therein, wishing them to accept of their certificate of her Majesty's pleasure as an earnest of a further warrant which afterward should be to them granted by her Majesty. 

Whereupon the said adventurers, in full and ample number assembled, did give their general consent by erecting of hands that they would go forward in the said voyage; and to the end that they might the better dispose thereof and of all preparations necessary for the same, both for shipping, merchandise, and money to be employed therein, they did make choice of the sev eral persons hereafter named to be committees and directors of all the preparations and business concerning the said voyage; reposing themselves wholly upon their fidelities and provident handling and ordering thereof, which committees or the greatest number of them, from time to time assembled, are by the general consent of the said adventurers authorized and warranted according to their discretions to set forth and manage the whole voyage upon the proportion of stock and adventure generally contributed and set down, and upon any occasion for the furtherance of the said voyage to use the help of any adventurer in any employment requiring the same in time convenient. C.

THE CHARTER OF THE COMPANY 

The original charter has never been found, and the text printed here has been taken from a printed collation of several of the oldest manuscript copies. The document bears the title, "A Privilege for Fifteen Years Granted by Her Majesty to Certain Adventurers for the Discovery of the Trade for the East Indies," and is dated December 31, 1600.

Repetitious phrases and lists of names have been omitted and paragraphing has been added in the reproduction of the text given here. (8) 

Elizabeth, by the grace of God, Queen of England, France, and Ireland, defender of the faith, etc. To all our officers, ministers, and subjects, and to all other people, as well within this our realm of England as elsewhere, under our obedience and jurisdiction, or otherwise, unto whom these our letters patent shall be seen, showed, or read, greeting. Whereas [a list of 218 names follows] have of our certain knowledge been petitioners unto us, for our royal assent and license to be granted unto them, that they, at their own adventures, costs, and charges, as well as for the honor of this our realm of England, as for the increase of our navigation, and advancement of trade of merchandise, within our said realms and the dominions of the same, might adventure and set forth one or more voyages, with convenient number of ships and pinnaces, by way of traffic and merchandise to the East Indies, in the countries and parts of Asia and Africa, and to as many of the islands, ports and cities, towns and places, thereabouts, as where trade and traffic of merchandise may by all likelihood be discovered, established, or had; divers of which countries, and many of the islands, cities and ports thereof, have long since been discovered by others of our subjects, albeit not frequented in trade of merchandise. 

Know ye therefore, that we, greatly tendering the honor of our nation, the wealth of our people, and the encouragement of them, and others of our loving subjects in their good enterprises, for the increase of our navigation, and the advancement of lawful traffic, to the benefit of our commonwealth, have . . . given and granted . . for us, our heirs and successors, do give and grant unto our said loving subjects, .. that they and every of them, from henceforth be, and shall be, one body corporate and politic, in deed and in name, by the name of the Governor and Company of Merchants of London, Trading into the 

East Indies. 

We do declare, . . that by the same name of

Governor and Company of Merchants of London, Trading into the East Indies, they shall have succession, and that they and their successors, ... be and shall be, at all times hereafter, persons able and capable in law, and a body corporate and politic, and capable in law to have, purchase, receive, possess, enjoy, and retain lands, rents, privileges, liberties, jurisdictions, franchises, and hereditaments of whatsoever kind, nature, and quality so ever, they be to them and their successors. And also to give, grant, demise, alien, assign, and dispose lands, tenements, and hereditaments, and to do and execute all and singular

Problem IX: The Establishment of the East India Company other things, by the same name that to them shall or may appertain to do. And that they and their successors . . . may plead and be impleaded, answer and be answered, defend and be defended, in whatsoever courts and places, and before whatsoever judges and justices, and other persons and officers, in all and singular actions, pleas, suits, quarrels, causes, and demands whatsoever, . . . in such manner and form, as any other our liege people of this our realm of England, being persons able and capable in law, may or can. ...

And that the said Governor and Company of Merchants of London, Trading into the East Indies, and their successors, may have a common seal, to serve for all the causes and business of them and their successors. . . ... ... 

And further, . . . we do ordain, that there shall be, from henceforth one of the same company to be elected and appointed, in such form as hereafter... is expressed, which shall be called the governor of the said company and that there shall be from henceforth twenty-four of the said company, to be elected and appointed, in such form, as hereafter. . . is expressed, which shall be called the committee of the said company, who, together with the governor of the said company for the time being, shall have the direction of the voyage, of or for the said company, and the provision of the shipping and merchandises thereto belonging, and also the sale of all merchandises returned in the voyages, of or for the said company, and the managing and handling of all other things belonging to the said company. ... 

And further we will and grant . . . unto the said governor and company that it shall and may be lawful, to and for the said governor and company, for the time being, or the more part of them, present at any public assembly, commonly called the court, held for the said company, the governor of the said company being always one, from time to time, to elect, nominate, and appoint one of the said company, to be deputy to the said governor. ... 

And further we will and grant . . . unto the said governor and company . and their successors, that they or the greater part of them, whereof the governor for the time being, or his deputy to be one, from time to time, and at all times hereafter, shall and may have authority and power, yearly and every year, on the first day of July, or at any time within six days after that day, to assemble and meet together, in some convenient place, to be appointed from time to time by the governor, . . . and that they being so assembled, it shall and may be lawful to and for the said governor, or deputy of the said governor, and the said company for the time being, or the ... greater part of them, which then shall happen to be present, whereof the governor of the said company, or his deputy for the time being, to be one, to elect and nominate one of the said company, which shall be governor of the said company for one whole year, from thence next following, which person, being so elected and nominated to be governor of the said company, as is aforesaid, before he be admitted to the execution of the said office, shall take a corporal oath before the last governor, being his predecessor or his deputy, and any six or more of the committees of the said company for the time being, that he shall . . . well and truly execute the office of governor of the said company, in all things concerning the same; and that immediately after the said oath so taken, he shall and may execute and use the said office of governor of the said company, for one whole year, from thence next following. ...

And in like sort, we will and grant, that as well everyone above-named to be of the said company or fellowship, as all others hereafter to be admitted, or free of the said company, shall take a corporal oath before the governor of the said company, or his deputy for the time being, to such effect, as by the said governor and company, or the more party of them, in any public court to be held for the said company, shall be in reasonable manner set down and devised, before they shall be allowed or admitted to trade or traffic, as a freeman of the said company. 

And further we will and grant . . . unto the said governor and company and their successors, that the said governor, or the deputy of the said governor, and the company and their successors, for the time being, or the greater part of them, whereof the governor, or the deputy of the governor, from time to time, to be one, shall and may, from time to time, and at all times, hereafter have authority and power, yearly and every year, on the first day of July, or at any time within six days after that day, to assemble and meet together. . . . And that they being so assembled, it shall and may be lawful, to and for the said governor or his deputy, and the company for the time being, or the greater part of them, which then shall happen to be present, whereof the governor of the said company, or his deputy for the time being, to be one, to elect and nom inate twenty-four of the said company, which shall be committees of the said company, for one whole year, from thence next ensuing, which persons, being so elected and nominated to be committees of the said company, as aforesaid, before they be admitted to the execution of their said offices, shall take a corporal oath, . . . and that immediately after the said oath so taken, they shall and may execute and use their said

Part 1: The Formation of the Company 

217 offices of committees of the said company, for one whole year, from thence next following. 

And moreover . . . we do grant unto the said governor and company . . . and to their successors, that when and as often as it shall happen, the governor of the said company for the time being, at any time within one year, after that he shall be elected to the office of the governor of the said company, . . . to die or to be removed from the said office, which governor, not demeaning himself well in his said office, we will to be removable at the pleasure of the said company, or the greater part of them, which shall be present, at any of their public assemblies, commonly called their general court, held for the said company, that then and so often it shall and may be lawful, to and for the residue of the said company for the time being, or the greater part of them, within convenient time after the death or removing of any such governor, to assemble themselves in such convenient place as they shall think fit, for the election of the governor of the said company. [The same provision was also made for the election of successors to deceased or removed committee members.] 

And further we do. . . will and grant unto the said governor and company and their successors, that they, and all that are or shall be of the said company . . . and every of them, and all the sons of them, and every of them, at their several ages of one and twenty years or upward; and further, all such the apprentices, factors, or servants of them, and of every of them, which hereafter shall be employed, by the said governor and company, in the said trade of merchandise, of or to the East Indies, beyond the seas, or any other the places aforesaid . . . shall and may, by the space of fifteen years, from the feast of the birth of our Lord God last past, before the date hereof, freely traffic and use the trade of merchandise, by seas, in and by such ways and passages already found out and discovered, or which hereafter shall be found out and discovered, as they shall esteem and take to be fittest, into and from the said East Indies, in the countries and parts of Asia and Africa, and into and from all the islands, ports, havens, cities, creeks, towns, and places of Asia and Africa, and America, or any of them, beyond the Cape of 

Bona Esperanza, to the Straits of Magellan, where any trade or traffic of merchandise may be used or had, and to and from every of them, in such manner, order, form, liberty, and condition, to all intents and purposes, as shall be, from time to time, at any public assembly or court, held by or for the said governor and company, by or between them of the said fellowship or company of merchants, . . or the more part of 

them... present at such assembly or court, the governor, or his deputy, being always present at such court or assembly, limited and agreed, and not otherwise, without any molestation, impeachment, or disturbance, any statute, usage, diversity of religion or faith, or any other cause or matter whatsoever, to the contrary notwithstanding; so always the same trade be not undertaken, nor addressed to any country, island, port, haven, city, creek, town, or place already in the lawful and actual possession of any such Christian prince or state, as at this present is, or at any time hereafter shall be in league or amity with us, our heirs, or successors, and who doth not or will not accept of such trade, but doth overtly declare and publish the same, to be utterly against his or their good will and liking. And forasmuch as the said governor and company . . . have not experienced of the kinds of commodities and merchandises, which are or will be vendible, or to be uttered in the said parts of the East Indies, and therefore shall be driven to carry to those parts, in their voyages outward, divers and sundry commodities, which are likely to be returned again into this our realm, we therefore . . . for the better encouraging of the said governor and company . . . and for the advancement of the said trade, do grant unto the said governor and company, and to their successors, that they and their successors, during the four first voyages, which they shall make, or set forth, for or toward the said East Indies, shall and may transport, and carry out of our realm of England, all such and so much goods and merchandises, being goods and merchandises lawfully passable and transportable out of this realm, and not prohibited to be transported by any law or statute of this realm, as shall be by them, their factors, or assigns, shipped in any ship or ships, vessel or vessels, to be employed in any of the said four first voyages, free of custom, subsidy, or poundage, or any other duties or payments, to us or our successors, due or belonging, for the shipping or transporting of the same, or any of them. And for that, the ships, sailing into the said East Indies, must take their due and proper times, to proceed in their voyages, which otherwise, as we well perceive, cannot be performed in the rest of the year following: therefore we ... do grant, . . . that, in any time of restraint, six good ships and six good pinnaces, well furnished with ordnance, and other munition for their defense, and five hundred mariners, Englishmen, to guide and sail in the same six ships and six pinnaces, at all times, during the said term of fifteen years, shall quietly be permitted and suffered to depart, and go in the said voyages .. without any stay or contradiction, by us, our heirs, or successors, or by the lord high admiral, or any other officer or subject of us, our heirs, or successors, for the time being, in any wise, any restraint, law, statute, usage, or matter whatsoever to the contrary notwithstanding. Problem IX: The Establishment of the East India Company Part II. 

A. 

THE FIRST VOYAGE PREPARATIONS FOR THE VOYAGE 

Each voyage was conducted as a separate venture. The company's job was to raise capital, purchase ships and supplies, and arrange for any necessary documents of authorization. 

These were usually four: the royal commission for the expedition, the commission to the admiral in charge, a warrant for coinage of money if necessary, and lastly letters from the sovereign to foreign kings. Special documents of authorization were issued when desirable. Copies of these documents were recorded in a book called the "Register of Letters."

2. Council Order for the Payment of Over due Subscriptions, January 1601. (10)

Upon complaint made the lords by the new authorized company of merchants preparing to trade to the East Indies that certain persons which heretofore promised and assured by their subscriptions, when the said voyage was first projected, to advance certain sums of money for the proceeding in the same, upon confidence and assurance whereof the preparation for the said voyage has been undertaken and advanced to a full readiness, and yet nevertheless that the said persons would since, upon some undue pretenses, retract their former promises in that behalf, whereof would ensue that by the want of their promised contributions the voyage must break.

Their lordships upon due consideration realizing how greatly it does import the honor of the realm and the state of the present affairs thereof that the said voyage should not be hindered or overthrown by any such default and indirect means, and considering also how weak allegations of excuse have been made by the persons refusers, it has been therefore this day ordered by their lordships that, notwithstanding the pretenses of the aforesaid persons, they shall without further delay and namely by Saturday next, furnish their promised contributions, or otherwise that order shall be taken by the lords with such as shall refuse the same to commit them to prison until they conform themselves and make satisfaction according to their subscriptions. 

3. Queen Elizabeth's Circular Letter to the Kings of the East Indies, February 1601. (10) 

Elizabeth by the Grace of God Queen of England, France, and Ireland, Defender of the Faith, etc.: to the great and mighty King of 

Whereas Almighty God in His infinite and unsearchable wisdom and gracious providence has so disposed of His blessings and of the good things of this world created and ordained for the use of man, that the same however they be brought forth and do either originally grow and are gathered, or otherwise composed, and made some in one country and some in another, yet are they, by the industry of man directed by the hand of God, dispersed and sent out into all the parts of the world, that His wonderful bounty in His creatures may appear unto all nations. His Majesty having so ordained that no one place should enjoy as the native commodities thereof all things pertaining to man's use, but that one country should have need of another, and out of the abundance of the fruits which some region enjoys, the necessities of wants of another should be supplied; by which means men of several and far remote countries have commerce and traffic one with another and by their interchange of commodities are linked together in amity and friendship.

This consideration, most noble King, together with the honorable report of your Majesty for the well entertaining of strangers that visit your country in love and peace with lawful traffic of

Problem IX: The Establishment of the East India Company merchandise, has moved us to give us license to divers our subjects who have been stirred up with a desire by a long and dangerous navigation to find out and visit your territories and dominions being famous in these parts of the world for honorable merchandising, and to offer you commerce and traffic in buying, bartering, and interchanging, . . . if your Majesty shall accept of and shall receive and entertain our merchants with favor according to the hope that gave them encouragement to attempt so long and dangerous a voyage, you shall find them a people in their dealing and conversation of that justice and civility that you shall not mislike of their repair to your dominions. And upon further conference and inquisition had with them, both of the kinds of their merchandise brought in their ships and of other necessary commodities which our dominions may af ford, it may appear to your Majesty that by their means you may be furnished in their next return into your ports in better sort than you have been heretofore supplied, either by the Spaniard or

Portuguese, who of all other nations in the parts of Europe have only hitherto frequented your country with trade of merchandise, and have been the only impediments both to our subjects and diverse other merchants in the parts of Europe that they have not hitherto visited your country with trade, whilst the said Portuguese pretended themselves to be the sovereign lords and princes of all your territories and gave it out that they held your nation and people as subjects to them, and in their styles and titles do write themselves "Kings of the East Indies." 

And if your Majesty shall in your princely favor accept with good liking this repair of our merchants unto your countries, resorting thither in peaceable traffic, and shall entertain this their first voyage as an introduction to a further continuance of league and friendship between your Majesty and us and of commerce and intercourse between your subjects and ours, we have given order to this our principal merchant, if your Majesty should be pleased therewith, to leave in your country some such of our said merchants as he shall make choice of to reside in your dominions under your princely and safe protection until the return of another fleet, which we shall send unto you, who may in the meantime learn the language of your country and apply their behavior as it may best sort to so converse with your Majesty's subjects; to the end that amity and friendship being entertained and begun, the same may the better be continued when our people shall be instructed how to direct themselves according to the fashions of your country.

And because in the consideration of the entertaining of amity and friendship in the establishing of intercourse to be continued between us, there may be required on your Majesty's behalf such promise or capitulation to be performed by us, which we cannot in these our letters take knowledge of, we therefore pray your Majesty to give ear therein to this bearer and to give him credit in whatsoever he shall promise or undertake in our name concerning our amity and intercourse; which promise we for our parts in the word of a prince will see performed, and will be ready gratefully to requite any love, kindness, or favor that our subjects shall receive at your Majesty's hands. Praying your Majesty for our better satisfaction of your kind acceptance of this our love and amity offered your highness, you would by this bearer give testimony thereof by your princely letters directed unto us, which shall give us great and wonderful content.

Know ye therefore that I, the said Charles, Earl of Nottingham, lord high admiral, . . . do license and authorize the said governor and assistants and Company of the Merchants of London Trading for the East Indies to set forth to the seas the said ship called the Susan . . and therewith to set upon and by force of arms to stay and apprehend of the ships, goods, and merchandises of the King of Spain or any his subjects in as ample manner as if it were in the time of open war between her Majesty and the said King of Spain; and the said ships, goods, and merchandises so taken and brought into some port of this her Majesty's realm of England, and thereof an inventory taken, appraisement made, and judgment given in the said High Court of the Admiralty, . . . then the said ships, goods, and merchandises to keep and detain in his or their possession and to make sale and dispose thereof in open market or howsoever else to their best benefit... . ; so that neither the said captain, master, nor any the company thereof that shall in his or their own person serve in the ship aforesaid, or otherwise bear charge in the adventure, or in any other sort further or set forward the said enterprise in manner and form aforesaid, shall not be reputed or challenged for any offender against her Majesty's laws and that also it shall be lawful for any manner of person to buy the said goods, ships, and merchandises . . . without any danger, loss, hindrance, trouble, molestation, or encumbrance whatsoever.

Provided always that if by color of this commission there shall be taken any ships, goods, and merchandises of any her Majesty's loving subjects, the subjects of the French king, the kings of Scotland, Denmark, or Sweden or any the inhabitants of the United Provinces of the Hanse towns or Low Countries or the subjects of any other prince or potentate being in good league and amity with her Majesty and the same, or any other ships taken by authority hereof shall be spoiled, sold, embezzled, or diminished before they shall be adjudged in her Majesty's High Court of the Admiralty to belong to the King of Spain, or any of his subjects, that then this commission to be void and of no sufficient authority, either to take the said ships and goods or to warrant or to save harmless such as shall receive, buy, or intermeddle therein, but that also both the prizes so taken and the ships of war shall be confiscated to our use.

Provided also that the said ships, goods, and merchandises so as is aforesaid, after an inventory taken, appraisement made, and judgment given in manner and form aforesaid, shall be equally divided into three parts, whereof one part to go to the merchants and owners of the said ship, another part to the victualers, and the third part to the captain, master, mariners, and soldiers thereof.

Provided further that this commission shall remain and be in force during this present voyage and no longer. In witness hereof I have hereunto caused the great seal of my office to be affixed.

Problem IX: The Establishment of the East India Company 

B. 

THE RETURNS FROM THE FIRST VOYAGE 

James Lancaster, who had voyaged to India around the Cape of Good Hope in 1591, commanded the first fleet of the East India Company. Leaving England on April 22, 1601, he arrived in Sumatra on June 5, 1602. There he delivered the Queen's letter and was allowed to trade. The pepper crop had failed in Sumatra, but Lancaster made up for this loss by using the commission of reprisals and successfully attacked a Portuguese vessel and seized its rich cargo. More spices were obtained at Bantam and a factory, or trading post, established there. Lancaster returned to England on September 11, 1603. Immediate and large profits were expected from the venture, since the pepper which had been purchased in Bantam for 6d. might fetch up to 8s. in London. But because of a variety of unexpected factors, it was not until 1609 that the affairs of the first voyage were wound up and the profits distributed. These amounted to 95 percent on the original subscription. 

1. A General Court, June 16, 1603, after the

Arrival of the First Ship. (13) 

There is propounded to this generality the choice of a convenient place of receipt of the goods returned in the Ascension which is now come into the river. And for their better direction what places are likely to be hired for that purpose, there is nominated these several places or houses hereafter following, out of which the committees may make their choice upon the view of the fittest [6 warehouses listed]. 

At this court the generality have agreed that the committees according to the general trust which is reposed in them for the managing of the merchandise brought home in this voyage, shall appoint such men as they shall think meet to go aboard the Ascension and to attend there from time to time until the ship be unloaded. 

The general court being broke up, the committees did stay together in conference to give order for the disposing of the merchandise aboard the ship; and thereupon did resolve for the present that of these committees the persons hereunder nominated shall presently go down to the ship and there take order that no mariner or any other shall presume to deliver and carry from the ship anything whatsoever unless it be visited upon pain of detaining in the company's hands the wages of every such mariner or other officer [4 names]. 

And besides the committees who are to take their turns as occasion shall serve to go aboard the ship, these persons of the generality hereunder named are appointed to go down and to take their turns of warding aboard when they shall be appointed [17 names]. . . . 

It is thought meet by the committees above mentioned touching the tenths belonging to my lord admiral for the prize which the company's ships have taken in the East Indies, that his lordship shall be made acquainted with the advice which Captain Lancaster has written in that behalf wherein it may appear that the commodities taken are not vendible here but more fitter to be sold in the Indies. 

Mr. Ferrers and Mr. Lynge are entreated by this assembly to provide 50 or 60 pieces of poldavis [coarse canvas or sacking] for the making of bags for the bagging of the pepper brought home in the ship and to put them out to making. And also to provide 6 suits of canvas doublet and hose without pockets for 6 porters to be employed in the filling of the pepper.

2. A Letter from the Company to Its Fac tors at Bantam, December 2, 1603. (14)

At your departure out of England you may remember the state of our country was troubled in the cause of the deceased Earl of Essex, since whose death and your departure hence, God has taken away our late Queen. And although therein he visited this kingdom with a capital trial, yet he left us not thereby in any . . . trouble, but instantly upon the death of the Queen, with solemn proclamation first in divers places in London and afterward in the several counties of the realm was proclaimed King of England James the First, before King of Scots, with so general a consent that no opposition or question was once particularly made to the contrary. And thereby this kingdom so peaceably established that this wonderful blessing of God upon us was admired by all the neighbors' kingdoms adjoining.

Notwithstanding since, as times have their change and as God does many times humble his people lest they should forget themselves in pros-

perity, it has pleased Him to chastise this kingdom with great sickness and mortality in divers places thereof and especially in the city of London where there have died between December 7, 1602, and December 1, 1603, 38,138 people and as may appear by the bills of the weekly report of people deceased, there died in one week in the city, liberties, and suburbs, 3385 persons; by occasion of which mortality, trade has utterly ceased within the city for almost this half year, and merchants and all others of any estate and account have departed into the country; yet now, God be thanked, do resort unto the city again, the contagion being well ceased so as the number that now die of all diseases in the city and suburbs are about 200 a week. And touching our ships they are all, God be thanked, returned in safety and their goods in good condition. Howsoever, the time and great quantity of goods of the same kind brought from the Indies by the Hollanders yields but slow sale and utterance of them. But we hope for better opportunities of sale when men may freely and safely resort to the city. The meanwhile our trade being to be continued and followed we are preparing with all speed our four ships to return again to the Indies and to set forward in their voyage about two months hence, by God's assistance, at the furthest. And we are desirous that regard be had as far as possible may be that the pepper be large and smooth, and that the nutmegs be cleansed from rumps, and that no commodity be brought from so long a voyage that shall not be clean and commend itself. And thus much together with your good care whereupon we rely shall suffice for advice touching the preparing of the goods to be returned. 

3. A Letter from the King of Dachem and Sumatra to Queen Elizabeth Brought Back by James Lancaster. (15) 

I, most mighty King of Dachem and Sumatra, to all persons that shall read this present writing, Greeting. 

In token of our especial friendship and upon ... many good considerations us moving, and chiefly upon the contemplating of the gracious letters received from the most famous Queen of England, we . . . do signify and declare to all people, that we have entertained into our friendship and whole league our well-beloved the Serinissima Regina de Engla Terra, to hold and keep true and faithful league with her according to the commendable course and law of all nations, unto whose subjects we wish much felicity and therefore to give and grant by these presents for us our heirs and successors as much as in us lies to the said subjects of the most noble Queen of England our confederate and every of them these articles, grants, and privileges hereafter expressed and declared.

First we do give and grant free license, authority, and power to all the people, factors, merchants, or subjects of the Queen of England that they may at all times hereafter forever surely and safely come into any ports or elsewhere into these our dominions and kingdom of Sumatra with their ships, goods, and merchandise without any detainment or hindrance to them or to their goods; and there to abide, sojourn, buy and sell, barter and exchange according to their own manner and fashion with all manner of nations whatsoever as well as with our own natural subjects, both in spices and all other merchandise, and so they may tarry in our country so long as they will and go away when they list without any impediment, let, or hindrance, paying all such debts as they shall owe to any of our subjects within our said dominion.

Furthermore, our will and pleasure is that all such goods and merchandise as any of the subjects of the Queen of England shall bring into this our kingdom or any the parts thereof, shall be free of all custom or payment whatsoever as well for that which shall be brought into these our dominions as for all manner of merchandise they shall transport out of the same for any foreign port whatsoever.

Item, if any of their ships in tempest of weather shall be in danger to be lost and perish and thereupon shall stand in need of our help, we will and command that our vessels with all speed do help and succor them, to save the same ships and goods; and what may be saved to return to the said merchants or their assigns they paying reasonable consideration for their travail. 

Item, if any Englishman shall make his will and testament to whomsoever he shall give his goods, the party shall have them accordingly; and if he die intestate, he to whom the chief factor or governor shall say the goods of the dead to belong, he shall possess the same. 

Item, that every bargain made by the said merchants with any manner of person for any kind

Item, if any English merchant, factor, or servant shall offend the agent or chief governor of the factory, it shall be lawful for the said governor to do justice upon the said party, or to send him home into England at his pleasure. And further we grant unto the said governor power and authority to end any controversy that shall arise between them and to do justice according to their own laws and customs. 

Item, we do grant the said merchants and to their successors, that if any of them or of their servants shall be wounded or be slain in any part or place of our dominion, then information thereof being given, we, our justices, and other officers will execute due correction and punishment without delay according to the cause of the offense, so that it shall be an example to all others not to offend in the like. And if it shall happen the factors, servants, or ministers of the said merchants do trespass or offend, whereby they or any of them shall incur the danger of death or of punishment, that then the goods, wares, or merchandises of their seniors shall not, therefore, be forfeited, confiscated, seized upon, nor spoiled by us, our heirs, or successors or by any of our officers, ministers, or subjects, but shall remain frank and free as discharged of all punishment and loss. 

Item, we do promise the foresaid merchants, granting it forever for us and our heirs, that if any shall bring any manner of goods or merchandise meet for treasury that we will not cause any stay or arrest to be made of their said goods or merchandise to us or for our uses without present content to be made by our treasurer at such reasonable prices as the merchant could sell them for ready money, and that no price or valuation shall be set upon their goods by us or any officers of ours. 

Item, we of our goodness have granted to the said English merchants . . . that do or shall remain in any part of this our kingdom of Sumatra . . freely to keep their own law, and in any wise none of ours to force them to our law or faith against their wills 

Item, if any man shall say that these, being

Christians, have spoken anything to the derogation of our holy faith and religion, and have slandered the same, in this matter as well as in all others there shall no false witness in any case be admitted. 

Last of all, to the intent that this league with her Majesty and the aforesaid grants and privileges with her subjects may the better be observed and inviolably be performed, we, by the grace of God, great King of Dachem and Sumatra, for us, our heirs, and successors, do promise by our princely word instead of any oath, inviolably to maintain and preserve; and will cause to be inviolably kept, preserved, and maintained from time to time and at all times hereafter. And for the more ratification we command all our captains, judges, customers, governors, and servants, wheresoever these letters or privileges shall be seen throughout all our dominions that they be obeyed in all points; accordingly, as long as the Queen of England of her part shall duly keep and observe this league and holy peace expressed in this privilege with us and our subjects, we also of our royal part do charge and command the same so long to be straitly kept and observed. And the contrary to this divine league and privilege, let no man presume to do or say anything.

INTRO DUCTION TO THE PROBLEM 

In the history of English constituronal development, the Petition of Right has been considered the most important document after Magna Carta. Like 

Magna Carta, the Petition was a protest against royal misrule, a protest produced by a crisis in the relationship between ruler and subject. 

In 1628 the grievances of the subject were many. The first two Stuarts had not been able to maintain the popularity of the monarchy which the Tudors had achieved. This was due in large part to changing economic conditions. In the latter part of Elizabeth's reign and increasingly in the seventeenth century, economic opportunities of Englishmen were expanding. The court was no longer the only road to wealth and power, and there came into being a Puritan group who, regarding their hard-earned profits as God-given, looked with scorn on what they considered the ill-gotten gains of courtiers. This spirit of independence changed the shape of kingcraft, and, while both James and Charles made mistakes which Elizabeth might have avoided, the problems which they faced were of a different nature than those which had confronted their predecessor. The friction between subject and sovereign became intense. The government operated in an atmosphere of suspicion, and Parliament was summoned not so much to aid in government by counsel, as to grant funds. 

In 1628 Charles summoned Parliament with great reluctance. On bad terms with his two previous Parliaments, he was persuaded to issue writs in 1628 only by his desperate need for money to support his foreign ventures. Some preparations were made by the Crown to smooth the way of the session. The election of four privy councilors to the Commons was secured, and they and the lesser courtiers were given careful instructions. But it was idle to think that they would be able to steer a course favorable to the King. Recent measures of the royal administration had aroused the antagonism of many Englishmen to a high pitch, and it was a belligerent House of Commons and an only slightly more agreeable House of Lords that met on March 17, 1628, to air their grievances and demand reforms.

This Problem is designed not only to analyze the grievances of the subject and the reforms by which they could be alleviated but also to provide an understanding of the political theories and the governmental machinery in existence when this great constitutional milestone was erected. 

At the head of the English political machine was, of course, the King. In his own estimation Charles was a monarch by divine right; as a matter of cold fact he possessed extensive if vaguely defined powers. He could summon or dismiss 

Parliaments at will, and the very fact that he did call a Parliament in 1628 gave rise to some hopes that a better relationship would be established between King and subjects. Associated with the King in the daily administration of the government was the Privy Council. Under Elizabeth the Council had also been an effective policy-making organ and had been extensively used to steer Crown legislation through Parliament. But both James and Charles, while they made appointments to the Council as a mark of favor and rank, paid little attention to its advice and allowed its parliamentary functions to fall into disuse. For major decisions on policy the Stuarts relied on favorites, the most outstanding of whom was George Villiers, Duke of Buckingham. In 1628 the Council was consulted on parliamentary affairs more frequently than had been the case for years, but, since it was composed almost entirely of Buckingham's dependents, its decisions were largely his. 

The diminution of the Council's influence in Parliament permitted the growth of an organized opposition, particularly in the House of Commons. Moreover, [ 231 ]

parliamentary privileges and procedures had developed to a point where the opposition could be much more effective than in earlier days. One of the most useful procedural devices was the Committee of the Whole House. When the 

House went into committee, debate was free and no official record was kept of the discussions. Men did not have to rise to speak, and timid members aired their views more freely. Another advantage of the Committee of the Whole 

House lay in the fact that the Speaker withdrew and a private member of the House took the chair. The Speaker was always the King's man and had in his power the control of debate, since it was he who recognized speakers and who put questions to a vote. In his absence an opposition leader in the chair might use the same powers to good effect.

Not only had procedure developed and become more efficient, but the organization of the Opposition had also taken definite shape. In the Lords, William 

Herbert, Earl of Pembroke, and George Abbot, Archbishop of Canterbury, were leaders against Buckingham, and both of these men kept in touch with the Opposition leaders in the Commons. Many of the peers had found cause to dislike Buckingham and his tremendous power at one time or another, but in 1628 their opposition was less strong because Buckingham had attempted to conciliate them by the promise of positions or marriage alliances. In contrast to the Parliament of 1626, when the Lords joined the Commons in the attack on Buckingham, the Parliament of 1628 opened with the Lords reasonably united and ready to resume their usual position of go-between for Commons and King. 

In 1628 the Opposition leaders in the House of Commons held a meeting before the opening of the session to decide their course of action. Sir John Eliot wanted to attack grievances by renewing the impeachment proceedings against Buckingham. The others decided that the protection of the liberties of the subject was more important, and this was decided upon. The leaders had learned to work together, though it was at this time that Sir Thomas Wentworth made a great effort to wrest the leadership of the Commons from Eliot. But personal feelings were subordinated to the great work at hand. In addition to the lesson of cooperation, the leaders had learned the value of the backing of public opinion and saw to it that good speeches were publicized. Of these there were many, for one tremendous advantage which the Opposition had was the support of the orators and skillful parliamentarians. They were men who could think on their feet. The manner in which they conducted their campaign against the Crown is revealed in the documents which follow. 

BIOGRAPHICAL SUPPLEMENT 

Printed below are brief biographical sketches of the principal speakers in the debates in the Lords and Commons. 

Abbot, George (1562-1633) was Archbishop of

Canterbury. He favored Puritan views and was opposed to Laud. He introduced George Villiers at court and undoubtedly regretted this action. 

He was opposed to Charles's arbitrary government and 1627 was ordered to withdraw to Canterbury while his authority was given to a commission of five bishops. He was restored to favor in 1628 but after that lived in retirement. 

Alford, Edward was a lawyer who sat for the city of Colchester from the last days of Elizabeth.

He was an outstanding parliamentarian and a strong member of the opposition. 

Bristol, Earl of. See Digby, John 

Buckingham, Duke of. See Villiers, George 

Canterbury, Archbishop of. See Abbot, George 

Cavendish, William (1591?-1628), second Earl of Devonshire, served in the House of Commons in the 1621 Parliament and also in 1626. He was a leader of court society and had been a close friend of James. In the House of Commons he consistently supported the government until 1626,

Biographical Supplement 

233 when he joined the attack against Buckingham.

He was a close associate of the Earl of Pembroke and continued his hostility to Buckingham in the Lords. It is interesting to note that the Cavendish family had gained wealth and prestige at the time of the dissolution of the monasteries. 

Clare, Earl of. See Holles, John 

Coke, Sir Edward (1552-1634) was a great jurist. He got his start through Burghley and in 

1593 was Speaker of the House. In 1606 he was made chief justice of the Common Pleas and then of the King's Bench. He did not get along with 

Bacon, who was his great rival in the interpretation of the law. In 1616 Coke threatened the 

King's prerogative by his decisions and was dismissed from office. He was recalled to the Council, but in 1621 he became a leader of the parliamentary opposition. He was imprisoned in 

1622. After 1628 he lived in retirement and worked on his Reports and Institutes. In every 

Parliament he was the great legal authority, and his speeches are full of legal terms and precedents. He was a great believer in the common law and the privileges of Parliament. 

Coke, Sir John (1563-1644) was made secretary of state in 1625. He was an honest, faithful, and industrious bureaucrat and the trusted agent of the Crown. He showed great ability in the administration of naval affairs, but was constantly blundering in the House of Commons, where he sat from 1621 to 1629. He lacked imagination and was rather scorned because he always gave very carefully prepared speeches in the House. 

Digby, John (1580-1653), first Earl of Bristol, was a diplomat who had been sent on a number of fruitless missions to Spain. There he deeply offended Charles and Buckingham. He was a moderate member of the Opposition but by 1644 had become very unpopular. He went into exile in 1646 and died in Paris. 

Digges, Sir Dudley (1583–1639) was one of the more conservative opposition leaders. He was much interested in trade and founded a company to trade with the East by the supposed northwest passage. He opened the case against the

Duke of Buckingham in 1626. He was against 

Stuart innovations, but he wanted to be on the good side of the Court. During the period when 

Charles governed without Parliament, Digges held several offices. 

Dorset, Earl of. See Sackville, Edward 

Edmondes, Sir Thomas (1563-1639) was treasurer of the royal household and a member of the Council. He had been a diplomat and owed his advancement to Sir Robert Cecil. He was intensely loyal to the King, and though he admitted that grievances were serious, he constantly stressed 

Charles's good intentions. 

Egerton, John (1579–1649), first Earl of Bridgewater, served in the House of Commons before he was raised to the peerage. He was a patron of Milton. 

Eliot, Sir John (1592-1632) entered Parliament in 1614. It was not until 1625 that he turned his energies against the government. He hated Buckingham bitterly and was active in the attack in 1626. In 1627 he was imprisoned for refusing to pay his share of the forced loan. In 1629, while the Speaker, who was trying to adjourn the House, was held in the chair, Eliot read resolutions against innovations in religion, against the King's right to take tonnage and poundage without Parliament's consent, and against any who might yield such payments. For this he was committed to prison where he died. There is some question about his predominating leadership in the House. 

His sufferings and final martyrdom have undoubtedly enhanced his greatness.

Erle, Sir Walter was a close friend of Lord Saye and Sele. He was one of the five knights who was imprisoned in 1627 for refusing to pay the forced loan. 

Exeter, Bishop of. See Hall, Joseph 

Fiennes, William (1582–1662), first Viscount

Saye and Sele, refused to pay the forced loan in 1626. He was an outspoken Puritan and was consistently opposed to Buckingham. He was interested in colonies but decided not to settle in New England because his suggestion that an hereditary aristocracy should be established there was rejected by the Massachusetts government. He was on the Parliament side in the rebellion. 

Glanville, John (1586-1661) was a distinguished lawyer and a member of the opposition. He was made Speaker of the House in 1640, the Short Parliament, in an effort to start Parliament off in a good frame of mind. He was an able man and a good orator. 

Grimston, Sir Harbottle (1603-85) was a great lawyer. He was a Puritan and was very active in the Long Parliament until he was excluded by 

Pride's Purge. Then at the time of the Restoration, he was made speaker of the Convention Parliament and held offices under Charles II. 

Hall, Joseph (1574-1656) was Bishop of Exeter at this time. His attitude toward the Puritans was conciliatory. In 1641 he defended the use of liturgy and was impeached and imprisoned. 

Harsnett, Samuel (1561-1631), Bishop of Norwich, was very unpopular with the Puritans. He was suspected of being no friend to Buckingham because he was not advanced rapidly enough. He was made Archbishop of York in 1629. 

Herbert, Philip (1584-1650), Earl of Montgomery and fourth Earl of Pembroke, was not so fine a character as his brother William Herbert.

He was on the Parliament side in the rebellion. 

Herbert, William (1580-1630), third Earl of

Pembroke of the second creation, was the wealthiest peer in the realm. He had many constituencies at his disposal, and therefore his opposition to Buckingham carried great weight. He was very much interested in colonial enterprise. He was not an office-seeker. As lord steward he swore in the members of the House of Commons. 

Hoby, Sir Thomas was a courtier. 

Holles, John (1564?-1637), first Earl of Clare, was a soldier as well as a politician. He served against the Armada and fought the Turks in Hungary. He was opposed to Buckingham. His son John changed sides several times during the rebellion, but his second son Denzil was a staunch member of the Opposition. He was on the Parliament side in the rebellion. 

Hoskins, John (1566-1638), sergeant-at-law, was known as a great wit. He had been imprisoned for attacking the Scottish favorites of King James. 

Howard, Thomas (1586–1646), second Earl of 

Arundel, was made earl marshal in 1621. He opposed Buckingham and for this was imprisoned from 1626 to 1628. He escorted the Queen to the Continent in 1642 and thence lived in exile in Italy. He forwarded large sums to the royalist cause. He was an art collector and was considered queer by his contemporaries. 

Jermyn, Sir Thomas was a courtier of minor rank who was made a councilor in 1630. 

Lincoln, Bishop of. See Williams, John

Littleton, Edward (1589-1645) was another great lawyer. He was made chief justice of the 

Common Pleas in 1640 and lord keeper in 1641. 

Marshal, the Earl. See Howard, Thomas 

Marten, Sir Henry (1562-1641) was a judge of the Admiralty Courts. In the 1626 Parliament he had a very telling argument with Sir John Coke over naval affairs. Marten's speeches showed Coke in a very poor light. Marten was a great friend of Eliot. His son was vehemently opposed to the 

King in the Civil War and was one of the regicides. 

May, Sir Humphrey (1573-1630) was chancellor of the duchy of Lancaster and a councilor in 

1625. He was not in favor of Buckingham's policies, but he was loyal to the King and constantly hoped for higher offices. He was a good speaker and quite well liked by the members of the Opposition. He was the ablest councilor in the House. 

Mildmay, Sir Henry (d. 1664?) was master of the King's Jewel House. He was a lukewarm courtier and in 1641 deserted the King. He was a member of the state councils, 1649-52. When 

Charles II returned, Mildmay tried to escape when called to account for the King's jewels. He was sentenced to life imprisonment in Tangier and died on the way there. 

Montagu, Henry (1563–1642), Viscount Mandeville and first Earl of Manchester, as chief justice of the King's Bench condemned Sir Walter Raleigh. He was made lord high treasurer in 1620.

He was interested in the colonies. He did not hold the office of lord high treasurer long but was president of the Council, a rather empty honor.

He was a great friend of the Puritans. 

Montgomery, Earl of. See Herbert, Philip 

Norwich, Bishop of. See Harsnett, Samuel 

Pembroke, Earl of. See Herbert, William 

Phelips, Sir Robert (1586?-1638) entered Par liament in 1604 when his father was Speaker of the 

House. By 1621 Sir Robert was one of the leaders of the Opposition. He was outstanding in 1625.

He was removed as a justice of the peace and had good reason to be of the Opposition.
