President of the Council. See Montagu, Henry 

Pym, John (1584-1643) entered Parliament in 1614 and became a leading speaker in 1621. He was a Puritan and very active on the Committee for Religion. He was a great leader in the Long 

Parliament and shaped the attack against Strafford and Laud. His religious views were fairly moderate, though he finally consented to the extirpation of episcopacy. He was an able manager of Parliament, and even his opponents recognized his ability and admired him. 

Rich, Sir Nathaniel (1585?-1636) was a merchant-adventurer and helped form a number of companies for colonial ventures. He had been a friend of Buckingham but went over to the Opposition after 1626. 

Rudyerd, Sir Benjamin (1572-1658) was a poet as well as a politician. He was an intimate friend of Ben Jonson. More important for this study, he was a friend of William Herbert, Earl of Pembroke. He was knighted and appointed surveyor for life of the court of wards. He was considered a courtier, but in 1628 his role was that of mediator between Charles and his subjects. In the 

Long Parliament he attacked Charles's evil counselors and identified himself with the Puritans. 

He was especially interested in colonial enterprise. 

Sackville, Edward (1591–1652), fourth Earl of

Dorset, served in the Commons before he succeeded his brother as earl. There he was a member of the Opposition. He was made a councilor in 1625 and was suspected of not favoring Buckingham, though he managed to keep himself clear. He continued to hold offices under Charles and supported him in the Civil War. The family derived wealth from monastic lands gained in the time of Henry VIII. 

Saye and Sele, Viscount. See Fiennes, William 

Scudamore, Sir John (1601-1671) became ambassador at Paris in 1635. He was made high stew-

Biographical Supplement 

235 ard of the city and cathedral of Hereford in 1639 but surrendered to the parliamentary forces in 1643. 

Seymour, Sir Francis (1590?-1664) was an Opposition leader. He was very much against Buckingham and seems to have followed Wentworth's policies. He was identified with the popular party until 1642, when he went over to the royalist side. 

He kept out of politics during the Commonwealth and Protectorate and was given a minor post at the Restoration. 

Steward, the Lord. See Herbert, William 

Villiers, George (1592-1628), first Duke of

Buckingham, rose from cupbearer to lord high admiral and the King's chief advisor. His foolhardy policies made him intensely unpopular, and in 1628 he was assassinated. 

Wentworth, Sir Thomas (1593-1641) entered

Parliament in 1614. He was consistent in opposing the financial demands of both James and Charles and, though he did not share the enthusiasm of most of the Opposition for Puritanism, he was united with them firmly by his belief in the need for reforms in administration. In 1627 he was imprisoned for refusing to pay the forced loan. In 1628 he made a strong bid for the leadership of the House of Commons. After the session of 1628 he was taken into court favor and made president of the Council of the North. He was one of the great landowners in Yorkshire. Eventually he was made lord lieutenant of Ireland and there was considered an arbitrary governor. 

He was made Earl of Strafford and became the King's chief adviser in 1640. He thought he could manipulate Parliament and recommended calling it. He was very able but had no respect for the abilities of others. Later his pride and arrogance made him unpopular. He was executed in 1641. 

Weston, Richard (1577–1635), Baron Weston of

Neyland and first Earl of Portland, served in the Commons before he was raised to the peerage. He was greatly disliked. He was suspected of Catholic sympathies, though he aroused the anger of the Queen because he would not give grants to her favorites when he was chancellor of the Exchequer. In 1628 he was made lord high treasurer. He was noted for his timidity. He made many enemies and was always in great fear of what they might do to him.

Wilde, John (1590-1669) was a Puritan and was made chief baron of the Exchequer in 1646. He was a member of the council of state in 1649-50. 

Williams, John (1582-1650) was Bishop of Lincoln and lord keeper in 1625. He disliked Buckingham and was in touch with the members of the Opposition in the House. In 1628 he was charged with betraying secrets of the Council and in 1635 he was accused of perjury. From 1637 to 

1640 he was imprisoned in the Tower. Then, in 

1641, he was made Archbishop of York. At the outbreak of war he was retired and later made terms with the Parliamentarians.

A.

THE PROTECTION OF THE LIBERTIES OF THE SUBJECT THE ROYAL APPEAL FOR FUNDS 

As was customary on the opening day of a session, the King and the lord keeper addressed Parliament in order to indicate the royal purpose in summoning the members. 

The session of 1628 marked the third attempt by Charles to gain adequate parliamentary support for the war against Spain. Lack of supply had led him to try forced loans and to quarter soldiers on his subjects. With inadequate forces and funds the prosecution of the war was ineffectual, and in the fall of 1627 a most unpopular disaster occurred. Buckingham made an unsuccessful attempt to capture the Isle of Rhé in the harbor of La Rochelle and thus relieve the besieged French Protestants. The expedition served only to arouse the hostility of the French king and increase England's enemies. The speeches which follow are printed in the Journals of the House of Lords, the official record of action of the Upper House and of all matters which concerned Parliament as a whole. 

1. The King's Speech. (1) 

I am sure you now expect from me both to know the cause of your meeting, and what to resolve on; yet I think there is none here but knows what common danger is the cause of this Parliament, and that supply at this time is the chief end of it; so that I need but to point to you what to do. 

I will use but few persuasions; for, if to maintain your own advices and . . . the true religion, the laws, liberties of this state, and the just defense of our true friends and allies, be not sufficient, no eloquence of men or angels will prevail. 

Only let me remember you, that my duty most of all and every one of yours according to his degree, is to seek the maintenance of this Church and commonwealth; and certainly there was never a time in which this duty was more necessarily required than now. 

I, therefore, judging a Parliament to be the ancient, speediest, and best way, in this time of common danger, to give such supply as to secure ourselves, and to save our friends from imminent ruin, have called you together. Every man must do according to his conscience; wherefore if you (which God forbid) should not do your duties in contributing what this state at this time needs, I must, in discharge of my conscience, use those other means which God has put into my hands, to save that that the follies of particular men may otherwise hazard to lose. 

2. The Lord Keeper's Speech. (2) 

tion of our religion, our King and country; and what can be greater? Urgent it is; it is little pleasure to tell or think how urgent; and to tell it with all material circumstances were a long work. 

I will but touch the sum of it and in few words. 

The Pope and House of Austria have long af fected, the one a spiritual, the other a temporal monarchy; and to effect their ends, do join together to serve each other's turns. The House of 

Austria, besides their vast and rich territories in both the Indies and in Africa, are become masters of Spain and the great country of Germany; and although France be not under their subjection, yet they have now environed it all about, and ... have gotten such a party and such interest in the government, that by pretense of aiding to root out the Protestants and our religion, they have drawn that King to their adherence so far, that albeit upon his Majesty's interposition by his ambassadors and engagement of his royal word for just performance the war between that King and his subjects of the religion were quieted. . yet against it and the strict alliance between his Majesty and that King, the treaty has been broken and those of the religion put to all extremities and undoubtedly will be ruined without present help. . . . Other potentates that in former time did balance and interrupt the growing greatness of the House of Austria are now removed and diverted. The Turk has made peace with the Emperor and turned himself wholly into wars in Asia. The King of Sweden is embroiled in a war with Poland, which is fomented by the Spanish practices to keep that King from succoring our party. The King of Denmark is chased out of his dominions on this side the sound; so as the House of Austria is on the point to command all the seacoast from Danzig to Emden and all the rivers falling into the sea in that great ex- [ 236 ] You are here assembled in Parliament, by his 

Majesty's writ and royal commandment, to consult and conclude of the weighty and urgent businesses of the King and kingdom; weighty it is and great, as great as the honor, safety, and protec-

Part 1: The Protection of the Liberties of the Subject 

237 tent; so as besides their power by land they begin to threaten our party by sea to the subversion of all our trade in the Baltic sea. They are now providing and arming all the ships they can build or hire, and have at this time their ambassadors treating at Lübeck to draw into their service the Hanse towns; whereby taking from us and our neighbors the Eastland trade by which our shipping is supplied, they expect without any blow given to make themselves absolute masters of the sea.... 

I speak not this to increase fear, unworthy of 

English courages, but to press provision worthy of the wisdom of a Parliament. 

I might press many reasons to this end. I will but name a few. 

First, for his Majesty's sake it requires it. Great is the duty that we owe him by the law of God, great by the law of nature and natural allegiance, great for his own merit, and the memory of his ever blessed father.

I do but point at them; but methinks, if our thoughts but recoil on one consideration touched by his Majesty, which to me seems to sound like a parliamentary pact or covenant, a war was advised here, assistance professed, yea, and protested here, I do but touch it. I know you will deeply think of it, and the more for the example the King has set you. His lands, his plate, and jewels he has not spared to supply the war. What the people have protested, the King on his part has willingly performed. 

Secondly, for the cause's sake, it concerns us in 

Christian charity to tender the distresses of our friends abroad; it concerns us in honor not to abandon them that have stood for us; and if these come not close enough, you shall find our interest so woven and involved with theirs, that the cause is more ours than theirs. If religion be in peril, we have the most flourishing and orthodox 

Church. If honor be in question, the stories and monuments of former ages will show that our ancestors left as much as any nation. If trade and commerce be in danger, we are islanders; it is our life. All these at once lie at the stake, and so does our very safety and being.

Lastly, in respect of the manner of his Majesty's demand which is in Parliament, the way that has ever best pleased the subjects of England; and good cause for it, for aid granted in 

Parliament works good effects for the people; they be commonly accompanied with gracious pardons and the like. Besides, just and good kings, finding the love of their people and the readiness of their supplies, may the better forbear the use of their prerogatives and moderate the rigor of their laws toward their subjects. B.

THE GRIEVANCES OF THE SUBJECT 

The source for the debates which follow is known as the "Borlase Account." The Journals of the House of Commons did not contain a record of debates when the House sat as a committee, but notes taken by individuals were circulated as daily news-letters. "Separates," or single speeches or reports were issued separately. The "Borlase Account" is a set of news-letters. It is in manuscript and the name on the title page of the volume is 

William Borlase, Knight. He was a member of this Parliament, but his name probably indicates ownership rather than authorship. 

1. The Opening Debate on Grievances in the House of Commons, March 22. (3) 

Mr. Robt. Goodwin: We are now at leisure, and we cannot but remember the chief cause of calling this assembly. His Majesty and the lord keeper gave it us in ample relation. We cannot think on them too soon, for time is precious and the occasions are urgent. I humbly move that this day may frame a beginning and that we may lay other businesses aside to perfect the better this grave and important work. 

Sir Francis Seymour: This is the chief council of the kingdom. Here, if not here alone, is the truest looking glass. We are to give counsel and not flattery. The commons that send us expect we should sit here without fear, not like Cambyses' judges, who finding no law, answered that the 

Persian kings might do what they pleased. But in case of giving, how shall we know what to give, when we do not know what we enjoy, since his Majesty is pleased to take what he thinks fit. This has been lately done by billeting of soldiers, as ill for the service of the King as the ease of the people. Then imprisonments, wherein the setters-on had their ends, and raised a cloud betwixt the King and us. It has been preached, or rather prated in pulpits, that all is the King's. Their doctrine, mere ambition, to change their conscience for a bishopric and flatter by keeping truth from a prince. Thus not only the people suffer but the King also to the hazard of that maxim, that those princes have wanted most that have exacted most. And now I am in speech of

wants, I cannot forbear to say that there wanted experience in those that were trusted by his Majesty in his late wars, and here wanted discretion in those that gave away their goods against their wills. Let us keep that which is hereditary to us to defend us and humbly to present to his Majesty, etc.

Sir Thomas Edmondes: We have had too much experience of late miserable distractions of Parliaments. If we meet with the like now, we are to expect nothing but ruin. The desperate affairs of Christendom press us, and accordingly, let us take care. Here let us bury all former ill passages, and think which way we may restore all and offer such a present to his Majesty, as may invite him to meet us halfway. The sympathies are yet good. 

Let not doubts arise, for as this Parliament succeeds, all our allies are either blessed or broken. 

Sir Humphrey May: All spirit of words ought to be laid aside. What counsels have passed are such as have been counsels of extremity. I am sure it is in the power of the House to do well, and I am as sure that the King brought a benevolent heart. 

Sir John Eliot: I would avoid all occasions of diversion, and yet I know not on what quality to speak. These unhappy times make us unworthy of our own privileges. Is it for myself I speak? It were nothing. Is it for the country [county] I serve? It were not much. Is it for all our countries? It is yet more. 'Tis for our ancient law, our liberties, our lives that call to us for protection. 'Tis not the cry of money that thus terrifies us, our lands and goods are all involved, the law, the very judgment of the law questioned, as fundamental, as that what Magna Carta itself decides to be meum et tuum is now no meum et tuum. All that is ours is engaged under a mighty power. 

What is once done may be often done, and the Lycurgan laws . . . worse than the Lycurgan wars. The causes have proceeded from two forms: (1) that of projectors themselves; (2) their instruments. The first plot it, the second put it in practice, and from the unnatural motions of these orbs, as under ill planets, vile diseases have been produced. I humbly move this business may be considered upon by a committee. 

Sir Benjamin Rudyerd: If we be thankful, all is well. By this we shall know whether Parliament will live or die. This is the crisis. By this we ourselves and all Christendom with us to whom we have any relation, must stand or fall. His Majesty does no less than proclaim that he will rely upon our loves. If we fail him we are unworthy of his. We are not now upon questions of our bene esse, but our esse only. Is it a small matter that we have provoked two mighty enemies and not hurt them? Made them friends to themselves to agree to destroy us? Is there no balm in Gilead?

Then is there none if not here. One Parliament may instruct another as one day does another. 

Avoid contestations, for it is comely that princes should have a precedency, and without a mutual confidence betwixt King and people none of this can be effected, and he that is not safe in his goods and his person is not at home. First, therefore, let us begin to trust the King that he may trust us; secondly, give ample supply, for counsel without money is but a speculation. 3. Prostrate our grievances at his feet, that all may appear to be done in duty to him, and let us all labor to bring the King on our side. 

Sir Thomas Wentworth: May this day be as happy as it is hopeful. This is a time to contemporate. King and subjects, though both innocent from guilt, yet both injured and both to be cured. 

Surely these illegal ways past of imprisonments, moneys, billeting of soldiers, etc., cast a stain upon a prince's crown. They have gone farther, extended prerogatives, rent from us our liberties, vitiating our wives and daughters, and ruined the comely and everlasting fruits of law and justice and protection, ravishing at once all those left to us by our sires. The shepherd is smitten and the sheep are scattered; the primum mobile is out of frame. Now we have lost our liberty, what have they left us to give our King? I shall make bold to propound some remedies: first, to vindicate all our vital liberties by reviving ancient laws, and set a character that never shall be eclipsed. Shall this break a Parliament? 2, Freedom from imprisonment or commandment to be sent abroad contrary to their wills and the ancient laws. 3ly, Upon our goods no levy to be made but by Parlia ment.

Sir Robert Phelips: Amongst the Romans once a year there was a feast for bondmen and slaves, wherein they had freedom of speech to complain of any ill usages they had suffered the year before. We are not bondmen yet. They returned again to slavery, but we I hope shall not. I am glad to see such a sense of our miseries and find such a concurrency from all parts to acknowledge the subject's wrong. All confess him wronged; all wish him righted; and would have an amnesty amongst us. Let him not prosper that wishes not so. Yet so as to sit secure there is no way least to perfect remedies as to forget past injuries. This is now a critical Parliament. Dangers abroad, distractions at home, he is not an Englishman that thinks not on them. These are no chimeras. We have joined two enemies to make them both ours, yet I fear more home violence than foreign forces. 

Must we give money to secure ourselves abroad and do nothing to defend ourselves at home? 

Take heed of fear; we are yet Englishmen. But oh, Mr. Speaker, our religion, our religion is dispensable. A toleration of conscience is granted by a pecuniary commission. I have not seen it, but have heard of it, and will produce good witnesses to avouch it. Preachers have sycophanted the King

Part 1: The Protection of the Liberties of the Subject 

239 and abused his ears. The people ought to suffer no more than what they voluntarily assent unto here, but now there are acts of power against acts of law. Levies of money, imprisonment, though the Parliaments tell us no man's good can be taken without consent. Did ever king of England violate this open way and damn that statute of Rich. III that damned all illegal means of raising money? What a miserable grievance is that of lieutenancies, when by an arbitrary warrant, I shall have my goods taken from me as if I were a poor snake! . . . Who sends there warrants, levies, money, imprisons their persons. As concerning his Majesty, I will first clear him, for necessity is a strong and strange counselor. But we now little differ from the course in Turkey. 

Where the Janissary sets his halberd there he is master without resistance. Soldiers are laid upon us now as if we were the poorest slaves living. 

Fortescue, De Laudibus Legum Angliae [written about 1470], tells us that no subject is by force to receive any person, only into inns, and there to pay for what they have. But what talk I of law where there is scarce any penalty? Therefore I humbly move we may petition his Majesty for regulating lieutenancies. For conclusion, consider his Majesty and people. One calls, the other comes. One asks, the other hopes. And now we are here let every man hie him to make up his part and portion in the walls of peace. We are branded with a mark of facti oneres. Let us carry home with us the mark of peace. We seek liberty, but we will not forget subjection. Let us labor for an unanimity. The kings of England were never deceived when they trusted to their subjects. I wish there might be a committee to consider both for election and moderation in these grievances. When this is done, I doubt not but the supply will be exceeding great. For we shall present to his Majesty our purses and our hearts with such a gift as never king of England received, for we shall give him a new people being yet such a one as does no more than breathe. 

Sir Edward Coke: I will speak nothing but what concerns my own profession. I am for giving, yet conditionally. To tell of dangers, I will not. Here are loans haut et bas, sans Parliament. To what end is it to give now if we must give again by compulsion? But the King cannot command a loan. I will vouch you records. . . . 34 Henry 

VIII no tax, no tallage but by Parliament. Every man may lend to his friend, but no man may be constrained. I would wish to represent to the 

King this by way of grievance and I have drawn a bill to that effect and a preface to the subsidy. 

It is admirable. 'Twill make the people I fear run too fast. This preamble is worth all eloquence, and let the loan and the subsidy go together. I will not despair of such a King so attentive to divine service. But Mr. Speaker, these loans are cuttings. 

Sir John Coke [Secretary Coke]: I hope you do not expect I should answer such learning as you have heard. My desire is to quiet, not to provoke any. I petition every man to question his own heart and to settle all in unity by taking away all scandals. Every man speaks out of his own abundance. Charity is good for all. Every man agrees the King should be relieved, and grievances heard, neither need there many arguments to prove that that is confessed. Only the manner, not the matter, of guilt is to be argued. In repairing of buildings all men are not of a mind. One would have a door, one a window altered. But if we find a fire abroad is not to be thought upon. The danger is confessed; what course, then, is fittest to go about to prove the unlegality of what is past, is labor lost. You cannot think of it but as counsel of necessity. It is propounded that we should begin with grievances. I wish a preparation, but will you begin with these? Will not this way seem conditional? Do not you think the King jealous of his honor? Will not standing upon such terms estrange him? 2ly, you would have fruit, a good answer. But the King must be judge. You may speak your grievances, but what think you of being differed? I advise rather to proceed by way of committee, but first to meet his Majesty. Bellum constat fama. All our subsidies do not so much good as the people's readiness to relieve their King, and the report of that abroad. Therefore, begin with him. I am sorry to except against any man. Yet I heard a complaint made in matter of religion, whereof we ought to be sensible that idolatry is exercised and tolerated. I know none, and if this hand ever gave way to any, I would it were cut off. If this be spoken by instructions I desire the witnesses may be produced; if of the gentleman himself, I desire he may be questioned. 

Sir Robert Phelips: I have about me two affections: one of sorrow, if any way I have failed in my tongue; another of thankfulness to that noble gentleman, to call upon me openly in this House, not privately traducing me, but giving me leave to clear myself there where I was accused. I do acknowledge again that the liberty was great, and will make it good by witnesses as I promised, and I desire to be censured by this House. 

Sir Dudley Digges: In everything I concur with those gentlemen that spake last. But I hear the cries of necessity. I desire to give no color of differing, and I will speak my conscience freely. I am afraid (and I have too great cause to fear) that our King is told he is no great king unless he be told so. But I believe his greatness lies in the observance of his laws. That king that is not limited, rules slaves that cannot serve him. The 

Turk and Egypt have no other. In all my employments I know by experience that there is no success where there is calling upon against laws. The 

Muscovites are so cowed with these arbitrary com-

mands, that I know the time when a few English and Scots have beaten I know not how many thousand of their best horsemen out of the field. 

The Low Country men are poor at land . . . but at sea where they have such encouragements, you see what a brave people they are. The King cannot lose more than by degenerating us. I humbly desire his Majesty may be moved to these considerations, and that a committee touching our goods and liberties may be appointed, that we may be settled in the good will of his Majesty. 

Sir Henry Mildmay: I desire my fellows of the court to make a good relation of what has passed this day. I see a great deal of obedience in every man. I find also some mistakings. For if I be not deceived, that worthy gentleman's meaning was mistaken by this noble gentleman here, and thus it may be also that the King may be misinformed. 

Concerning the proposition of grievances and donation, which should proceed, I humbly move that the dispute may end by ordering them to go together hand in hand, and a committee to be appointed for them both. 

2. Debate on Forced Loans, March 26. (4) 

Sir Robert Phelips: I will not play the lawyer though they should lead us. The goods of the subject are his own, and cannot be taken law- C. fully from him, though he consent without Parliament. Even our neighbors, the French whereof du Haillian, the historian, is one, can tell us as much. We have two authors at home for us, Fortescue, Henry VI, and Sir Thomas Smyth, secretary to Queen Elizabeth. They say that the kings of England cannot make laws nor raise money but in Parliament. I move this in hope to set the lawyers awork to deliver their knowledge and their opinions. 

Sir Nathaniel Rich: I will leave law to the lawyers. I am for reason and example. One authority

I will add. King James himself professed that whosoever should bid the King go against law was a viper. . . . This I think good to remember for reasons. If there be no property, no meum and tuum, then there is no justice. When there is no justice what is there left to establish a king's throne? Those that pull it down pull down the king. No propriety, no industry, all beggars; no propriety, no valor; no valor, all in confusion. 

You may enlarge and add to these as you please. . . . The question is thus put: All those that are of opinion that the subject of England has such property and right in his own goods according to ancient custom as that no levy nor tax may be made upon the said goods without act of Parliament, say aye. All of that opinion.

GRIEVANCES versus SUPPLY 

For several days debate continued on imprisonment and the liberties of the subject. Then on April 1 and 2 the results of debate were formulated into resolutions and on April 3 these were sent to the Lords. These debates had produced no supply, and the King decided to hasten matters by a message. The source used for the report of the King's mes sages is John Rushworth, Historical Collections of Private Passages of State, Weighty Matters in Law, Remarkable Proceedings in Five Parliaments Beginning the Sixteenth Year of King James, Anno 1618, and Ending the Fifth Year of King Charles, Anno 1629. Rush worth (16122-90) was clerk-assistant to the House of Commons in 1640. He served first as 

Fairfax's secretary and then as Cromwell's. In the reign of Charles II he was several times a member of Parliament. As an historian he was especially interested in the background of the Civil War. His source for the Parliament of 1628 is a parliamentary compilation of news-letters and separates called The True Relation. 

1. A Message from the King Delivered by 

Secretary Coke, April 3. (5)

His Majesty having understood that some rumors were spread abroad of a sharp message yesterday delivered by me, and of some malicious words that the Duke should speak yesterday at the Council board, he commanded me to tell you of the malice of those false reports, for that nothing fell from the Duke or that board, but what was for the good of this assembly; he would have you observe the malice of those spirits that thus put in these jealousies; had the Duke so spoken, he should have contradicted himself, for all of us of the Council can tell, he was the first mover and persuader of this assembly of Parliament to the King. Esteem of the King according to his actions and not these tales; his Majesty takes notice of our purpose, that on Friday we will resolve upon supply, which his Majesty graciously accepts of, and that our free gift without any condition should testify to the world that we will be as far from encroaching upon his prerogative, as he will be to encroach upon our liberties; and this shall well appear, when we present our grievances to him, and then we shall know that he has no intention to violate our liberties, only let us not present them with any asperity of words;

Part I: The Protection of the Liberties of the Subject 

241 he counts it his greatest glory to be a king of free men, not of villeins. He thought to have delivered this message himself, but that he feared it would take us too much time. (Then Sec. Coke added a word of his own.) Yesterday after dinner we attended his Majesty, and he asked us what we had done. We said we had entered into the consideration of supply, and that the final resolution was deferred till Friday; and that this was done for just reasons, to join the business of his Majesty's and our countries together, and this would further his Majesty, and it would give content to the country, and that this union here might be spread abroad in the world. His Majesty answered, "For God's sake, why should any hinder them in their liberties? If they did it not I should think they dealt not faithfully with me." You may see a true character of his Majesty's disposition; let us proceed with courage, and rest assured his Majesty will give great ear unto us, and let us all join to make a perfect union to win the King's heart; we shall find a gracious answer from the 

King, and a hearty cooperation from those that you think to be averse to us. 

2. Resolutions to be Sent to the House of 

Lords, April 3. (6) 

First. Resolved, upon question, that no free man ought to be committed, or detained in prison, or otherwise restrained, by the command of the King, or the Privy Council, or any other, unless some cause of the commitment, detainer, or restraint be expressed, for which, by law, he ought to be committed, detained, or restrained. . . . 

2ly. Resolved, upon question, that the writ of habeas corpus may not be denied, but ought to be granted to every man that is committed, or detained in prison, or otherwise restrained, though it be by command of the King, the Privy Council, or any other, he praying the same. 

3ly. Resolved, upon question, that if a free man be committed, or detained in prison, or otherwise restrained, by the command of the King, the Privy Council, or any other, no cause of such commitment, detainer, or restraint, being expressed, for which, by law, he ought to be committed, detained, or restrained, and the same be returned upon an habeas corpus, granted for the said party, that then he ought to be delivered, or bailed. 

4ly. Resolved, upon question, that the ancient and undoubted right of every free man is, that he has a full and absolute property in his goods and estate; and that no tax, tallage, loan, benevolence, or other like charge ought to be commanded or levied by the King, or any of his ministers, without common assent by act of Parliament. 

3. A Message from the King Delivered by 

Secretary Coke, April 4. (7)

His Majesty has again commanded me to put you in mind, how the eyes and interest of the Christian world are cast upon the good or evil success of this assembly. He also graciously takes notice of that which is in agitation amongst us, touching the freedom of our persons and the property of our goods; and that this particular care (which he no way mislikes) may not retard our resolution for the general good, he wills us cheerfully to proceed in both, and to express our readiness to supply his great occasions, upon assurance that we shall enjoy our rights and liberties, with as much freedom and security in his time, as in any age heretofore under the best of our kings; and whether you shall think fit to secure ourselves herein, by way of bill or otherwise, so as it be provided for with due respect of his honor and the public good, whereof he doubts not but that you will be careful, he promises and assures you that he will give way unto it; and the more confidence you shall show in his grace and goodness, the more you shall prevail to obtain your own desires. 

4. Debate on Supply, April 4. The source for this debate is the unpublished diary of Sir Edward Nicholas, who entered Parliament in 1620 as a servant of the court. In 1624 he was made secretary to the lord high admiral, and throughout his parliamentary career he was undoubtedly a government scout. He was a clear-headed man of business. In his first 

Parliament he took copious notes, but in this session he was briefer. He apparently took notes on a speech as the speaker reached his main point. Skillful in compressing substance, he did not bother with irrelevant speeches or with those of unimportant men. (8) 

Sir Francis Seymour: Whosoever seeks to advance the supply or the liberty of the subject, the one before the other, loves neither; and to join them, seeing we demand but what is our own, cannot be thought to put conditions on his Majesty. 

The King's message has wrought much in him. He declines fifteens, considers five subsidies fit to be given in so short a time. 

Sir Roger North: Would have us sweeten the

King with a supply, albeit he did never think to have given supply in the infancy of a Parliament, for that he has ever observed such lamentable effects of it. Would have us give four subsidies and two fifteens. 

Sir Thomas Wentworth: This as weighty a cause as ever came into this House; would have us proceed evenly and equally between the King and his subjects. He likes not this pressing upon the

House for supply at the beginning of a Parliament, and hopes hereafter the King will calm so pleasurably as that we may not be put on the rack of necessity but drawn on by the cords of affection. . . . There is a fair offer of the King's part of reconciliation; would not have us neglect it. 

If this Parliament should succeed amiss it would be the greatest blow that was ever given to this kingdom. Will put no condition on the King but looks for assurances of liberties. . . 

Mr. Pym: Would give five subsidies because it is the most proposed to be given. 

Sir John Eliot: That he knows not how five subsidies will be levied without soldiers; would give but four subsidies. 

Resolved by this Grand Committee on the Question that we shall give to his Majesty five subsidies in a parliamentary way. 

Sir Thomas Wentworth: That there may be no report now to the House of this resolution; for this gift is upon an assurance that the King will settle the fundamental liberty of the subject. 

Would have the Grand Committee appoint a subcommittee to draw into a law what may assure us of our liberty of our persons and property of our goods, before we report the resolution of our gift. 

5. The King's Message Delivered by Secretary Coke and Its Reception, April 12. (9) 

His Majesty having given timely notice to this House, as well of the pressure of time as of the necessity of supply, has long since expected some fruit of that which was so happily begun; but finding a stop beyond all expectation, after so good beginning, he has commanded me to tell you that without further or unnecessary delay any he would have you to proceed in this business. 

For, however he has been willing and consenting his affairs and ours should concur and proceed together, yet his meaning was not that the one should give interruption to the other, nor the time to be spun out upon any pretense, upon which the common cause of Christendom does so much depend. He bids us therefore take heed that we force not him to make an unpleasing end of that which was so well begun. . . 

This message was very unpleasing to the House and many debates succeeded thereupon. And Sir 

Robert Phelips said he hoped their moderation would have given a right understanding to his Majesty of their loyalty. Others proposed to find out a way by God's Providence to make this message happy to King and people, it concerning the 

King's honor abroad and our safety at home that this Parliament be happy. Let us prevent (say they) these mischiefs which by frequent messages thus obstruct us. Let those gentlemen near the chair see that we have endeavored to apply ourselves to his Majesty's service, notwithstanding this message.

Nothing so endangers us with his Majesty as that opinion that we are antimonarchically affected; whereas such is and ever has been our loyalty, if we were to choose a government we would choose this monarchy of England above all governments in the world. 

D. 

THE ACTION OF THE LORDS ON THE RESOLUTIONS OF THE COMMONS 

Between April 8 and April 25 the Lords gave serious consideration to the Commons' Resolutions. They listened to the attorney general, judges, and the House of Commons' lawyers on the subject of imprisonment. The stumbling block in the way of agreement was the advisability of expressing the cause of commitment. Many were of the opinion that in cases of treason it would not be expedient to express the cause lest plots be revealed before all those involved were apprehended. 

1. The Counterproposals of the Lords, April 

25. (10) 

First. That his Majesty would be pleased graciously to declare, that the good old law called Magna Carta, and the six statutes conceived to be declarations and explanations of that law [temp. 

Edward I and Edward III], do still stand in force to all intents and purposes. 

2ly. That his Majesty would be pleased graciously to declare, that according to Magna Carta, and the statutes aforenamed, as also according to the most ancient customs and laws of this land, every free subject of this realm has a fundamental property in his goods, and a fundamental liberty of his person. 

3ly. That his Majesty would be graciously pleased to declare, that it is his royal pleasure to ratify and confirm unto all and every his loyal and faithful subjects, all their ancient, several, just liberties, privileges and rights, in as ample and beneficial manner to all intents and purposes, as their ancestors did enjoy the same under the best of his most noble progenitors.

Part 1: The Protection of the Liberties of the Subject 

243 4ly. That his Majesty would be further pleased graciously to declare, for the good content of his loyal subjects, and for the securing of them from future fear, that in all cases within the cognizances of the common law concerning the liberties of the subject, his Majesty would proceed according to the common law of this land, and according to the laws established in the kingdom, and in no other manner or wise. 

5ly. As touching his Majesty's royal prerogative, intrinsical to his sovereignty, and betrusted him withal from God, . . . that his Majesty would resolve not to use or divert the same, to the prejudice of any his loyal people in the property of their goods, or liberty of their persons. 

And in case, for the security of his Majesty's royal person, the common safety of his people, or the peaceable government of this kingdom, his Majesty shall find just cause for reason of state to imprison or restrain any man's person, his Majesty would graciously declare, that within a convenient time he shall and will express the cause of his commitment or restraint, either general or special: and upon a cause so expressed, will leave him immediately to be tried according to the common justice of the kingdom. 

2. The Consideration of the Lords' Counter proposals, April 26. (11) 

Mr. Wilde: That he observes these defects of these propositions. Unless these propositions be required to move particulars it will do us little good. For the first two propositions, we shall not need to stand much on them: for we shall not [have] to have any renovation of that Great Charter and those statutes. For the third proposition, would have it to be supplied with further words of negative, that there may be nothing done therein but according to the common law; the fourth proposition, it is too short; for it is and has been a question, what is lex terre; and doubts unless some further words be expressed to declare what that law is, it may be extended to prerogative which may be called a law. For the fifth, that "convenient time" has no limitation which should be ascertained, and there is no way in this proposition set down for help of the subject in case the prerogative be extended; which we do desire may be set down by habeas corpus or otherwise; would have confinement put down as well as imprisonment. And would have us put it down propriety in our goods and estate. 

Sir Nathaniel Rich: Said that the Lords said they were not out of love with our propositions, and there was no offer to us to recede from them; and therefore would have us stick to our propositions. . . . [For] the fifth proposition he would have us leave it out entirely, for they imply speech of matter of law and matter of state, which he understands not, but so as the sense is, he doubts will be little for our good. He wishes we should extract what is for our advantage in these propositions and retaining it, add it to our own. 

Sir Edward Coke: That he would not have us to recede from our own resolutions for our liberties of our persons, which is, according to his knowledge, good and wholesome; and would not have us recede from it. As for the Lord's propositions, concludes nothing. That there are in those propositions divers statutes of the liberty for the subject omitted. Generally he likes well that word, but it is our right that those laws should be confirmed, and when the King does a thing of grace it implies that it is not our right. Lex terre is the common law of the land. He understands not fundamental and therefore will not assent to it. 

That our just liberties shall be confirmed; what are our just liberties, is the question; and the thing has been here disputed under the best kings of England, whether he were the most religious, most rich, wise, or just. There must be added predecessors as well as ancestors, for bishops have no ancestors but predecessors, or else they are excluded. All things done within cognizance of the common law, it must be added "or statutes of the realm"; and it is also the law established within the realm. Martial law and civil is established in the realm, and by the fourth proposition the common law must yield to the martial law. For the fifth, he understands it not, for intrinsical prerogative, it seems by this proposition, is entrusted in him from God; which shows it is done to him jure divino, which then cannot by any human law be taken from him. Who shall judge of "convenient time"? This is the thing for which Magna Carta was first made. . . . The end of our conference with the Lords was that their lordships would declare with us. If they shall, out of their doubtfulness, use any hesitation, then that we go on by ourselves, and wishes that they would declare with us or say no. Wishes we should not recede from anything.. 

Mr. Ball: Would have a subcommittee to consider of the propositions. ... 

Sir Thomas Wentworth: Would have a subcommittee but thinks things are not yet ripe for it; hopes that it shall never be a question here whether the King or the law are above each other. 

Would have us to get an act and not a petition of right which will lie still in a parliamentary roll unprinted. Princes do rather gather than lose any ground, and what may be moved upon the heels of the fifth proposition, and would not have any ground given to it; would have subcommittee to take into consideration to expand lex terre. When we have a law that none shall be committed without showing cause, he would have a mark set on such a law that it may not on all occasions be broken, and when it shall, on any emergent cause, no man . . . will find fault with it.

Part II. 

A. 

THE KING ATTEMPTS TO DIRECT LEGISLATION 

Six weeks had elapsed since the King made his request for a supply. His supporters in the 

House of Commons having been unable to bring matters to a conclusion, Charles decided to use direct methods of bringing pressure to bear on the dilatory Commons. 

RELATIONS WITH THE COMMONS 1. Speech of the Lord Keeper to Both 

Houses of Parliament by the King's Command, April 28. (12)

My Lords, and you the knights, citizens, and burgesses of the House of Commons, you cannot but remember the great and important affairs concerning the safety both of the state and religion, declared at first from his Majesty's own mouth, to be the causes of the assembling of this Parliament; the sense whereof, as it does daily increase with his Majesty, so it ought to do, and his Majesty doubts not but it does so with you, since the danger increases every day, both by ef fluxion of time, and preparations of the enemy. 

Yet his Majesty does well weigh, that this expense of time has been occasioned by the debate which has arisen in both Houses touching the liberty of the subject; in which, as his Majesty takes in good part the purpose and intent of the Houses, so clearly and frequently professed, that they would not diminish or blemish his just prerogative, so he presumes that you will all confess it a point of extraordinary grace and justice in him to suffer it to rest so long in dispute without interruption; but now his Majesty considering the length of time which it has taken, and fearing nothing so much as any future loss of that whereof every hour and minute is so precious, and foreseeing that the ordinary way of debate, though never so carefully husbanded, in regard of the form of both Houses, necessarily takes more time than the affairs of Christendom can permit, his Majesty out of his great princely care has thought of this expedient to shorten the business, by declaring the clearness of his own heart and intention; and therefore has commanded me to let you know that he holds the statute of 

Magna Carta, and the other six statutes insisted upon for the subject's liberty, to be all in force, and assures you, that he will maintain all his subjects in the just freedom of their persons, and safety of their estates; and that he will govern according to the laws and statutes of this realm; and that you shall find as much security in his 

Majesty's royal word and promise, as in the strength of any law you can make; so that hereafter you shall never have cause to complain. The conclusion is, that his Majesty prays God, Who has hitherto blessed this kingdom, and put into his heart to come to you this day, to make the success thereof happy, both to King and people. 

And therefore he desires that no doubt or distrust may possess any man, but that you will all proceed unanimously to the business. 

2. Debate on the Lord Keeper's Speech, 

April 28. This debate is taken from the unpublished diary of Sir Richard Grosvenor, who entered Parliament in 1620 as M.P. for

Chester. His diary is very full, for he was diligent and painstaking in his note-taking. He tried to get exact words rather than their significance, a fact which sometimes makes his meaning obscure. (13) 

Sir John Coke: Observe his Majesty's most gra cious moderation in interpreting our proceedings; that we have the same sense of the affairs of Christendom; his moderation be three subsequent degrees: (1) that the expense or time by the debate touching the liberty of the subject; whereby we see how indulgent he is to us, that has not taken ill that notwithstanding the great affairs of Christendom, we have neglected them; (2) he takes in good part our proceedings that we go not about to blemish his prerogative; (3) the King hopes that we will confess that he has used an extraordinary justice to us that we have had leave to dispute so long about matters so nearly concerning the Crown. . . . In the speech of the lord keeper I observe five degrees, wherein there is more assurance of what we desire than by any law. That his Majesty confirms, confesses, declares the fundamental laws of the kingdom; this is not the first time that the liberties of the kingdom have been infringed, a hard matter so to limit power as not to blemish it, so to limit liberty not to advance it. But his Majesty goes further. He, according to the sense of those laws, promises to retain his subjects in the just freedom and liberties of their persons and estates. By "just" he acknowledges this a matter of right, not of grace. [The] third degree [is] that he will govern according to the laws and statutes of the realm. (4) that we shall find as much security in

his promise as in the strength of any law we can make; a law passed here must come to his Majesty; if he shall find that his government is blemished by that law, may not his Majesty, as his predecessors, use the benefit of a dispensation?

Make the law with any penalty, the King has power to pardon the penalties. The best expedient his Majesty thought to this business was to express his heart, which we now have expressed, and bind all with his royal word. What prince can express more affection, wisdom, care? Fifth clause; beyond all these, so that hereafter you shall never have cause to complain, can we expect this from law or anything but the heart of the King? Is not this promise sufficient satisfaction for all past? . . . Moved that we would show ourselves the best of subjects as he has shown himself the best of kings, and without further interruption proceed in the King's business. 

Sir Benjamin Rudyard: The business is great and the manner of handling as great as the thing. 

Liberty is precious, and he that does not value it deserves to be valued accordingly. We have resolved according to law, and if any judge of a contrary opinion, we should have heard of it before now. The end of Magna Carta to reduce the regal to a legal power. .. The King has intimated that he would have the abuses of power reformed, a happiness to us. I shall be glad to see Magna Carta walk abroad with vigor attended by those other six statutes; and I doubt not but we shall fall to a fit accommodation with the Lords for a liberty of the person and goods; and that we have a law in the point that we may not be imprisoned for forced loans and privy seal. . ...

Sir John Eliot: I speak nothing upon the para phrase given upon this great text, but I observe the great grace for the King, in so excellent a manner, and I begin with a prayer that that God who put it into his heart will make it happy and successful to him and us. I will not insist too consciously upon particulars, nor to stand upon that grace for confirmation of those laws, now his just profession to allow them to us in their just sense. We doubt it not. I resort to that work of satisfaction to clear us how we come to him and how to preserve the liberties of the subject. . . 

From our conclusions we intended to report to the Lords, so to a law to be passed by the King. 

I know no reason why we should recede thence. 

We moved then to hear if any scruples remained with them. We hear of none, so I take it as granted (they not being denied) that they are admitted. The King allowed his laws, but the difficulty still rests upon the word "just," what interpretation it shall bear, who shall expound it. 

Moved to apply ourselves to the framing of a bill where our own conclusions and the propositions from the Lords may be so interwoven that we may give them satisfaction and proceed to the great work desired by his Majesty. . 

Mr. Glanville: He concurred for a bill propounded generally. He found no cause to recede one jot from our resolutions and would not have a bill to prejudice anything. . Moved for a committee to draw a bill; no great matter; it may be ready tomorrow morning. Ordered, that a select committee should be named to draw a bill wherein should be contained the substance of Magna Carta and the best of those laws concerning the liberty of the subject, in their persons and goods, and to make use of the resolutions in this House. 

3. A Draft of the Bill of Right, April 29. (14) 

An act for the better securing of every free man touching the property of his goods and liberty of his person. 

Whereas it is declared and enacted by Magna

Carta that no free man is to be convicted, destroyed, etc., and whereas by a statute made in 

E:1, called de tallagio non concedendo, and whereas by the Parliament 5 E:3 and 14 E:3 and 

29 E:3 etc., and whereas the said Great Charter was confirmed and that the other laws [were confirmed], etc. Be it enacted that Magna Carta and the same acts of explanation and other the acts be put in due execution and that all judgments, awards, and rules given are [or] to be given to the contrary shall be void. And whereas by the common law and statutes it appears that no free man ought to be committed by command of the King, etc.; and if any free man be so committed and the same returned upon an habeas corpus, he ought to be delivered or bailed. Be it now enacted that no free man shall be committed by the command of the King or the Privy Council but the cause ought to be expressed and the same being returned upon an habeas corpus, he shall be delivered or bailed; and whereas by the common law and statutes every free man has a property in his goods and estate as no tax, tallage, etc. Be it now enacted that no tax, tallage, loan shall be levied etc. by the King or any minister without act of Parliament and that none be compelled to receive any soldier into his house against his will, etc. 

4. Debate on the Bill of Right, May 1. (15) 

Sir Dudley Digges: I say the King ought not to do this, but I like not to put it in a law that the King ought not. Never act spoke in such a language. ...

Sir John Scudamore: Behold our sovereign is ready to declare our liberties in our goods and persons; that he will govern us by his laws where-

by we claim our rights. Besides we have his word that we shall not have cause hereafter to complain. That king that will break his word will be no punctual observer of his law. . . . If a prince after shall break our liberties let them at that time proceed for themselves. I am afraid (yet no coward) lest we suffer the substance steal away while we catch at the shadow. . . . 

Sir Francis Seymour: This bill without a penalty, we take only the shadow and leave the substance. In all those things wherein we suffer, none more faulty than deputy lieutenants and justices of peace who are willing to execute what comes out. Moved for a penalty; such are more fearful to lose a little authority than the liberty of the subjects. 

Sir Thomas Wentworth: Moved: take this law as it lay in proposition 2; the ancient [statutes] fully confirmed; a security that we shall be bailed; the judges shall do their duty; that we have a property in our goods. No such law of consequence to the commonwealth since Ed. 3 time. How can you answer your country if you refuse it?

Sir John Coke: A message from the King. The 

King commanded me to desire this House clearly to let him know whether this House will rest upon his royal word delivered by former messages, especially by that speech made by my lord keeper in his presence which he assures us if we do he will royally and really perform. . . .

Sir Edward Coke: To take this message into consideration tomorrow morning. 

Sir John Eliot: I wonder that this message has been so long within these walls without acquainting us with it, to suffer us go on with other business; prejudice to his Majesty's service; as supposition not fit to be presented in this place if you will and to yourselves; if you will dictate from the King.

Sir John Coke: He that gave him the message gave him the time and directed him how to carry himself. 

5. The Debate on the Answer to the King, May 2. (16) 

Sir Walter Erle: This message invites us to frame an humble remonstrance of what we have done and what we have framed in our bill, and in what manner we have done it. 1. What we have done in passing those laws which conserve the liberty of the subjects in the property of goods and liberty of person and therein no new thing. 2. Why we have done it; and in an humble manner plainly to lay down that it is conceived that the subject has suffered more in his liberty in two or three years than in many hundreds before; and let the blame of this light upon the authors and actors and not on his Majesty. These heads framed into a remonstrance may serve for ... so many heads of an answer; withal to show his 

Majesty what proceeding we had then in hand when we received this message from him, and that we were encouraged to go by way of bill from a message we received from him that we might go by bill or otherwise. . . 

Mr. Wilde: I conceive this message proceeds not from any greed but from that fountain of grace and goodness which has flowed upon us which if it had been poured out sooner would have produced better effect. . . . Our speediest way presently to return an answer, without much debate; the effect of it thus; that we have taken into consideration his messages heretofore, the last by lord keeper, and this last, that we have duly considered of them and have taken notice what he pleased to say, that he would join with us by bill or otherwise to settle our liberties. . . . ... 

Mr. Browne: The King has promised his word; where the word of a king is there is power. His word is the greatest security can be given us. I of opinion to trust the King and his word. . . . 

Sir Thomas Wentworth: A present answer in part and a future message hereafter. Presently to be sent by Sir John Coke, that after by the House and Speaker. That presently: that we present most humble thanks to his Majesty for his gracious declaration in Parliament of his purpose to govern according to his laws; that never 

House did more trust in the goodness and royal word of a king than we as private men; but yet that we are ambitious that his goodness may live to posterity; that he would be pleased to consider that we are accountable to a public trust to our country; and so do beseech that he would give us leave to lay hold of his former messages and that we may in all duty present unto him that when there has been a public violation by his ministers, there cannot be less satisfaction than by a bill.

Sergeant Hoskins: Against a remonstrance be cause that implies a protestation and claim of a right which we have no cause to complain of especially in this message being but a request. . . 

Sir Francis Seymour: Our relying upon the

King's word has occasioned the resolutions of the King's word; and to move a bill never to doubt of that word because he has told us he would consent to a bill. . . . ... 

Mr. Crew: To have Sir Thomas Wentworth's words set down and presently sent by Secretary 

Coke. . . .

Sir Edward Coke: Though I trust the King as a private man, the King speaks but by record. 

Sir Thomas Hoby: Moved to have this message propounded by Sir Thomas Wentworth to be set down in parts. 

Sir Thomas Wentworth: That we should from this House return most humble thanks for his

Majesty's gracious declaration in the Lord's 

House. 2. That never House did more trust in the words and goodness of a king than we as private men, but that we are ambitious that his goodness might live to posterity. With some modest provision for illustration, execution and performance. That we have not yet agreed upon a bill. So soon as we have debated it (wherein we will lose no time) we shall crave his grace clearly to represent the same to his Majesty by our 

Speaker with the whole House.

Sir Dudley Digges: Took exception against 

"doubt as private men." I would have no limitation. Let nothing be there that may give question as though we distrusted as public persons.... 

Sir John Coke: You lay a charge that his Majesty must acknowledge that there has been a public violation of the laws. Wished the committee to put this in a style fit for the King's ear. . . . 

Sir Thomas Wentworth: It was far from me to charge anything upon his Majesty, for my words were: by his ministers, which cannot be denied.

That language becomes this House and who shall inform him if we do not? 

Sir Francis Seymour: Nothing laid down in this but what has been confessed by the counselors in this Parliament, that it has been illegal. I fear the King never hears truth in any place so well as from here.

Sir John Coke: Message from the King. 

Wherein as his Majesty will rank himself amongst the best of our kings, and show he has no intention to invade or impeach our lawful liberties, or rights; so he will have us to match ourselves with the best subjects, not by encroaching upon that sovereignty or prerogative which God has put into his hands for our good, but by containing ourselves within the bounds and laws of our forefathers, without restraining them, or enlarging them by new explanations, interpretations, expositions, or additions in any sort, which he tells us he will not give way unto. That the weight of the affairs of the kingdom, and Christendom, do press him more and more, and that the time is now grown to that point of maturity, that it cannot endure long debate, or delay; so as this session of Parliament must continue no longer than Tuesday come sevennight, at the furthest, in which time his Majesty for his part will be ready to perform what he promised; and if the House be not as ready to do that is fit for themselves, it shall be their own faults. 

6. The Answer or Remonstrance to the 

King Based on Wentworth's Suggestion, May 5.(17) 

Your loyal and obedient subjects, the Commons now assembled in Parliament, by several messages from your Majesty, and especially by that your declaration delivered by the lord keeper before both Houses, have to their exceeding joy and comfort received many ample expressions of your princely care and tender affections toward them, with a gracious promise and assurance that your Majesty will govern according to the laws of this realm. . . ...

True it is they cannot but remember the public trust for which they are accountable to present and future times; and their desires are that your Majesty's goodness might in fruit and memory be the blessing and joy of posterity.

They say also that of late there has been public violation of the laws and the subjects' liberties by some of your Majesty's ministers, and thence conceive that no less than a public remedy will raise the dejected hearts of your loving subjects to a cheerful supply of your Majesty, or make them receive content in the proceedings of this House. 

From these considerations they most humbly beg your Majesty's leave to lay hold of that gracious offer of yours which gave them assurance that if they thought fit to secure themselves in their rights and liberties by way of bill or otherwise, so it might be provided with due respect to God's honor and the public good, you would be graciously pleased to give way unto it. 

The way how to accomplish these their humble desires is now in serious consideration with them; wherein they humbly assure your Majesty they will neither lose time nor seek anything of your 

Majesty but that they hope may be fit for dutiful and loyal subjects to ask, and for a gracious and just King to grant. 

7. Answer of the King to the Remonstrance, Delivered by the Lord Keeper, May 5. (18) 

Mr. Speaker, and you gentlemen of the House of Commons, his Majesty has commanded me to tell you, that he expected an answer by your actions, and not delay by discourse. 

Yet to show clearly the sincerity of his Majesty's intentions, he is content that a bill be drawn for a confirmation of Magna Carta, and the other six statutes insisted upon for the subjects' liberties, if you shall choose that as the best way, but so as it may be without additions, paraphrases, or explanations. . . . Lastly I am commanded to tell you that his Majesty's pleasure is, that without further replies or messages, or other unnecessary delays, you do what you mean to do speedily, remembering the last message that Secretary Coke brought you in point of time; his Majesty always intending to perform his promise to his power.

8. Debate on the Lord Keeper's Speech, 

May 6. (19)

Mr. Alford: We are in a great strait. . . . To go by bill with these limitations I like it not; for to go on thus barely what will the subject be the better; and yet we give our money, and decline this robs the statutes. Second by petition. These messages and these proceedings have not been done in a parliamentary fashion; and that is the way to err. I propound (according to the ancient course) I would reduce these messages into petitions of Parliament, and then the King according to ancient fashion answers the King will have it done no more so. Add to that the billeting of soldiers; keeping of the seas. Then because these 

Parliament rolls are not published, I would have all these entered into the preamble of the Act of 

Subsidy. . . . 

Mr. Littleton: I am so far from believing we shall have benefit by this confirmation that I am confident we shall lose by it. You know what we have resolved; from which I know no reason in point of law to recede a tittle. . . . 

Sir Nathaniel Rich: For confirmation of the law without interpretation we have but shells and shadows for kernels and substance. 

Mr. Pym: Moved to the question whether a naked confirmation on the King's word generally given be sufficient satisfaction for us. 

Mr. Ball: That an explanation is necessary. Useful to have those laws confirmed which will be useless and senseless without explanation and this has been done when there was a breach against Magna Carta. . . . A general confirmation would do no good. . . . Proposed: that all might be done in one bill of subsidies. To have his Majesty's gracious declaration inserted; to have these laws recited in the bill; and a declaration of the particulars for billeting soldiers. This has been done 18 Ed.3. . . . ...

Mr. Pym: If we had nothing but the King's word were enough if we knew how far he meant to express that word. A comfort to us to hear the 

King. If he understood the laws, he would not err. We have a greater tie on him at his coronation in his conscience. If the King should say that he is better satisfied in the law than he was the last year and apply it to our business, I should rely upon it. But I hear not the King say that we shall have no more imprisonments for loans; nor that his name shall not be used in such like; that it shall not be pretended to be matter of state when it is not so. The Lords have a rule of conscience and religion to rule them; if they were not persuaded of the lawfulness of these commitments, I think they would not do it. I hear it not said that soldiers shall not be exempted from ordinary jurisdiction. . . . 

Sir John Coke: To say that the King's word added no strength to a law not fit to be used. 

Forbear negatives that trench upon the King. 

Mr. Pym: Expounded himself that the King's word could add no strength to his obligation by oath at his coronation.

Sir Harbottle Grimston: I rely as much upon the King's word as any, but what his minister will do I know not. 

Sir John Coke: The cause of all our griefs has been imprisonment for loans. If we petition it, he doubted not but the King would graciously express that he holds it unlawful.

Sir Edward Coke: To set us into a parliamentary way, which we are out of yet. First to the point of trust; second to the point of confirmation.

For any man not to rely and trust the King, it is all the confidence we have under God, Whose lieutenant he is. Were general words ever a satisfaction to particular grievances? . . . Did ever 

Parliament rely upon messages? Nay, they ever put up a petition of right, and the Lords joined. with them. Liked not to put the King's messages into the bill of subsidy; for then future kings may say, you trusted such a king, why not me. Concluded: when the King has done his gracious messages, that we go to the Lords for a petition of right. For this matter of trust, I would trust the King in a parliamentary way, because we are parliamentary men. . . 

Sir Francis Seymour: That we may know in what to trust his Majesty to go to him ourselves with the Upper House with a petition of right, therein to declare our right. What trust is reposed in us for the commonwealth, to waive that, is to do the King ill service. . 

Mr. Glanville: My opinion with Sir Edward 

Coke's motion. . . . Moved that we may votc that these instructions for loans were against law. To vote this and then petition of right as the manner and truth is. A committee to pen a petition to present to the King. 

Ordered by question: that the way and manner of proceeding concerning our liberties shall be by a petition of right, and that in a parliamentary way.

B. 

THE ATTEMPT TO WIN THE LORDS 

Once the decision to proceed by petition had been reached, the Commons lost no time. 

On May 8 the petition had two readings in the House and on May 9 it was sent to the Lords. The Lords had shown greater sympathy for the protection of the King's prerogative and quite naturally Charles relied on them to help him check the Commons. The debates in the Upper House printed here are taken from Notes of Debates in the House of Lords. It was customary for the clerk in the Lords to take notes, and from these and the documents handed to him he made a preliminary draft of the Journal. This was corrected by a committee of Lords and finally inscribed on parchment. In this period Henry Elsing was the clerk, and he was assisted by his son and one other. 

1. Debate in the Lords on the Petition, May 

9. (20) 

Pembroke: Concurs with the petition. Moved to sweeten the manner, not to lie down the particulars so at large. . .

Dorset: Words not to destroy matter. (1) The first part read touching the statutes recited. (2) 

The commissions for loans etc. read. Much debated whether this particular shall be omitted or retained. Some propounded to refer this to a committee. To consider (1) how this particular may be retained, but yet so as they may be presented to the King without offense or distaste to his Majesty. (2) How to proceed that the Commons may agree therein also, by conference, etc. 

Others, that the particulars may be taken away.

Others to leave it to the committee, and not to conclude that the committee shall not omit the particulars and only put them into better words.

Lord Saye and Sele: Objected. It will appear to posterity that such commissions, etc. and such particulars were done against the laws, for they are recorded. Therefore it is necessary to express these particulars, otherwise it may be said, no exceptions were taken against them, and so they remain for precedents to posterity to be used again.

All agreed the conclusion of the petition to be good. 

Dorset: To have such particulars wholly omitted as may distaste the King.

Some to have the particulars read, and to agree which shall stand, and which shall be left to the committee to consider of. . . . ... 

Pembroke: As many of the particulars to stand as may stand. None to be omitted but such as will distaste the King. 

Buckingham: Give a latitude to the committee herein. 

2. The King's Letter to the House of Lords, 

May 12. (21)

We, being desirous of nothing more than the advancement of the peace and prosperity of our people, have given leave to free debate upon the highest points of our prerogative royal, which in the time of our predecessors, kings and queens of this realm, were ever restrained as matters that they would not have discussed; and in other things we have been willing so far to descend to the desires of our good subjects, as might fully satisfy all moderate minds, and free them from all just fears and jealousies, which these messages which we have heretofore sent into the Commons' House will well demonstrate unto the world. Yet we find it still insisted upon that in no case whatsoever, should it never so nearly concern matters of state or government, we or our Privy Council have power to commit any man without the cause shown; whereas it often happens that should the cause be shown, the service itself would thereby be destroyed and defeated, and the cause alleged must be such as may be determined by our judges of our courts at Westminster, in a legal and ordinary way of justice, whereas the causes may be such as those judges have not capacity of judicature, nor rules of law to direct and guide their judgment in cases of that transcendent nature; which happening so often, the very encroaching on that constant rule of government for so many ages within this kingdom practiced, would soon dissolve the very foundation and frame of our monarchy. Wherefore as to our Commons we made fair propositions, which might equally preserve the just liberty of the subject, so my Lords, we have thought good to let you know that without the overthrow of sovereignty we cannot suffer this power to be impeached; notwithstanding, to clear our conscience and just intentions, this we publish, that it is not in our heart, nor will we ever extend our royal power lent unto us from God, beyond the just rule of moderation, in anything which shall be contrary to our laws and customs, wherein the safety of our people shall be our only aim. And we do hereby declare our royal pleasure and resolution to be, which, God willing, we shall ever constantly continue and maintain, that neither we nor our Privy Council shall or will at any time hereafter commit or command to prison, or otherwise restrain the persons of any for not

lending money to us, nor for any cause which in our conscience does not concern the public good and safety of us and our people, we will not be drawn to pretend any cause wherein our judgment and conscience is not satisfied with. Base thoughts we hope no man can imagine will fall into our royal breast; and that in all cases of this nature which shall hereafter happen, we shall upon the humble petition of the party or address of our judges unto us readily and really express the true cause of their commitment or restraint so soon as with conveniency and safety the same is fit to be disclosed and expressed. And that in all causes criminal of ordinary jurisdiction, our judges shall proceed to the deliverance or bailment of the prisoner according to the known and ordinary rules of the laws of this land and according to the statute of Magna Carta and those other six statutes insisted upon, which we do take knowledge stand in full force and which we intend not to abrogate and weaken against the true intention thereof. This we have thought fit to signify, the rather to shorten any long debate upon this great question, the season of the year being so far advanced and our great occasions of state not lending many more days for longer continuance of this session of Parliament. 

3. Debate in the Lords on the King's Letter. (22) 

May 12

President of the Council [the Earl of Manchester]: A glass of the King's heart. No debate, but a conference with the Commons to conclude somewhat...

Devon: To acquaint the Commons that we had considered of their petition, etc., this day to debate one point of it, received this letter, a conference. ...

Bristol: To show the Commons how far we have proceeded. And, that we having appointed to debate this matter this morning; we received this letter from the King, which we thought good to communicate unto them. .. ... 

Pembroke: We to persuade the Commons that at this time, considering the times, they would bring their petition within the compass of this letter for this session. . . .

Clare: Our endeavors to be only persuasive, not conclusive or exclusive, but only by way of persuasion, without prejudice either to the petition or proposition. 

May 14 

Buckingham: Yesterday appointed to move the

Commons to make their petition according to the King's letter. To prepare our reasons against our meeting with the Commons. And the lord steward to deliver what he has drawn. 

Bishop of Exeter: The petition of the Commons incompatible with the King's prerogative. To propound to the Commons whether they had any intent to diminish the prerogative of the King. 

Bristol: It was never said that the petition of the 

Commons is incompatible with the King's prerogative. Doubts not but both may be reconciled. 

The Commons demand their ancient right without addition. The King promises their immunities as free as in any of the best times. It may be so done that both may be reconciled. It was agreed on Monday last to move this moderation, etc., but without concluding the proposition or petition of the Commons. 

Report on the First Conference with the Commons

Lord Keeper [Baron Coventry]: At the begin ning they expected it from us. I delivered the substance agreed on. Sir Ed. Coke began. Expressed their joy for the correspondence. Added endeavor to continue. . . . The eyes of Christendom on us. Never doubted a good success. Questioned not the prerogative. Grounded their proceeding on records and laws. . . . Concluded that we declare the reasons of these propounded alterations. Touching the letter, thanks. . .

Found that time ran away. This no parliamentary course, this letter no answer or record. To husband time. If you will enter into the other parts of the petition, they will show good reason to satisfy us touching the petition without the alteration. . . 

Buckingham: Not only the copy of the letter, but the letter itself was shown them. Besides they said, they have voted the petition of right and will not recede from it. Then why should we confer about it any more. Considering in what manner our offer was. . . . 

Lord Keeper: To consider what is to be done.

The main point is the King's letter. (1) Conservation of time. (2) Not a parliamentary way.
