The Same to the Same 

My noble Lord. ... 

December 1, 1733

As to elections going on I find the hearts of the people to be mostly inclined to Sir Miles. I look upon it that the other party must buy a great many if they carry in any great numbers. 

I think if Mr. Wortley would set up it would be one way to secure Sir Miles, by breaking Lord 

Malton's interest in our quarter. But if Lord

Burlington stands fast, and considering who is for us that was against us the last election, it will be easy to carry two against Sir Rowland and Turner, especially by laying out a little money northward about Sedborough or thereabouts where are great numbers of freeholds, but at such a distance they will not come, unless something be given toward their charges. 

Lady Londonderry has the command of several votes at both Cudworth and at Bolton, if your Lordship would pleasure to secure them, and I will speak the freeholds. . . 

The Same to the Same 

My noble Lord, December 18, 1733

I postponed in expectation to hear some particular accounts from the north of Sir Miles's success there. Sir Miles desired we would write to him how votes stand, and we should hear from them; but no account is come, only one letter from Mr. Robinson, Lord Thanet's steward, who writes to Mr. Fenton to take care of Boulsterston votes, and further says that without boasting with them there are forty to one for Sir Miles.

We increase our votes here upon which we have lately had a very sufficient proof by Lord Malton's making a countermarch upon us at Sheffield which was done by the advice of Mr. Shore &c., who told Lord Malton that if another treat was made at Sheffield those votes Sir Miles had got would come over to his Lordship again; so on 

Wednesday last they came to Sheffield to treat

with wine. And in answer to this there is a gent. that lives near Sheffield whose name is Bampford, of estate about £800 per annum, not married, about 23 years of age, one of Samuel Fleming's sons is his steward, who espouses Sir Miles's interest; I have been with him at several places. So 

Mr. Bampford hearing of Lord Malton's design went to Sheffield that day, and likewise sent for me to meet him, but I was gone to Barnsley to end the affair of Fenton and Morton which I did. 

But I went the next morning to Sheffield to see how matters stood, where I found Mr. Bampford who had been treating Sir Miles's men with ale only, and their numbers had increased five for Sir Miles, who all sign a paper to stand fast and true, so that we hope to have a balance against their molten images; we do very well and much better than could be expected. Sir Tho. Saunderson, if he gives Sir Miles his interest he will cramp Lord

Malton on that side. I can't find Lord Malton's interest is anything like the last time; I think half will not be carried in by him as was then. 

Lord Malton's servant, who went to treat this time at Sheffield, told Lord Malton that the money would be spent in vain which proves so. 

We have not been at Rotheram yet, only Mr. 

Bampford and I is to go. 

I humbly conceive by your Lordship's letter that as to some money toward managing the election that I leveled particularly at your Lordship. 

I meant the whole body at a general meeting, which should be as soon as could be. Mr. Wortley bore Mr. Travis' charges and mine and furnished me with some money to spend at some other places; those on the place are always actors. . .

I don't think what has been spent is anything considerable by any that has attended Sir Miles. 

I believe Bampford has spent as much as any. 

Lady Winn brings everything about this election up to a quarrel. Mr. Matthew Wentworth, who designs to stand for the register office, went to ask 

Sir Rowland to give him leave to stand neuter, which Lady Winn resented so much that when 

Mr. Matt. Wentworth was going away she sent a servant after him to desire him to come no more there, which has displeased all Matt. Wentworth's friends. Lady Winn was ridiculing a gentlewoman in York, and the lady was present unknown to

Lady Winn; but the gentlewoman fell upon her ladyship so warmly that Lady Winn made her exit. 

These things do Sir Rowland harm. Sir Rowland told Justice Norton that he would have the election or it should cost him dear, upon which Norton said, "Take notice, gentlemen, a man that will buy his country will sell it, so I hope no wise person give Sir Rowland his vote, and I now tell 

Sir Rowland I will make all the interest I can for Sir Miles."

I tell people Geneva [a popular name for gin] is a dangerous liquor, and Sir Rowland was educated there. I do whatever I can. .. I hear for truth that there are several gent. that are upon 

Sir Rowland's side who say that they will have 

Sir Rowland swore before they give their votes that he will not vote for any excise. Sir Tho. 

Saunderson has 96 votes in Tickhill which Lord 

Malton had the last time. 

Richard Wardman to the Earl of Strafford 

Wentworth Castle, March 12, 1734 

My Lord, ... 

As this day is Sunday I galloped over to Wakefield to see what time Mr. Fox and Mr. Wentworth voters was to meet, and the day; so it is set out for next Wednesday morning at six o'clock; and I called upon Mr. Wentworth of Woolley in my way home, and he told me the same. And we are to join Mr. Wortley and Mr. Travis with their company at Tadcaster the same day, and so go all together in to the city of York; which I hope will be the greatest number of men and a greater show than the ribbon and black coats can make. . . . Mr. Phipps we know him and so does all mankind that ever see him, and his great talent is of bragging and telling of lies so that nobody minds him, nor, if your Lordship will believe me, he is not much taken notice of by nobody; but I think your Lordship not putting him into no power he will be out of temper, for he did expect to have seen your Lordship in Yorkshire, for I always told him that I expected your 

Lordship every day. As to horses for the voters, we must let them that wants have some from our tenants, for Mr. Wortley has got one hundred horses off his tenants and other people and gives twelve pence a day for them, so I must get one of some of our tenants for old Rook. 

Mr. Wentworth of Woolley has sent seventy pounds to help Mr. Bampford with his men, and they want to know what Mr. Wortley will do, for he has not declared his mind yet. 

My Lord, The Same to the Same 

Wentworth Castle, April 20, 1734 

I received your Lordship's letter of the 16th.

As there will be a meeting of a great many gentlemen at York the 26th to consider how to bring in their men at proper times, and to consult with Sir Miles to do everything for his interest, and with all to save their money; so till that day is over we can't judge the time or day our country men must go into York. I was sent for to Silkson yesterday by Mr. Fenton and Mr. Walker to give a small treat to some freeholders and we spent five shillings apiece, and Mr. Fenton thinks that

if we had a meeting at Barnsley before Lord Malton comes down, that with spending a guinea or two your Lordship might spirit them up again; for since the post office is not got, my 

Lord Malton is not much looked upon amongst them, but they are all riding about and do not leave a stone unturned, for we do think here that their hearts fail them, and if due care be taken of Sir Miles's men, Sir Rowland must lose it. Your Lordship and Mr. Wortley has been expected very much in Yorkshire about this election. If Mr. Wortley had known of the meeting at York very likely he would have gone; if he does not come down our interest about Sheffield will sink, for Mr. Bampford is not able to support the charge, and what advice to give your Lordship about spending your money I am not wise enough to judge; but a little at Barnsley and at Wakefield would look well, and the world would see your Lordship did do great things and stir about. It is thought Mr. Spencer does not spend his money freely nor does not take much pains; and indeed if your Lordship do join with 

Mr. Wortley they will expect you to join your purse with him, for that is the chief thing our county gentlemen wants, your Lordship and Mr. 

Wortley to be at the most expense. If your Lordship would have me go over to York, or Mr. 

Travis, perhaps they will be bringing one in for such and such towns in the wapentakes [divisions of a county] to take care of the men belonging to those places; but I will not pretend anything without your Lordship's orders. 

My Lord, The Same to the Same 

Wentworth Castle, May 5, 1734 

I received your Lordship's letter dated the 2nd instant, and a whole sheet of paper pays no more post than half a sheet, so I hope to fill this sheet before I have done writing. Every letter I have from your Lordship costs seven pence. The first thing I shall begin with is-elections. Last Thursday we had a great meeting at Barnsley, the great 

Mr. Wortley, Mr. Wentworth of Woolley, and some gentlemen from Sheffield and Darfield. Mr.

Wentworth sent for me and Mr. Travis and we went all over the town of Barnsley, and I hope we got the better half of the voters. We had a good dinner and every one paid their shares and then parted, and tomorrow Mr. Wortley and Mr. 

Wentworth go to Sheffield, and laid their commands of Mr. Travis and me to meet them there. 

So Mr. Travis and I have considered that he shall go and I stay at home, for it's of a Monday and a good excuse for me, it being our sale day in the woods.

This time of election will soon be here, and I cannot write to your Lordship above once or twice before it begins, and should be glad to have your orders about the tenants and other people that is for your Lordship's interest. Abraham 

Rock, he will want a horse, and two more at Barnsley that will want horses. It will be of great expense if your Lordship was to treat those people yourself and yet more I doubt if you was to make a purse with Mr. Wortley or Mr. Wentworth. Mr. Travis will go with all your tenants and friends about Wentworth Castle and Barnsley at the time when Mr. Wortley and Mr. Wentworth goes, and that will be of the fifteenth instant; and I believe that very day all Wakefield that is for Sir Miles goes. There is an old man they call Johnson, your Lordship's tenant, that lives at Wakefield, he will want a horse to York; or else I think they are all rich enough at Wakefield to bear their own expenses. Mr. Travis I doubt will want money, but he is modest and does not say anything; I am afraid his tenant does but pay him badly. We both appear for your Lordship, and is as sparing and as careful as we can, and what orders your Lordship gives us we shall take care not to exceed. 

Yesterday after the other parties had heard so many gentlemen had been for Sir Miles, came Sir Rowland Winn and all his crew of people to Barnsley, and a great dinner at Tom Hackworth's, but we had ours at your Lordship's inn at Roper's; but we had a great deal of better gentlemen, but they was more freer of their money, and spent a great deal more money than we did; and I doubt got one or two of our men that had promised us. Mr. Wortley takes a great deal of pains about this affair, and this day a great many gentlemen is to dine with him at the 

Lodge. Just now Mr. Wentworth of Woolley called here to know how your Lordship did, and with his humble service to your Lordship. So he is gone to dine at Mr. Wortley's; and so goes to 

Sheffield tomorrow to make what interest they can for Sir Miles; but I doubt my Lord Malton's purse strings open more easily than theirs will do, and he has sent and been at Sheffield before them, for he does not spare his money, and I think he will bring in Sir Rowland at last, for it is thought they begin to get men of us now-so much for elections. 

George Phipps to the Earl of Strafford 

My noble Lord, May 6, 1734

Mr. Wortley is very hot for Sir Miles and has not rested one day but Saturday last. On Thursday we went to Barnsley and was met by Mr. 

Wentworth of Woolley, Mr. Nevile of Chevett,

Mr. Beamont of Darton, Mr. Fenton, and several

others, and we had great success. Sir Rowland came to Barnsley on Saturday, upon which a great part of the voters left the town. On Friday we went into Handsworth parish and some adjacent towns. Mr. Bampford attended, Mr. Stacy of 

Balyfield, Mr. Williams and several others. This parish joins Eckington parish where Mr. Griffith lives and pretends great interest there; but we find ours much superior for Sir Miles. This day we are at Sheffield with Mr. Wentworth and the same gentlemen who dined with Mr. Wortley yesterday; with a further addition of gentlemen, Mr. Wrightson and others, we shall run them hard; but not without hopes of carrying a majority. But where we go next it will be considered of this night.

There has been a large subscription at York, and some of the money sent to Mr. Bampford, for a great part of the poorer sort must have horses sent, &c. or they can't go.

Mr. Wrightson tells me than an express is just come in to Mr. Nevile to acquaint him that Sir 

William Milner has declined the poll at York, so Sir John Kaye must be chosen with Mr. Thompson. 

The gentleman wishes that your Lordship's affairs would allow your Lordship so much time as to take a step into Yorkshire before the election. 'Tis supposed that either Turner or Winn will give up before the election. But I take this to be only grounded upon Milner's giving up at 

York. Lord Malton went to York yesterday to meet gentlemen upon Turner's and Winn's account to settle the time of their men's coming into York. I find by reports in the country that person is afraid of being mobbed; he has put all his own servants into new liveries, and the old ones he has put upon farmers' sons, so he is double manned. Sheffield mob huzza'd Mr. Jessop out of the town last night, "Sir Miles forever and no excise," but could not quiet them [sic] but followed to the end of the town. I am glad to hear Mr. Connolly is chosen and that Northampton election went so well.

My Lord, The Same to the Same 

York, May 22, 1734

Never was such an election as this, for we cannot make an end of it I doubt this day. We have been night and day a-riding for voters, and just now we have got the better of them; and the numbers of voters stands thus: 

Sir Miles Stapleton is 

Wortley is 

Winn is 

Turner is 7899 5901 7702 7877 So it certainly will be Sir Miles and Turner which all the world of our side will be very well pleased. They have just now shut up their books, but it is supposed that the other side will have a scrutiny and are very hot upon it, but Mr. Wortley stands to Sir Miles and backs him out bravely; but what the consequences will be at last I cannot tell at present, for all the gentlemen that is 

Sir Miles's friends is desired to stay by him to the last pinch and indeed, everybody that is Sir Miles's friends has been very active, for it has been the hottest election that ever was in England.

Your Lordship's interest and Mr. Wortley has spoiled my Lord Malton, that he could not nor did not bring in by a great number they expected [sic], which I believe has been a great grief to my Lord Malton and Lady Malton, and it is said that Sir Rowland Winn's lady frets very much now. My Lord Bruce is in the town, Mr.

Duncome, Mr. Hazelbee [Aislabie], Mr. Went worth of Woolley, and twenty more I do not know, who does not spare money nor horse; as likewise on the other side my Lord Malton has taken as much pains and come every day to the grand jury room, but this day he has not com'd, for he feared all was over.

The Rev. David Travis to the Earl of Strafford 

My Lord, Barke, May 24, 1734

I would have wrote to your Lordship from York the last post, could I have given an account so exact as I could have wished for. The books were closed on Tuesday last in the evening, but with much difficulty, and proclamation was made by agreement of the candidates to meet the morning following by 9 o'clock; which accordingly they did and held their conferences till about 

6 in the evening. Sir Rowland strenuously insisted upon a scrutiny, and Sir Miles and Mr. 

Wortley insisted upon £10,000 bond as a security that Sir Rowland should defray all expenses that might attend it. Warm disputes arose amongst them, but nothing brought to a final determination. At last it was unanimously agreed upon that the candidates should meet upon the 30th instant, in order to make a final decision, and proclamation was made accordingly, and the high sheriff immediately declared that Sir Miles had a majority of voices, as your Lordship may perceive by the following account-for Sir Miles 7899; 

Mr. Turner 7877; Sir Rowland Winn 7702; Mr. 

Wortley 5901.

Mr. Wortley has done singular service to the cause; and indeed all gentlemen in the interest of their respective candidates have excited their best endeavors. Messengers were continually sent into every quarter who brought the halt and the blind in coaches, chairs, and wagons. Mr. Wortley, my Lord, insinuates as if there would be no scrutiny, and that Sir Miles must indisputably be a sitting member, which is the sincere wish of all true patriots and particularly of your Lordship's most humble chaplain.

Sir Miles was the only candidate that was chaired. 

Richard Wardman to the Earl of Strafford 

Wentworth Castle, May 24, 1734 

My Lord, I got home last Wednesday night, God be thanked, and am alive and my poor mare, I doubt I have almost killed her; and two horses we borrowed, one of John Crawshaw, one of

Tomey Walker, and they have broke both their backs and I doubt will both die. Sir Miles has had the honor of being the very first man chose at this great election, and was carried in the chair about York. He outpolled Mr. Turner 17 men and Sir Rowland 109 men, which is a very great affliction to my Lord Malton, and Sir Rowland wants to have a scrutiny; but I hope they will consider better of it and will let it end with nine nights' wonder. When their hot blood is

cooled once they will consider that they will be in the wrong, or at least will consider that money will grow cost [sic].

My charges will come to about four or five pounds, and if these two horses die it will make the journey so much dearer. I cannot tell what

Mr. Travis has spent, but he has lost his horse, he was stole, I believe, out of the stable the first night, and I left him at York in a sad fret. There was three horses killed or died one night at York.

Mr. Wortley's tenants has two horses by us that is almost dead, but this is owing to carelessness. 

I lent two of your Lordship's old horses, and sent them to grass at Streethouses, where they was well taken care of, and is no worse at all. 

I have found your Lordship's letter dated the 

14th instant, and you mention that if Sir Miles loses the election you will be railed at, and if he carries it your Lordship expects no great thanks; but I cannot think no such thing, for Sir Miles was pleased to see us, both Mr. Travis and me, and I am sure I took as much pains as any man, and rid to Wakefield all night and fetched up all the old men I could get; and indeed so did everybody that was concerned, and if we had not been so very active as we were we had lost the day. Mr. Phipps he hopped about and told everybody Mr. Wortley would come in before Sir Rowland; and I will do him justice that if anybody asked what number your Lordship sent in, he cracked and lied well enough, and so did Mr. 

Travis, so that nobody did know how many or how few we had. I cannot say but your Lordship will come pretty well off, and if you had joined any of them, more money had gone, and would not have looked no better than what your Lordship did by sending Travis and me; and [since] we have got in Sir Miles there no danger but he will return his thanks to everybody at his proper time, and so farewell elections. .

The Rev. David Travis to the Earl of Strafford Barke, June 1, 1734 

My Lord, On Wednesday last I accompanied Sir John 

Bland and Mr. Wentworth of Woolley to York.

There was really a very great appearance of gentlemen in the interest of Sir Miles Stapleton. The day following the sheriff publicly declared the adjournment unnecessary, and that it was occasioned by bad advice, but had since obtained the best counsel, and that he thought himself obliged in honor as well as duty to return Sir Miles Stapleton and Mr. Turner. Upon which declaration Sir Rowland Winn immediately and indeed very abruptly left the court. Mr. Turner did not appear. Sir Miles's success is certainly to be attributed to Mr. Wortley as acting in conjunction with him. Mr. Wortley is vastly caressed by the gentlemen. My Lord Malton has been imposed upon by his agents; his lordship was made to believe that he would have 1500 voters, but the number did not answer the calculation. His lordship had only about 400. 

George Phipps to the Earl of Strafford 

My noble Lord, June 11, 1734

Mr. Wortley went from York to Newcastle, and he is not returned, but I expect him in a week or less. Sir Miles was at Leeds races, and was upon a scaffold, and gentlemen crowding upon it the scaffold shot an end, but going gradually down no person was hurt except two men that was below.

Lord Malton went to Malton, and his Lady, on Friday after the poll ended, and returned on 

Thursday morning, when the sheriff declared Sir 

Miles and Turner. I think Lord Malton got home the first inst., or night before; but I think 

Lady Malton never stopped in York in their way from Malton; at least if she did, she never appeared, that I could see; as I wrote before, Lord 

Malton was in town but never appeared at the windows as usual in the great room at the George Inn. If Rowland and Turner had carried their point there was to have been fine balls, and venison to be sent from Woodhouse; and then have took a tour to Scarborough. There was one or two of their creatures had patched up little equipages for that purpose, but we spoiled their dancing, &c. and at last Sir Rowland or Lord Malton, or both are to pay the piper without dancing, for as I am told, and I am satisfied 'tis so, they agreed to pay Mr. Turner all the expense he should be at if in case Turner would join Sir

Rowland. I take that to be the chief motive of 

Turner joining Sir Rowland.

Lord Malton, I am told for certain by his workman, that as soon as he got home turned off all his workmen except Marke Smith, and a few of other sorts of workmen, who are finishing the bargains. We have a neighbor's daughter, who 

Lady Malton turned away last Thursday; the girl says that another servant informed Lady Malton that she joined in the cry at York (a Stapleton forever), and the girl said when she went out of the house she said to one of the servants, now she would cry "Stapleton forever." The girl says that Lady Malton bought a fine suit of clothes but, losing the election, the clothes was never unpacked and her ladyship's Scarborough journey was put off. The girl says that for some time past her ladyship has pleased herself with the thoughts of a petition being lodged next sessions; but such a thing would make Lord Malton more ridiculous and hated than he is. The girl I

spoke of was at Malton with Lady Malton, and what vexed her ladyship very much was the mob all the road to Malton and those voters which had been at York affronted them all the way "Down with the Rump, no bull beef, a Stapleton and Wortley forever." "Tis said that Mr. Westby of Ranfield left Lord Malton at York upon some words; Lord Malton was so il vexed that he stuck at nothing, so Mr. Westby did not altogether like his going on, upon which spoke his opinion which Lord Malton did not like, so parted in a civil way as 'tis said. Mr. Griffith has complained against the housekeeper and the steward at Woodhouse for not treating the freeholds as they should have done; so they both are C. in disgrace. They say Lord Malton is very much out of temper and sour. Sir William Rooke is gone mad upon this election; Mr. Witton is very much disordered; one Doctor Lee of Divinity of 

Halifax is disordered; and Col. Foley behaved himself very oddly. They are like people just awakened from a dream, they can scarce believe the election is lost, they made themselves so sure of it. Lord Malton is very much vexed at bonfires which are made at every little town round about; never such bonfires and rejoicing I never see upon any occasion, and people gives money to drink. 'Tis reported Turner is dead, but I can't affirm it; but, if so, Mr. Wortley will outpoll Sir 

Rowland 1000 men.

THE CORRESPONDENCE OF THE EARL OF CARLISLE 

Charles Howard (1669-1738), third Earl of Carlisle, came of an old Cumberland family. 

Before he succeeded to his earldom in 1692 he had been M.P. (Whig) for Morpeth and he subsequently held many places in the court and in the government, being, at various times, a gentleman of the bedchamber, deputy earl marshal, privy councilor, and first lord of the Treasury. In 1733, however, his only office was that of "Master of the Harriers and 

Foxhounds," a post which, as a keen sportsman, he thoroughly enjoyed. The following letters, written to the earl, are preserved at Castle Howard and have been printed by the 

Historical Manuscripts Commission. (3) The Archbishop of York to the Earl of Carlisle 

Downing Street, November 3, 1733

I shall serve Sir Rowland Winn to the utmost of my power. Of any other person I shall be silent till I hear what the York meeting of 

Wednesday last will have produced; and shall hope that our friends in the country will thereupon come to some such proper resolution as 

Mr. Turner's behavior shall suggest. ...

Sir Thomas Robinson to the Earl of Carlisle 

Albermarle Street, December 24, 1733

The last time I was at Chiswick I had a good deal of talk with Lord B[urlington] about our county contest. He says he is not engaged any way, and is still entirely master of his interest; commended the matter my kinsman writ to him, and said Sir R[owlan]d was a very indifferent one. He talks of going soon into Yorkshire, and in my opinion, if he stirs in the election, 'twill be for the former. He has quite quitted London, sent for all his pictures from Burlington House, and is making very great and beautiful additions to 

Chiswick. . . . 

The Tories are exceeding angry with Mr. Turner, and say they should not have made an opposition but by his giving the strongest hints he would not stand, or at least not join with Sir R[owland]. I find the great ones here are full as angry with him, and wish we had pinned him to his first declaration, when he at first declared he would not stand, and seem very unwilling he should come again into Parliament. A few months will now soon bring us to the field of battle, and I believe the struggle will be as warmly maintained on both sides as ever was known in the memory of man; and I think it demonstrable the loss [result?] of the ensuing elections will not only be the entire loss of the 

Whig interest, but no one knows what may be the farther fatal consequence of it. . . .

Colonel Charles Howard to the Earl of Carlisle January 24, [1734] Mr. Turner desired me to acquaint you [that] 

Mr. Lonsdale, attorney at Bernard Castle, and agent for the Duke of Devonshire and you, has received no directions from you; that Mr. Bowes is very zealous in making interest against him in that part of the country; and that this person is very well inclined to him, but only waits for orders from your Lordship. I told him I dare answer any agent of yours have [sic] had notice before this, but that I would send you word.

He [Mr. Turner] divided with us yesterday in an address that was moved to be presented to the King, to lay before the House letters writ to the courts of France and Spain at the time of the making of the Treaty of Seville, which was debated for two hours. Upon the division, for the question, 105; against it, 195.

D.

NEWSPAPERS AND BALLADS 

Thomas Lashley was apparently a tradesman in York, for in the preface of his little book, the York Miscellany, he speaks of his shop in Upper Ouse Gate. He wrote several ballads to promote the election of Stapleton and Kaye, and he collected these, along with other ballads and newspaper accounts of the campaign, into the York Miscellany which he published in 1734. He stated that his purpose was to present both sides, but his own sympathies were clearly revealed. (4) 

The York Courant, Dec. 4, 1733

Being informed by letters from several parts of the country that it has been industriously reported that I had promised to join the late Sir 

John Stapleton, I do hereby declare that report to be utterly groundless, and that I heartily choose to offer my services as a candidate at the ensuing election in conjunction with Sir Rowland Winn to the gentlemen, clergy, and freeholders of this county; and shall always gratefully acknowledge the favor of their votes and interest.

CHO. TURNER 

The York Courant, March 19, 1734 

We hear that on Saturday, the second instant, Sir Miles Stapleton, Bart., one of the candidates for this county, attended by several persons of distinction, in his way to Skipton in Craven was met by a great number of gentlemen, clergy, and freeholders, who conducted him to town where he was received with ringing of bells, drums, music, and all possible demonstrations of joy. 

He afterward, with all his friends, dined at Skipton Castle, the ancient seat of the right Honorable, the Earl of Thanet, where a very splendid and elegant entertainment was prepared for his reception. After dinner his Lordship's good liquor of all sorts went plentifully round when the following healths were drunk, viz. the Church and

King, the present happy establishment, the Earls of Thanet and Burlington, Lord Bruce, Sir John 

Kaye, George Fox, and Thomas Lister, esqs. Sir

Miles's behavior, the spirit and great abilities he discovered upon the occasion gave infinite pleasure and satisfaction to that great meeting of gentlemen; who, in return not only gave him the warmest and fullest assurances of all the service in their power, but also assured him that almost all the freeholders in their respective neighborhoods would appear at the election and give him single votes.

The Saint James's Evening Post, April 2 

On Friday night last the Yorkshire meeting was at Lebeck's Head, pursuant to the advertisement; and it is remarkable that it was much the greatest that has been known upon the like occasion, the number of gentlemen then present being upwards of one hundred, amongst which were several dukes, earls, and lords; the Bishops of York, Durham, and Chester appeared by their proxies.

There were also present many baronets, gentlemen, and clergy of the best fortunes and interest in that county.

Lord Malton, in a proper manner, told them the intention of that meeting was to desire their concurrence to what the gentlemen had done at a former one at York, viz. the nominating of Sir 

Rowland Winn and Mr. Turner as joint candidates for that county: his Lordship observed that they were gentlemen of unblemished characters, of known zeal, both to their King and country, and strictly adhering to the Church of England; and that their personal qualifications and fortunes rendered them capable of truly representing the county of York. His Lordship then assured the company that he would support the interest of those gentlemen totis viribus and hoped that they would concur with him therein; to which he was answered they would to a man join with him in vigorously supporting the interest of those gentlemen; so there remains no doubt but they will both be chosen. 

The London Daily Courant, May 18, Date-lined 

York, May 8

This day came on the election of members of Parliament for this city, when Sir John Kaye, Bart. and Edward Thompson, Esq. were chosen without opposition. It was observable, upon their riding round the town, the populace appeared with Sir John L. Kaye in great numbers, with oaken boughs in their hats, hallooing "No excise, no Whigs, and no," what is not to be named without a charge too great. The company of substantial and loyal citizens that went with Mr.

Thompson wore orange colored cockades and carried a flag with the motto Navigation, in memory of his great service in obtaining a bill for the improvement of their river; hallooed "Thompson, liberty, and navigation"; yet he was outdone in numbers of freemen of the lowest rank, collected together by hire or the false and scandalous in-

sinuations of two or three insignificant men, who are no ways allied to the city, but who have fomented for some months past a spirit which will certainly tend to the disadvantage of it, if not to the hazard of his Majesty's person and government.

MILES STAPLETON 

"Old England" by Thomas Lashley 

Gentlemen, let us be merry and wise 

And send up a man to oppose the excise;

I wish all the freemen may firm by him stand For the good of their country, Old England. 

We'd as good go to Poland and there close our eyes As slave here for pensioners and the excise; 

To oppose them we'll send up a man that will stand

For the good of his country, Old England. 

Now is the time, if ever we do it, If we've honor or honesty now we must show it And vote for a man that we're certain will stand For the good of his country, Old England. 

If corruption or bribery dazzle our eyes,

We ought to be plagued with the greatest excise 

Or ever prove false to the man that will stand

For the good of his country, Old England. 

In spite of their gold we'll let them all see 

That worthy Sir John first chosen will be

And we, like brave citizens firmly will stand By him and his country, Old England. 

Now let's heartily wish that Sir Miles may be chose

In spite of Bob's men and our country's foes. 

May Sir John and Sir Miles go up hand in hand

For the good of the country, Old England. 

We'll drink to their healths and wish them success, And all their endeavors may kind Heaven bless, And each loyal soul that ever will stand

For the good of his country, Old England. 

To the Freeholders of the County of York Gentlemen,

It being much to be apprehended 

That it is traitorously intended 

To sap the Protestant Succession 

And eke the Protestant profession 

And under color of a cloak 

Called Country Interest; all a joke 

With dire design and black intent 

To blow up King and Parliament;

It behooves each freeholder to join 

And guard against that vile design.

Cant words and short deceitful phrases 

Confound your intellect and amazes 

And are but plausible pretenses 

To rob you of your very senses. 

The Country Interest is this cry; 

Believe me, 'tis a groundless lie.

The interest they have most at heart Nor King nor country has a part. 

And I aver on faith and troth

It tends to disunite them both. 

Does not our constitution tell us

That King and country are such fellows 

That, being strictly tied together, No man can find out whether's whether?

Country and King are sounding words And when these two make one, affords 

Delightful music to the ear

Of each true commoner and peer. 

Part 'em, they then oppose each other 

And soon begin a mighty pother.

The body which has lost its head, Is maimed and much disfigured, So a body politic we own 

Looks full as ill without a crown. 

May a true love to Church and state

Conduct and guide you in this strait, To set aside the candidate. 

And may each voter stand as tight

As I shall in my country's right 

Who am your servant, Yorkshire Bite.

XV The War of Jenkins' Ear 

BOTH Burke and Coxe have said that Jenkins never lost his ear from the stroke of a Spanish "cutlash"; a modern historian has shown it to be likely that he did. What, however, is more important than the establishment of this truth is the decision as to the exact amount of influence it had upon producing the war which followed. Jenkins' ear may be said to typify the feelings of the English public in their broad sense. . . The question is how far did these feelings influence the declaration of war; what were the main motives of the diplomats on either side? Did the English statesmen first truckle to Spain and then to England? The great interest of such an inquiry lies in the fact that the year 1739 was a turning point of history.

The year 1739 was a turning point in English history. From the declaration of war against Spain made in the fall of that year "issued in a clear and undeviating succession the series of wars which were waged between England and France during the eighteenth century-wars in which Spain was sometimes a passive spectator, oftener an active enemy, never the friend of England. Spain's alliance with 

France produced grave complications for England in 1743, contributed to the fall of the greatest of English Ministers in 1761, and to the loss of the greatest of English colonies in 1783." (1) The decision to make war was thus fraught with immeasurable consequences for England's future.

The monarchs and ministers in whose hands the decision lay made an odd assortment of characters. The King of Spain was Philip V, the Bourbon prince over whose title to the throne the War of the Spanish Succession (1701-13) had been fought. He was an indolent hypochondriac, who in 1738-39 suffered a mild fit of insanity which caused him to sing and howl vociferously at the dinner table. Consequently the direction of Spanish affairs fell largely to his wife, the impetuous termagant Elizabeth Farnese. She burned with an intense ambition. for the members of her family and the kingdom of Spain. She had employed 

Spanish power to win principalities for her sons in Italy, and under her influence the court was filled with grandiose notions of restoring the dwindling power of the Spanish monarchy. The comparatively drab chief minister, Don Sebastian de la Quadra, though stern and stubborn, was under the domination of the willful Queen.

The English King was George II. He loved his German principality of Hanover far more than England and fancied himself as a soldier in the tradition of the Hanoverian Electors. But he quite conscientiously performed his duties as a constitutional monarch, and during the war that began in 1739 he displayed a more intelligent view of England's interests than most of his ministers. At the outbreak of the war the English prime minister was the coarse and corpulent Sir Robert Walpole. He had been in office for eighteen years, a tenure secured by his construction of an effective, if corrupt, Whig political machine, and under his benign administration England had grown secure and prosperous through years of peace.

Between the two kingdoms, whose destinies were guided by these figures, there arose serious differences in the early eighteenth century. England and Spain engaged in desultory hostilities in 1718-21 and 1727-29, and friction continued to arise out of a multitude of clashes between the nationals of the two countries. 

Among these stood out one bizarre incident, of which contemporaries took considerable notice and which has caught the imagination of historians. A certain 

Captain Jenkins claimed that in 1731 Spanish guarda costas had amputated his ear and insulted his King. So gross did this alleged outrage appear that some chroniclers of a later date have looked upon it as a major casus belli and named the war of 1739 after the captain's missing member. Other writers consider the whole incident a hoax, invented as a pretext for an unjust war; still others have asserted that the alleged incident, though true, had little or no effect upon the course of events. The factor of Jenkins' ear is perhaps a parallel to the blowing up of the Maine in 1898. The ear was gone and so was the Maine, but in each case there remain the questions of responsibility for the loss and of whether or not the loss was, or even was considered, a cause for war. 

The purpose of this Problem is to analyze the crisis that resulted in the War of Jenkins' Ear. The materials in Part I provide an insight into the basic differences between the two kingdoms. In Part II the documents offer the student an opportunity to determine why the two kingdoms went to war. [367]

A.

THE DEVELOPMENT OF THE CRISIS ANGLO-SPANISH COMMERCIAL REGULATIONS 

From the Restoration to the accession of George II Spain and England had been frequently at war. So important were their commercial relations to each kingdom, both in the new and old worlds, that the treaties concluding their recurring hostilities almost invariably contained clauses regulating Anglo-Spanish trade. Whenever commercial disputes arose between the two countries, these clauses were invoked by the diplomats seeking a solution. In this section are printed the most important articles relating to seaborne trade in general and the West Indian trade in particular. 

1. Articles of Peace, Commerce, and Alli ance between the Crowns of Great Britain and Spain, Concluded in a Treaty at Madrid, the 23rd of May in the Year of Our 

Lord God 1667. (2) 

XIV. And if any ship or ships belonging to the subjects and merchants of the one or the other, entering into bays, or in the open sea, shall be encountered by the ships of the said Kings, or of privateers their subjects; the said ships, to prevent all disorders, shall not come within cannon shot, but shall send their longboat or pinnace to the merchant ship, and only two or three men on board, to whom the master or owner shall show his passports and sea letters, according to the form which shall be inserted at the end of this treaty, whereby not only the ship's lading, but the place to which she belongs, and as well the master and owner's name, as the name of the ship may appear; by which means the quality of the ship, and her master or owner, will be sufficiently known, as also the commodities she carries, whether they be contraband or not; to the which passports and sea letters entire faith and credit shall be given, so much the rather, for that as well on the part of the King of England, as of the King of Spain, some countersigns shall be given (if it shall be found necessary) whereby their authenticalness may the better appear, and that they may not be in anywise falsified. 

XV. If any prohibited merchandise or goods shall be exported from the kingdoms, dominions, and territories of either of the said Kings, by the respective people or subjects of the one or the other, in such case the prohibited goods shall be only confiscated, and not the other goods; neither shall the delinquent incur any other punishment, except the said delinquent shall carry out from the respective kingdoms or dominions of the King of Great Britain, the proper coin, wool, or fullers earth of the said kingdoms, or shall carry out of the respective kingdoms or dominions of the said King of Spain, any gold or silver, wrought or unwrought; in either of which cases the laws of the respective countries are to take place.. ... 

XXIII. And in case that within the said ships respectively be found, by the abovesaid means, any merchandise hereunder mentioned, being of contraband, and prohibited, they shall be taken out and confiscated, before the admiralty, or other competent judges; but for this reason the ship, and the other free and allowed commodities which shall be found therein, shall in no wise be either seized or confiscated. 

2. A Treaty for the Composing of Differences, Restraining of Depredations, and

Establishing of Peace in America between the Crowns of Great Britain and Spain, Concluded at Madrid the 18th day of July in the year of our Lord 1670. (3) 

VII. All offenses, damages, losses, injuries, which the nations and people of Great Britain and Spain have at any time heretofore, upon what cause or pretext soever, suffered by each other in America, shall be expunged out of remembrance, and buried in oblivion, as if no such thing had ever passed.

Moreover, it is agreed, that the most serene King of Great Britain, his heirs and successors, shall have, hold, keep, and enjoy forever, with plenary right of sovereignty, dominion, possession, and propriety, all those lands, regions, islands, colonies, and places whatsoever, being or situated in the West Indies, or in any part of America, which the said King of Great Britain and his subjects do at present hold and possess; so as that in regard thereof, or upon any color or pretense whatsoever, nothing more may or ought to be urged, nor any question or controversy be ever moved concerning the same hereafter. 

VIII. The subjects and inhabitants, merchants, captains, masters of ships, mariners of the kingdoms, provinces, and dominions of each confederate respectively, shall abstain and forbear to sail and trade in the ports and havens which have [368]

fortifications, castles, magazines, or warehouses, and in all other places whatsoever possessed by the other party in the West Indies; to wit, the subjects of the King of Great Britain shall not sail unto, and trade in the havens and places which the Catholic King holdeth in the said Indies; nor in like manner shall the subjects of the 

King of Spain sail unto, or trade in those places which are possessed there by the King of Great 

Britain. . . .

X. It is also agreed, that in case the subjects and inhabitants of either of the confederates, with their shipping (whether public and of war, or private and of merchants) be forced at any time through stress of weather, pursuit of pirates and enemies, or other inconvenience whatsoever, for the seeking of shelter and harbor, to retreat and enter into any of the rivers, creeks, bays, havens, roads, shores, and ports belonging to the other in America, they shall be received and treated there with all humanity and kindness, and enjoy all friendly protection and help; and it shall be lawful for them to refresh and provide themselves, at reasonable and the usual rates, with victuals and all things needful, either for the sustenance of their persons, or reparation of their ships, and conveniency of their voyage; and they shall in no manner be detained or hindered from returning out of the said ports or roads, but shall remove and depart, when and whither they please, without any let or impediment.

XII. But when it shall happen, that the ships of either (as is above-mentioned) through danger of the sea, or other urgent cause, be driven into the ports and havens of the other, if they be three or four together, and may give just ground of suspicion, they shall immediately upon their arrival acquaint the governor or chief magistrate of the place with the cause of their coming, and shall stay no longer than the said governor or chief magistrate will permit, and shall be requisite for the furnishing themselves with victuals, and reparation of their ships; and they shall always take care not to carry out of their ships any goods or packs, exposing them to sale, neither shall they receive any merchandise on board, nor do anything contrary to this treaty. . . ... 

XIV. No private injury shall in any sort weaken this treaty, nor beget hatred or dissensions between the foresaid nations, but everyone shall answer for his own proper fact, and be prosecuted thereupon; neither shall one man satisfy for the offense of another by reprisals, or other such like odious proceedings, unless justice be denied, or unreasonably delayed, in which case it shall be lawful for that King, whose subject hath suffered the loss and injury, to take any course according to the rules and method of the law of nations, until reparation be made to the sufferer. 

3. The Assiento, or Contract for Allowing to the Subjects of Great Britain the Liberty of Importing Negroes into the Spanish America, Signed by the Catholic King at Madrid, the 26th day of March, 1713. (4)

I. First then to procure a mutual and reciprocal advantage to the sovereigns and subjects of both crowns, her British Majesty does offer and undertake for the persons whom she shall name and appoint [the South Sea Company], that they shall oblige and charge themselves with the bringing into the West Indies of America, belonging to his Catholic Majesty, in the space of the said thirty years, to commence on the 1st day of May, 1713, and determine on the like day, which will be in the year 1743, viz. 144,000 Negroes, Piezas de India, of both sexes and of all ages, at the rate of 4800 Negroes, Piezas de India, in each of the said 30 years, with this condition, that the persons who shall go to the West Indies to take care of the concerns of the assiento shall avoid giving any offense, for in such case they shall be prosecuted and punished in the same manner as they would have been in Spain if the like misdemeanors had been committed there. 

II. That for each Negro, Pieza de India, of the regular standard of seven quarters, not being old or defective, according to what has been practiced and established hitherto in the Indies, the assientists shall pay 33 pieces of eight (escudos) and one third of a piece of eight, in which sum shall be accounted to be and shall be comprehended all and all manner of duties . . . whatsoever of importation or regalia that now are or hereafter shall be imposed, belonging to his 

Catholic Majesty. . 

...

XXII. When the said ships [of the assientists] shall have entered into any of the ports, they are to be visited by the governor and royal officers and searched to the bottom, even to the ballast; and having landed their Negroes in whole or in part, they may at the same time land the provisions which they shall bring for their subsistence, laying them up in particular houses or magazines, having obtained leave of the ministers who had searched the said ships; to avoid by these means all opportunities of fraud or controversy; but they shall not land, import, or vend any goods or merchandise under any pretense or motive whatsoever; and if there should be any on board the ships they shall be seized as if they were found on shore, excepting only the said Negro slaves and the magazines of provisions for their subsistence, under the penalty that those who are guilty shall be severely punished and their merchandise and effects confiscated or burnt, and they shall be declared for ever incapable of having any employment in the said assiento.

XXVI. They may not bring over in any of the said ships any silver, gold, or other effects than what shall be the produce of the sale of the Negroes, nor any Spanish passengers, they being forbid to receive on board any merchandise or other effects, on account of his Catholic Majesty's subjects in those dominions, without an express license first obtained from his Catholic Majesty; and they consent that if the captains, commanders, and officers do bring any such on board without such license, they shall be declared guilty and punished as having defrauded his Majesty's customs, and transgressed against the contents of this article and the orders which his Majesty shall have been pleased to give for the execution thereof, and for the avoidings of such frauds in the ports of the Indies, so that the offenders, being convicted thereof, shall be constantly punished. 

Additional Article 

Besides the foregoing articles stipulated on behalf of the English [South Sea] Company, his Catholic Majesty, considering the losses which former assientists have sustained and upon this express condition that the said company shall not carry on, nor attempt any unlawful trade, directly nor indirectly, under any pretense whatsoever; and to manifest to her Britannic Majesty how much he desires to pleasure her, and to confirm more and more a strict and good correspondence, has been pleased, by his royal decree of the 12th of March, in this present year, to allow to the company of this assiento a ship of 500 tons yearly, during the thirty years of its continuance to trade therewith to the Indies, in which his Catholic Majesty is to partake a fourth part of the gain, as in the assiento; besides which fourth, his Catholic Majesty is to receive 5 percent out of the net gain of the other three parts which belong to England upon this express condition, that they may not sell the goods and merchandise which each of those ships shall carry, but only at the time of the fair; and if any of these ships shall arrive in the Indies before the flotas and galleons, the factors of the assiento shall be obliged to land the goods and merchandise (with which they shall be laden) and put them into warehouses that shall be locked with two keys, one of which to remain with the royal officers, and the other with the factors of the company, to the end the said goods and merchandise may be sold during the continuance of the said fair only; and they are to be free of all duties in the Indies. 

4. The Treaty of Peace, Union, Friendship, and Mutual Defense, between the Crowns of 

Great Britain, France, and Spain, Concluded at Seville on the 9th of November, 1729. (5)

IV. It having been agreed by the preliminary articles that the commerce of the English and French nations, as well in Europe as in the Indies, should be re-established on the foot of the treaties and conventions antecedent to the year 1725, and particularly that the commerce of the 

English nation in America should be exercised as heretofore; it is agreed by the present article that all necessary orders shall be dispatched on both sides, without any delay, if they have not been sent already, as well for the execution of the said treaties of commerce, as for supplying what may be wanting for the entire re-establishment of commerce on the foot of the said treaties and conventions.

V. Although it was stipulated by the preliminaries that all hostilities should cease on both sides, and that if any trouble or hostilities should happen between the subjects of the contracting parties, either in Europe, or in the Indies, the contracting powers should concur for the reparation of damages sustained by their respective subjects; and notwithstanding this, it is alleged that on the part of the subjects of his Catholic Majesty, acts of disturbance and hostilities have been continued; it is agreed by this present article that as to what relates to Europe his Catholic Majesty shall forthwith cause reparation to be made for the damages which have been suffered there since the time prescribed by the preliminaries for the cessation of hostilities; and as to what relates to America, he will likewise forthwith cause reparation to be made for the damages which shall have been suffered there since the arrival of his orders at Cartagena on the 11th day of June, 1728. And his said Catholic Majesty shall publish the most rigorous prohibitions for preventing the like violences on the part of his subjects; their Britannic and most 

Christian Majesties promising on their part, if there be like cases, to cause reparation to be made for what shall have been so done, and to give like orders for the preservation of the peace, tranquillity, and good intelligence.

VI. Commissaries shall be nominated, with sufficient powers on the part of their Britannic and Catholic Majesties, who shall assemble at the court of Spain within the space of four months after the exchange of the ratifications of the present treaty, or sooner if it can be done, to examine and decide what concerns the ships and effects taken at sea on either side to the times specified in the preceding article. The said commissaries shall likewise examine and decide, according to the treaties, the respective pretensions which relate to the abuses that are supposed to have been committed in commerce, as well in the Indies as in Europe, and all the other respective pretensions in America, founded on treaties, whether with respect to the limits or otherwise. The said commissaries shall likewise discuss and decide the pretensions which his Catholic Majesty may have, by virtue of the treaty of 1721, for the restitution

of the ships taken by the English fleet in the year 

1718. And the said commissaries, after having examined, discussed, and decided the abovesaid points and pretensions, shall make a report of their proceedings to their Britannic and Catholic B.

Majesties, who promise that within the space of six months after the making of the said report, they will cause to be executed punctually and exactly what shall have been so decided by the said commissaries.

THE GROWTH OF FRICTION 

Despite diplomatic endeavors to regulate commerce peacefully, there was almost continual friction between English traders and the Spaniards in the West Indies. The following documents indicate the growth of this friction until it reached the proportions of a major crisis in 1738. 

1. A Petition to the House of Commons, 

March 3, 1738. (6) 

Mr. Alderman Perry presented to the House a petition of divers merchants, and planters, and others, trading to, and interested in the British plantations in America, on behalf of themselves and many others, setting forth, "That application was made to this House, in the year 1728, against the many unjust seizures and depredations, that had, for several years preceding, been committed by the Spaniards in America upon his Majesty's subjects, whilst they were carrying on their fair and lawful trade in those parts: upon which application, this House came to a resolution, 'That from the peace, concluded at Utrecht in the year 1713, to this time, the British trade and navigation to and from the several British colonies in America has been greatly interrupted by the continual depredations of the Spaniards, who have seized very valuable effects and unjustly taken and made prize of great numbers of British ships and vessels in those parts, to the great loss and damage of the subjects of this kingdom and in manifest violation of the treaties subsisting between the two Crowns'; and that this House was pleased humbly to address his Majesty thereupon. "And that the Spaniards continuing their depredations on the British subjects, and no satisfaction having been obtained for those before committed, a farther application was made to this 

House, in the year 1730, complaining of the great interruptions given by the Spaniards to the trade and navigation of this kingdom, and their cruel treatment of the British subjects; and that this 

House, having again taken this matter into their consideration, and examined into the same with the utmost deliberation, came to a resolution: "That an humble address be presented to his Majesty, that he will be graciously pleased to continue his endeavors to prevent the depredations of the Spaniards for the future; to procure full satisfaction for the damages already sustained; and to secure to the British subjects the full and uninterrupted exercise of their trade and navigation to and from the British colonies in America.' 

Which address was presented to his Majesty accordingly. "And representing to the House, that the Spaniards have paid so little regard to his Majesty's most gracious endeavors, that they have continued their depredations, almost ever since the treaty of Seville, and more particularly last year have carried them to a greater height than ever; they having arbitrarily seized several ships with their effects, belonging to his Majesty's subjects, on the high seas, in the destined course of their voyages to and from the British colonies, amounting to a very considerable value. "And that the captains or masters of some of the said ships were, according to the last advices of the petitioners, and are (as the petitioners believe) at this time confined by the Spaniards in the West Indies, and the crews are now in slavery in Old Spain, where they are most inhumanly treated. "And that that cruel nation make it their practice to attack and board all British merchant ships they meet within the American seas, under pretense of searching for goods, which they deem contraband or not, according to their own arbitrary will and pleasure, contrary to the law of nations and in manifest violation of the treaties subsisting between the two Crowns. "And that by these unjust and violent proceedings of the Spaniards, the trade and navigation to and from America is rendered very unsafe and precarious; insomuch that the insurance from 

Jamaica has greatly risen on these accounts only; and that without some speedy and effectual remedy, the American trade and navigation will be (together with the revenue of the Crown arising therefrom) very much diminished, if not entirely lost. "And farther representing to the House that, although his Catholic Majesty has stipulated by the treaty of Seville and by the declaration of 

1732 relative thereunto, to cause reparation to be forthwith made to the unhappy sufferers, yet there is no instance of its having been done; so far from it, that, whilst the British subjects have

been amused with vain and fruitless hopes of satisfaction, the Spaniards have committed farther insults and depredations upon them, and still continue the same unjust practices. "And that the cedulas or orders given by the court of Spain to their governors in America are only calculated (as the petitioners by experience have great reason to apprehend) to evade giving satisfaction to the British subjects; for there has never been one of the cedulas complied with, nor any governor recalled nor punished for his disobedience, as the petitioners ever heard. "And that for any nation to assume the power of detaining or rummaging the British ships upon their lawful voyages in the American seas under pretense of searching for contraband goods, is in effect (as the petitioners conceive) claiming and exercising the sole sovereignty of those seas; and that if the Spaniards be suffered to act in this injurious manner, to insult the persons of his Majesty's subjects, or to plunder them of their property, the petitioners apprehend the same will be attended, not only with great obstruction to this valuable branch of our commerce and navigation, but also with consequences very fatal to 

Great Britain itself. "And as the measures hitherto pursued have proved ineffectual, praying the House to take the premises into their mature consideration, and provide such timely and adequate remedy for putting an end to all insults and depredations on the British subjects, as to the House shall seem meet, as well as procure such relief for the unhappy sufferers, as the nature of their case, and the justice of their cause require." 

2. Pamphleteering in 1738. The agitation of the merchants in Parliament was paralleled by pamphleteering in the country. Following are selections from three pamphlets that appeared in 1738. (7) 

Reasons for a War against Spain

As the depredations of the Spaniards are become the topic of discourse, and as the trade to America is of such importance to the kingdom, I may say, every Englishman is deeply concerned in its destiny, I thought no juncture so favorable for giving my thoughts on that subject as the present, when things seem to be drawing to a crisis, a crisis which, we have reason to believe, will rouse Britons out of their lethargy and convince the Spaniards that we are still inspired with the same sentiments of valor, resolution, and intrepidity which often led us on, to vanquish their fleets, and conquer their cities and provinces. 

The same spirit still animates us, and it may be affirmed that the nation never discovered more unanimity than at this time, to revenge their country's wrong.. ...

In order to set this in a clear light, we must first examine whether such depredations, injuries, and indignities are allowed to be just motives by the law of nations for an offensive war; and on the nicest inquiry, we may take the liberty to affirm, that all the civilians and political writers, who have wrote on the subject of war and peace are unanimous for the affirmative. . . .

Since such violences are, then, allowed to be just causes of war, it may perhaps be expected that I should exhibit some proofs of those charged upon the Spaniards. But this would be, in my opinion, as superfluous as to employ much time in proving the most notorious and self-evident truths. All Europe may be cited for a witness of our wrongs. Our ships have been taken and condemned as lawful prize in the Spanish ports, others searched, stopped, and plundered; our seamen bastinadoed, treated with the most reproachful language, and our whole nation dishonored and made a subject of scorn and ridicule to Spanish insolence.

We have employed many years in negotiating with the Spaniards upon the topic which has given occasion for writing these sheets without any fruits of our labors; and I am persuaded it must be granted that we had more reason to promise ourselves success in a war against them ten years ago than we have now. Spain was then less formidable, and Great Britain in a better understanding with her allies; to which we must add the immense losses of our merchants since that period.

It may be inferred from the same considerations that no time can be more seasonable for a war with Spain than the present, since we have the strongest motives to think every year will augment her revenues, her alliances, or territories. 

The Queen of Spain is capable of forming the greatest designs; 'tis well known she has the plan of Cardinal Alberoni before her eyes, she has lately conquered two kingdoms for her eldest son, and we may well conclude from the towering genius of that princess that she is meditating upon the conquest of others for her younger, the elder of whom, Don Philip, is eighteen years of age, and no doubt, but the Queen his mother will contract a new alliance by marrying him to a princess of some potent house.

We must likewise observe that the Spaniards are daily improving their manufactures, forming new schemes for extending their commerce, and augmenting their naval force, which, with their possession of the silver of America, will soon render them one of the most formidable nations in the world.

Since a war with that Crown will consequently become every year more impracticable, it must be allowed that no juncture can be so favorable

for Great Britain as the present to make her utmost efforts, not only to obtain satisfaction for our losses, but to establish our American commerce on such a basis as will secure it from any future attempts.

Having now endeavored to prove that we have just causes of war with Spain, and that no time can promise us more success than the present, our next inquiry will be: whether we have a force sufficient for that end.

But this, in my opinion, will not admit of much debate, since our naval power is not only superior to that of Spain, but perhaps to the whole naval forces of all Europe, as well with regard to the number of ships as the bravery and skill of our seamen.

Common Sense: Its Nature and Use 

The sentence of common sense on the Spanish affair: "It is right to take care of the South Sea Company's effects, and of the general trade to Spain, as well as of that of the West India merchants. 

It is proper, before anything is done which may put a stop to the whole Spanish trade, as well as embarrass the Turkey and other Mediterranean trades, diligently to consider the consequences.

That the power of the British nation has been exerted in the year 1718 against the Spanish, but much more justifiably so in 1735 and 1736 in the 

Portugal affair. That it is right, before we take another military satisfaction, to be able to prove to the whole world the indispensable necessity of it. 

That we ought to guard against and inquire after any assistance the Spaniards may have. That the complaints of our merchants have been heard and admitted, application made to Spain, land forces sent away, and additional ships of great force, to enforce our legal demands. That France and Holland have been treated by Spain in the same manner as Great Britain, that they have not exerted more spirit (nor so much) as our government. That considering the whole and every part of the affair, our Ministry have acted as other wise and prudent people have acted and ought to act." 

Is it not as obvious that, no sooner did the merchants wronged acquaint the King by petition with it, that not a day was lost, a committee of Council was forthwith ordered thoroughly to examine into it, who not only found most of the complaints to be just, and so reported, but a redress was immediately taken in hand, viz. five ships (besides those already there) of more than usual force for those seas were directly put into commission and equipped, and are now visibly, and in the face of the world, sailed to see that the remedy demanded of the King of Spain be had, and to oppose with force those who resist it. 

A regiment of soldiers is also gone to Carolina to prevent any insults from the Spaniards, which might be expected to disturb our trade and settlement on that side. These facts show the opinion and the intention of the King and his Council, and demonstrably prove that their sentiments are the same and their resentments much stronger than those of the losers themselves, or they would not take such vigorous and extraordinary methods to procure satisfaction for the past, and preventions against future injuries, nor is it any question between the merchants and anybody of consequence, whether they have lost, and whether they ought not to have satisfaction. . . .

And what immediately offers itself to us in this view, is the effects of the South Sea Company who have many hundred thousand pounds value in New Spain, which the Spaniards can immediately lay hold on. Is it not worth our thinking on, then, what would be the lot of these merchants, and of a vast number of tradesmen engaged with them and depending on them? And if our ministers had not as careful an eye to this, as well as to the others, they would soon be justly told they wanted circumspection. Besides, might not too hasty a vengeance bring on a general war with Spain, before we are sufficiently prepared for it? 

Would not our Turkey and every other branch of the Mediterranean trade be immediately under very great difficulties, and a stop put at once to the whole Spanish trade, as well in Europe as in America? And might we not reasonably expect that a neighboring power would take the advantage to serve the Spaniards with most of those commodities they now have from us, and thereby get such a considerable part of this valuable trade out of our hands as we could scarce ever recover? And if the French did this, it would not be more dishonest in them than, in common trade, if a shopkeeper had a very good constant customer, by whom he made great profit every year, and they should fall out, would it be called dishonesty for a neighbor of the same business to endeavor to serve him? All these things the vigilant eye of our ministers must be constantly observing, and guarding against. . . ...

But I am so far from going to infer from hence that it is improper for our government to resent this behavior of the Spaniards, that I dare be bold to say, we shall find that ample satisfaction must be had for those ships taken in or near the Gulf of Florida, as also for any others as unjustly plundered or taken. And when we are once forced to call them to account, I am apt to think that their late demand of Georgia etc., will be one of the articles; for we shall then settle the whole account with them. And if they should depend on our being lately degenerated to such weak, indolent, and phlegmatic people, as our

daily, weekly, and monthly libelous newspapers say we are (and which, perhaps, is one of the causes of the Spaniards daring to do what they have), I say, they may at last be convinced that these libelers have misled them. And this we shall find will be the case, whenever things are ripe and we are properly prepared against all probable events; for then, and not till then, will it be consistent with right reason, that is with universal common sense.

Letter Addressed to Every Honest Man in Britain 

Notwithstanding the authors of several pamphlets lately published, as well as those of weekly and daily papers, have exerted their talents and public spirit in behalf of our plundered merchants, so inexhaustible a subject as that of the Spanish depredations will always have field. enough for a friend to Britain and her trade to glean in after them. As such, I will, without further ceremony, venture to defy all the posse of Spanish advocates together to produce any one period of time, since the Norman invasion, in which England was so affronted and insulted, and Englishmen so vilely robbed, so inhumanly abused by any single nation upon earth, as we have been these many years past by the Spaniards. ... For these reasons, sir, I shall take notice of a pamphlet now rouling in the public, which, to me, seems expressly calculated, had the author been furnished with abilities suitable to his intention, to entail disgrace, want, and slavery upon Britons, and to give victory and triumph to the Spaniards. ...

The hopeful piece I mean, is entitled Common 

Sense: Its Nature and Use. . . . This, sir, is the title of a piece, designed, as I have just said in other words, to put chains on our nobility and gentry, canvas frocks and wooden shoes on the people of Great Britain and Ireland; of a piece whose final determination, if we follow the worthy author's advice, is intended for our final destruction. But it is surprising that a man, who establishes common sense as a criterion by which to try all disputable cases in common life, should sin so egregiously against it in his title page, as to call the "Spanish depredations," the "Spanish affair." Depredations, it seems, was a word which the author did not care to meddle with; he thought it would sound harsh in the ears he was endeavoring to tickle and deceive. But I must take leave to tell him that the "Spanish depredations" are become a "British affair." For, when a man has received a box on the ear, or a kick on the bd, it is no longer the affair of the insolent giver, but ipso facto becomes the affair of the injured receiver to resent it. This I take to be our case at present; the Spaniards have been long enough boxing and kicking us about in

America; and, if there is any truth in the old proverb, that if a man does not wear a lion's skin, every ass will piss upon him; much more ought ministers to wear lions' skins, if they have no mind to see their country kicked and buffeted, and trampled into contempt by even the most contemptible of her neighbors..

Hitherto there appears nothing terrible in a war with Spain; but such another nine years' peace with her as we have lately had will sink us into contempt and ruin. The Spaniards will impute our patience and forbearance to nothing, but either to mere want of resolution in our court, or, what would be equally dangerous, to want of power to carry on a war; nay, it is to be apprehended they think so already by their insolence to us. This is an opinion out of which we must immediately beat them, and show that we neither fear them nor any pretender they may attempt to make a tool of. This will be necessary in order to prevent other powers of Europe from falling into the same frenzy. For, sir, it requires but a very little stock of politics to know that when a nation begins to dwindle in her fame, or any way to lose her reputation either in arms or trade, she finds very few friends; her neighbors are so far from desiring her alliance that they rather look upon her as a wreck out of which everyone thinks he has a right to pull plunder. But it is just the reverse with a nation that stands scrupulously upon her honor and is ever ready to return two blows for one; such a nation will always have friends, either through esteem or dread of her, and for these very reasons, were there no other, we ought to call Spain to an immediate account for all her past deeds. 

3. The Diary of the Earl of Egmont, 173638. To the friction in the Caribbean were added disputes in North America. In 1732 

James Oglethorpe founded the English Geor gia colony just north of the Spanish possessions in Florida. The difficulties which quickly arose are described in the following excerpts from the diary of the first Earl of Egmont (1683-1748), a member of the Georgia Society in London which sponsored Oglethorpe's colony. (8) 

June 16, 1736: This morning I went to the 

Georgia office . . . Mr. Lapautre in the chair, Lord Carpenter, Egmont, La Roche, and Hucks.

Many letters that arrived to us last Monday were read. They came to us enclosed from Mr. Oglethorpe and brought us very disagreeable news. 

The first was Mr. Oglethorpe's from St. Simon's 

Island, date February 15th, to the Spanish governor of Fort Augustine with offers of friendship. 

The second was from Captain Dempsy to Mr. 

Oglethorpe, dated from Augustine March 29th.

This gentleman was the bearer of the above-mentioned letter to the governor and by concert of 

Sir Robert Walpole and Mr. Geraldino, the Spanish agent at our court, accompanied Mr. Oglethorpe to Georgia, in order to assist in settling the limits between the Spanish dominions in Florida and the King of Great Britain's, which join them. In this letter he writes Mr. Oglethorpe that he arrived the 16th at Fort Augustine; that the governor received him very civilly and expressed great respect for Mr. Oglethorpe, but that he said he doubted whether friendship will subsist between his Catholic Majesty's subjects there and the King of Great Britain's, since we had settled ourselves upon his master's territories. 

He also complained that 300 of our white men, with a considerable number of Indians, had entered the province of the Uches, which belonged to his master, with the intention to build a fort there. Captain Dempsy replied he was confident 

Mr. Oglethorpe knew nothing of it, and would not have given such directions, but he would write to him upon it.

Another letter from Captain Dempsy from Augustine to Mr. Oglethorpe, date April 1st, brought him enclosed two letters from the Spanish governor, expressing great civilities. They were dated March 24th and 30th. These Mr. Ogle thorpe likewise sent us, but being wrote in Spanish we understood them not, but we gathered the sense from the substance of Captain Dempsy's letter above-mentioned, wherein he tells Mr. 

Oglethorpe that the governor had received fresh accounts that our Indians with five of the Creek nation had killed a Spaniard belonging to an outguard, and that satisfaction must be made; that he had said what he could to prevail on the governor to adjust these amicably if true, and that he replied he would send a person to Mr. 

Oglethorpe, that he told the governor things might be made easy, for Mr. Oglethorpe desired nothing more than harmony, but if that could not be compassed, Mr. Oglethorpe knew how to behave, having a sufficient strength, besides a power to draw all the militia of the province down upon occasion. N.B.-Note we observed in this letter that he said this according to Mr. 

Oglethorpe's directions, by which it seemed to us that Mr. Oglethorpe had received some instructions or powers from his Majesty at going over which were not communicated to us. He adds in this letter that when he dispatched his messenger, he heard the drum beat up for soldiers, and that the Spaniards came briskly in.

The next letter was from Oglethorpe to Dempsy, date April 10th, wherein he mentions a letter of thanks he had sent to the governor for his expressions of civility.
