You may say: Let us cease to struggle; let us leave the lands of the world to the races that cannot profit by them to the full; let us cease to compete in the markets of the world. Well, we could do it, if we were a small nation living on the produce of our own soil, and a soil so worthless that no other race envied it and sought to appropriate it. We should cease to advance; but then we should naturally give up progress as a good which comes through suffering. 

The man who tells us that he feels to all men alike, that he has no sense of kinship, that he has no patriotic sentiment, that he loves the Kaffir as he loves his brother, is probably deceiving himself. If he is not, then all we can say is that a nation of such men, or even a nation with a large minority of such men, will not stand for many generations; it cannot survive in the struggle of the nations, it cannot be a factor in the contest upon which human progress ultimately depends. 

The national spirit is not a thing to be ashamed of, as the educated man seems occasionally to hold. If that spirit be the mere excrescence of the music hall, or an ignorant assertion of superiority to the foreigner, it may be ridiculous, it may even be nationally dangerous; but if the national spirit takes the form of a strong feeling of the importance of organizing the nation as a whole, of making its social and economic conditions such that it is able to do its work in the world and meet its fellows without hesitation in the field and in the market, then it seems to me a wholly good spirit -indeed, one of the highest forms of social, that is, moral instinct. 

So far from our having too much of this spirit of patriotism, I doubt if we have anything like enough of it. We wait to improve the condition of some class of workers until they themselves cry out or even rebel against their economic condition. We do not better their state because we perceive its relation to the strength and stability of the nation as a whole. Too often it is done as the outcome of a blind class war. The coal owners, the miners, the manufacturers, the mill-hands, the landlords, the farmers, the agricultural laborers, struggle by fair means, and occasionally by foul, against each other, and, in doing so, against the nation at large, and our statesmen as a rule look on. That was the correct attitude from the standpoint of the old political economy. It is not the correct attitude from the standpoint of science; for science realizes that the nation is an organized whole, in continual struggle with its competitors. You cannot get a strong and effective nation if many of its stomachs are half fed and many of its brains untrained. We, as a nation, cannot survive in the struggle for existence if we allow class distinctions to permanently endow the brainless and to push them into posts of national responsibility. The true statesman has to limit the internal struggle of the community in order to make it stronger for the external struggle. We must reward ability, we must pay for brains, we must give larger advantage to physique; but we must not do this at a rate which renders the lot of the mediocre a wholly unhappy one. We must foster exceptional brains and physique for nation purposes; but, however useful prize cattle may be, they are not bred for their own sake, but as a step toward the improvement of the whole herd. . . .

Science is not a dogma; it has no infallible popes to pronounce authoritatively what its teaching is. I can only say how it seems to one individual scientific worker that the doctrine of ev-

Problem XVIII: Evolution and Ethics olution applies to the history of nations. My interpretation may be wrong, but of the true method I am sure: a community of men is as subject as a community of ants or as a herd of buffaloes to the laws which rule all organic nature. 

We cannot escape from them; it serves no purpose to protest at what some term their cruelty and their bloodthirstiness. . .

Mankind as a whole, like the individual man, advances through pain and suffering only. The path of progress is strewn with the wreck of nations; traces are everywhere to be seen of the hecatombs of inferior races, and of victims who found not the narrow way to the greater perfection. Yet these dead peoples are, in very truth, the steppingstones on which mankind has arisen to the higher intellectual and deeper emotional life of today.

XIX 

The Great Agricultural Depression 

FTER 1877 the price of wheat never touched 50s. again; in 1884 it dipped below 40s.; in 1894 it was at 22s., and the harvest in that year of panic sold at 19s. The grazing counties were stricken, it seemed, beyond recovery. Great wars have been less destructive of wealth than the calamity which stretched from 1879, the wettest, to 1894, the driest year in memory.

The changes which overtook Britain's economy in the years between 1870 and 1914 proved momentous in their consequences, for they combined to undermine fatally that proud position of the "workshop of the world," which Victorian England had won. It is perhaps unwise to label this a "crisis," for these changes occurred over almost half a century, along an extended front, and as a result of world-wide forces. But every branch of England's economic life-agriculture, industry, trade, and finance-in its turn suffered blows which ultimately proved irreparable, and they have combined with two world wars to reduce England to the most critical point in her history. 

The disaster which overtook British agriculture in the 1870's provides an excellent case study in miniature of the larger depression. On the one hand, this dramatic collapse of the historic leader of agricultural progress had distant beginnings back in the mid-century days of high farming. Similarly, the full explanation for the debacle must be sought in such apparently disconnected events as the railroad development in Illinois, the business activities of Cyrus McCormick, and the perfection of refrigeration techniques. Some of the reasons lay nearer to home, concealed in the prices and structure of England's agriculture during the period. 

But an England which as late as the middle of the century was nearly able to supply its own wheat in a year of good harvests and yet was importing 65 percent of its wheat supplies in the years 1880-89 had truly experienced a disaster. 

Like the larger crisis of which it formed a part, this agrarian crisis had widespread effects. The student will note for himself the social consequences of the resulting shifts in the distribution of England's population, and the eventual political implications of these changes for what Disraeli had labeled in 1843 the historic "preponderance of the landed interest" can also be discerned. And this collapse in agriculture was intimately linked from its very inception to England's industrial bid to be the "workshop of the world"; for if the latter was to flounder in the wave of exclusive tariffs which the European countries and the United States were to erect in the twenty years after 1879, England's lack of agricultural self-sufficiency would then have fatal implications.

In this Problem the student is called upon to determine for himself the causes and nature of this agricultural collapse. For this purpose he is provided primarily with some pertinent statistics, the raw materials out of which he must construct his explanation. The contemporary analysis of the disaster he will find useful as a contrast to and test of his conclusions drawn from the statistical material. 

Certain events in earlier agricultural history are vital to an understanding of the disaster of the 1870's. If her island position (which meant an absence of free frontier land) and her immense growth in population are accepted as given, certainly the two most formative factors in England's agrarian past were the enclosure movement and the repeal of the Corn Laws. The former was the process, accomplished in two great waves in the sixteenth and late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries, whereby the historic open fields and commons were consolidated into compact holdings under individual ownership and management. The human cost of this second wave (which saw one fifth of the land of England enclosed between 1761 and 1845) has been much in dispute, but its over-all significance is clear. Not only was British agriculture reorganized so that it could keep pace with the revolution in industry, but also in the process the gentry turned farming into a business where enlightened practice and increasingly scientific methods made England the model for the world. 

The enclosure movement, in that it hastened the tendency toward large farms and the dispossession of the small proprietors and the agricultural laborers, also [ 465 ] alonies Fration?

stamped a unique pattern on the structure of British rural life. In the words of the most eminent historian of nineteenth-century England, "by far the greater part of the island was owned by a comparatively small group of noblemen, gentlemen of family or gentlemen in the making." Beneath this landed aristocracy the small owner had tended to disappear, leaving a substratum of tenant farmers and farm laborers. This tripartite hierarchy on the English land was in striking contrast to the peasant proprietor so prevalent on the Continent or to the family farm. of America.

If enclosure "transformed subsistence farming into commercial farming under capitalist management," the repeal of the Corn Laws in 1846 went one step further, for it definitely subordinated the agrarian interest to the needs and interests of industry. The Corn Laws had long protected and encouraged the domestic producers of grain. Their repeal afforded the manufacturer cheap food (and correspondingly low wages) and the possibility of food imports as exchange for his own industrial exports. Although the repeal thus represented a political defeat for the hitherto supreme landed interest, the latter's gloomy prophecies of the economic results did not materialize for over twenty years, and English agriculture at least appeared to bask in unalloyed prosperity. 

Then came the crash, as described on the title page of this Problem. How it happened, why it happened, and what the people of the times thought was happening the student is now to discover for himself.

FACTS AND FIGURES 

Out of the materials presented in this Part the student must piece together the story of the collapse of British agriculture. Most of the evidence is of a statistical nature and requires careful scrutiny and comparison in order to extract the answers. If judiciously handled, with due attention paid to the variables and limitations inherent in this type of evidence, these materials can go far to explain the nature, extent, and causes of this depression. Most of this evidence was available at the time, and the student, once he has established his own conclusions, will be afforded the chance in Part II to compare his own explanations with those made by the witnesses of this debacle. 469 C. 

LIVESTOCK 

As important as wheat to the complete story of English farming during the period under consideration is the amount of livestock available. This is particularly true in view of the changes in the nation's diet during these years. In 1878 one agricultural expert estimated that "thirty years ago probably not more than one third of the people of this country consumed animal food more than once a week. Now, nearly all of them eat it, in meat, or cheese, or butter, once a day." (4) Certain accidents affected the livestock figures: in 186566 England lost 209,332 cattle to the rinder pest, or cattle plague; in 1871-72 there was a serious outbreak of foot and mouth disease, attacking cattle, sheep, and pigs. These diseases (which usually came in with imported live animals) and the general impracticality of such imports on any large scale acted to limit the importation of livestock on the hoof. 

The first successful shipment of frozen meat-40 tons of beef and mutton from Australiaarrived in London on February 2, 1880.

F. 

WAGES, PRICES, PROPERTY VALUES 

It is obvious that many aspects of England's economy must be considered in any attempt to understand such a complex phenomenon as an agricultural depression. Wages and prices are of course a subject in themselves, but even a most general knowledge of their activities during the period will prove helpful. Of importance for agricultural wages was the foundation in 1872 by Joseph Arch of the Agricultural Laborers' Union; its demands -16s. a week and a 9½ hour working day—had great appeal to the farm laborer and many strikes resulted.

H. G.

GENERAL TRADE CONDITIONS, 1855-1903 

English agriculture did not function in a vacuum but was intimately connected to every aspect of the nation's economy. In particular, since the repeal of the Corn Laws and the adoption of free trade in the first half of the century, England's foreign trade balance was of critical importance to its agricultural situation. The diagram of the excess of imports, 1855-1903, gives part of the story. The student should remember that imports include both the interest on British money abroad (estimated at nearly £90,000,000 in 1900) and the earnings of British shipping (which by 1900 almost equalled the return on foreign investments). In 1854 income from interest on British money abroad had stood at almost £27,000,000. When the two items-interest and shipping-are taken into account, the truly complex dependence of England on the rest of the world for its prosperity can be visualized, a dependence which was all too obviously rooted in the maintenance of a world at peace. AMERICAN AND FOREIGN COMPETITION 

As the student has already surmised, a major factor affecting British agriculture was the increasing competition from the vast prairies of the United States. Something of the nature of this pressure and the pattern of its impact on English farming can be gathered from the material which follows. In the case of foreign competition, both from the United 

States and the rest of the world, the student must recall here the close connection of political and economic factors. Certain political events in the history of the mid-nineteenth century combined to give English agriculture a most unexpected protection from foreign competition, a protection which technology and the course of events would not allow to become permanent. Thus, the delay in the arrival of foreign competition, as well as its eventual appearance, must be included as a factor in the situation. 

1. American Wheat Production, 1869–93. In the United States grains were the single most valuable crop, worth in 1883 twice the meat production of the country and over three times its cotton crop. When and how it became a serious competitor in the English market the student must discover for himself.
