Part II. 

A. 

THE WAY IT HAPPENED 

The following selections have been drawn from the mass of contemporary interpretation and explanation of the agricultural depression. The student should appraise this evidence and compare its quality and discernment with his own findings. His judgments should always be tempered with compassion, for his vantage point in time provides him with a hindsight not given to the contemporaries of the event. 

THE REPORT OF THE ROYAL COMMISSION, 1882 

As its troubles grew more complex and national in character, Victorian England resorted with increasing frequency to royally-appointed commissions of investigation and inquiry. 

In the Benthamite tradition of empirical examination of specific difficulties, these hardworking bands of legislators and public-spirited citizens probed into every corner of the land, listened to hours of evidence, and then reported back to Crown and Parliament their findings and recommendations, leaving as the residuum of their efforts the famous parliamentary “blue books" for the benefit of future historians. In 1879 the government saw fit to appoint such a commission "to inquire into the depressed condition of the agricultural interest." For the next three years the eighteen commissioners, with their assistants who scoured the countryside, were at work. Their final report in 1882 included three thick folio volumes of evidence and interviews. Portions from the summary follow. (27) 

In obedience to your Majesty's command, we now desire to report the conclusions at which we have arrived upon the effect of the evidence which has been submitted to us as to- 1. The depressed condition of the agricultural interest, and the causes to which it is owing; 

2. Whether those causes are of a permanent character, and how far they have been created or can be remedied by legislation. 

Whatever difference of opinion may exist as to the causes of agricultural depression, or as to remedies which may be suggested for it, it will be observed that there prevails complete uniformity of conviction as to the great extent and intensity of the distress which has fallen upon the agricultural community. Owners and occupiers have alike suffered from it. No description of estate or tenure has been exempted. The owner in fee and the life tenant, the occupier, whether of large or of small holding, whether under lease, or custom, or agreement, or the provisions of the Agricultural Holdings Act-all without distinction have been involved in a general calamity. It is important that this should be clearly understood, so that undue stress may not be laid upon suggestions for legislative changes, which, whether expedient or not, have no direct or immediate connection with the distress of the present time.

The two most prominent causes which are assigned for that distress are bad seasons and foreign competition, aggravated by the increased cost of production and the heavy losses of livestock.

The extent to which agriculture has been injuriously affected by an unprecedented succession of bad seasons is very clearly shown by the abundant evidence to which we have referred in a preceding part of this report. 

Bad Seasons 

Although farmers must always take their chances of the seasons, and accept the consequences as they come, yet in some districts and to some extent the worse effects of heavy rainfall may be mitigated by the prevention of floods and an extended system of arterial drainage, which would be a national benefit. 

Foreign Competition 

Next to a succession of unfavorable seasons, the effect of foreign competition is assigned by the majority of witnesses as a main cause of the embarrassments of the agricultural community. 

In considering the representations which have been made to us as to the effect of foreign competition upon the agricultural interest of this country, it is but just to recall the fact that the pressure of that competition is now found to be greatly in excess of the anticipations of the supporters, and of the apprehensions of the opponents of the repeal of the Corn Laws. 

Whereas formerly the farmer was to some extent compensated by a higher price for a smaller yield, he has had in recent years to compete with an unusually large supply at greatly reduced prices. ...

On the other hand, he has had the advantage of an extended supply of feeding stuffs, such as Indian corn, linseed and cotton cakes, and of artificial manures imported from abroad. 

Disastrous as the combined effect of bad seasons and foreign competition has been, the witnesses who speak in the interest of agriculture fully recognize the advantage to the community that food should be cheap. They contend, however, that the low price of agricultural produce, beneficial as it is to the general community, lessens the ability of the land to bear the proportion of taxation which has heretofore been imposed upon it.

Local Taxation 

The history of the various imposts that are now levied for local purposes is very fully given in the evidence to which we have already referred. The first and the most important of these is the rate for the relief of the poor.

This rate, the heaviest local impost to which real property is subjected, has been taken as the foundation upon which the whole system of local rating has been built up. Although, to adopt the words of a resolution of the committee of the House of Lords (1850) upon parochial assessments, "The relief of the poor is a national object, to which every description of property ought justly to be called upon to contribute, and the 

Act 43 Eliz. c. 2. contemplates such contribution according to the ability of every inhabitant”; and although the decisions of courts of law established the liability of personal property to rating for the relief of the poor, yet, since the most recent decision in that sense, it has continued to be exempted from such rating by the periodical Ex emption Act. 

The practical effect of this is, that personal property is exempted not only from rates for the relief of the poor, but from others, as the cost of public highways, police, and education. . . . 

We are of opinion— 

1st That the cost of the maintenance of the indoor poor, instead of being paid, as at present, by a Union rate upon real property alone, should in future be defrayed either out of the Consolidated Fund or by a rate or taxes equitably adjusted according to means and substance; in other words, upon the personal as well as the real property of counties or of areas wider than existing unions; “indoor poor" being deemed to include all lunatics, to whom the present subvention extends, and all children in district schools or boarded out under any order of the local government board. 

2d That a certain proportion of the local taxes should be assigned to the local authority in aid of local expenditure.

Rates 

Whatever change may be made in the incidence of local taxation, we are of opinion that, without disturbing existing contracts of tenancy, all rates should in future be borne equally by owners and occupiers.

Agricultural Labor 

The difficulties of farmers during the last few years have been greatly aggravated by the condition of agricultural labor.

Owing to a variety of causes, labor has been more costly and less efficient, so that the average labor bill of an arable farm is at least 25 percent higher at the present time than it was some twenty years ago.

This condition of things is undoubtedly attended with serious embarrassment to the agricultural interest.

So far as the high price of agricultural labor results from the competition of other industries it must be accepted, just as the low price of agricultural produce must be accepted as the effect of foreign importation.

While the difficulties of the farmers have been thus increased, higher wages and more general employment have proportionately improved the condition of the laborer. It is most satisfactory to be assured that the laboring class has been scarcely, if at all, affected by the distress which has fallen so heavily upon owners as well as occupiers. Provisions have been cheap and employment abundant, while wages in a few districts only have been slightly reduced. 

In connection, however, with the unsatisfactory supply of labor, our attention has been directed to the insufficiency of house accommodation, and to the present system of education as it affects that class.

Although it is generally admitted that within the last twenty years very great progress has been made, especially upon large estates, in providing better cottages for agricultural laborers, yet, in many districts the accommodation is still very defective. To a considerable extent the interest of owners in attracting labor, and retaining it upon the land, would no doubt operate as a sufficient inducement to provide cottages with gardens or allotments, at reasonable rents, for farm laborers. 

It is due to the owners of land to state that, irrespective of considerations of interest, many of them have expended, and continue to expend, large sums of money to supply good and sufficient cottage accommodation.

A large proportion of cottages are, however, in the hands of small owners, who have neither the means nor the will to expend money on their improvement. The sanitary authorities through-

out the country have certain powers to deal with cases of defective accommodation; and if these powers are exercised with judgment and impartiality, we may reasonably look forward to such improvement in the condition of laborers, as would render them less inclined to abandon the field for the town. Education

There is a very general complaint amongst farmers that the present system of education operates prejudicially to the interests of agriculture. 

Boys, it is said, are kept at school at an age at which they might be usefully employed upon the farm, and be thus acquiring habits and tastes which would fit them for farm service. As it is, the standard of education is so fixed that not only are the first years of industrial training lost before a boy can attain it, but when he does attain it, he acquires with it a desire for what he regards as more suitable occupation; so that the class which was formerly trained into farm service is now gradually absorbed into other industries. 

Farmers very naturally complain of this, as in districts in which there are school boards they have to pay for education which not only deprives them, for the present, of the labor of boys, and obliges them to pay men's wages for boys' work, but tends to drain from the land the sources of future labor.

Agricultural Education 

We have received a good deal of evidence upon the subject of agricultural education in Great Britain and foreign countries, and the desirableness of encouraging scientific together with practical instruction has been urged by several witnesses.

We concur in these opinions, and, whilst we are not prepared to suggest the manner in which this instruction should be supplied, we are of opinion that the subject is well worthy of consideration.... Rent

It has been suggested in the course of this inquiry that for many years previous to 1875 rents had been unduly raised. The weight of evidence, however, satisfies us that such a practice was exceptional, especially on large estates, and might be attributed in a great measure to imprudent competition on the part of tenants. It would also seem that this competition was to a considerable degree encouraged by the employment of capital in the shape of advances made by country bankers on personal security, as well as by cattle dealers, salesmen, and others. The sudden withdrawal of such accommodation, and the calling in of loans so made, have, in our opinion, greatly contributed to the late difficulties of the tenant farmers. 

Upon the important question of the effect of rent upon agricultural depression several witnesses have communicated their views. 

While we strongly object to any legislative interference with arrangements on the question of rent between landlord and tenant, we are of opinion that it will be for the interest of both parties that rents should be so fixed by voluntary agreement as to enable farmers to meet the difficulties of their position. 

Contagious Diseases (Animals) Act 

The evidence to which we have already referred proves that the effect of the Contagious Diseases (Animals) Act has been most beneficial. 

Wherever the local authorities have carried out its provisions with strictness, it has been successful in checking the spread of disease. The general effect is shown by the diminished number of outbreaks, and of animals attacked with foot-andmouth disease during the last eighteen months, compared with the former periods when the disease prevailed. 

Pleuropneumonia is steadily and rapidly declining throughout the country. 

These diseases, which are both of foreign origin, are brought into the foreign animals wharves from time to time. Although every precaution is taken, there can be no doubt that foot-and-mouth disease has been introduced into this country from abroad by these means. This has led to the demand for the exclusion of livestock from infected countries, which has been urged by so many of the witnesses to whose evidence upon the subject we have already referred. 

The evidence as to the discouragement which was given to the breeding of cattle and sheep in Great Britain, and the diminution in the supply of meat which arose from extensive disease in the country, appears to us to be conclusive. 

Looking to the great importance of the home supply of meat as compared with the supply of live animals from abroad, and to the facility with which dead meat can be imported in the place of animals that are alive, we recommend that the landing of foreign live animals should not be permitted in future from any countries as to which the Privy Council are not satisfied that they are perfectly free from contagious disease. . .

Railway Rates 

In a preceding part of this report we have directed attention to the complaints of producers, not only of the inequality of railway rates as affecting home producers, but of the still more serious disadvantage arising from preferential rates for foreign commodities.

The present law clearly contemplates that similar treatment should be accorded to similar goods carried under similar conditions, but the evidence before us shows that in many cases such equality does not exist; and we would recommend that the law should be so amended as to provide a cheap and speedy means of securing the equality contemplated by the existing law. 

We are not, however, prepared to recommend that railway companies should be debarred by legislative enactment from offering special terms for through traffic from abroad. 

Minister of Agriculture

With reference to the appointment of a minister of agriculture, we believe that a system corresponding to that which prevails in foreign countries would be attended with advantage, and we recommend that the administration of all matters connected with agriculture should be vested in one public department. 

In submitting to your Majesty the preceding recommendations we desire, in conclusion, to observe that- Of the immediate causes of agricultural depression it cannot be said that any one of them is necessarily of a "permanent character." Bad and good seasons appear to come in cycles, and with them alternations of agricultural prosperity or depression.

This, the main cause of depression, no legislation can control. 

How far foreign competition may affect the home producer in the future it is impossible to calculate with any degree of certainty. That its effect will continue to be felt may be assumed as certain.

It is to be hoped that the proposals which we have made will, if adopted, eventually place all classes connected with land in a better position to meet those difficulties to which they are necessarily exposed, and which are sure to be, as they always have been, of periodical recurrence. 

We have already indicated various matters upon which legislative interference can benefit directly the agricultural classes of this country. But no interference between classes, between owners and occupiers, or between employers and laborers, can render any one of them independent of the other. We cannot recall a period in our history in which the relations of these classes have been more severely tried than during the existing depression. Owners have, as a rule, borne their share of a common calamity, and they, as well as occupiers, have done much to avert the distress from the class who are least able to bear it. It is satisfactory to know that, as we have already observed, upon the laborer it has fallen more lightly than upon either owner or occupier. The best hope for the prosperity of agriculture lies in the mutual confidence and friendly relations of the three classes directly engaged in it, and in the common conviction that their interests are inseparable. B.

MINUTES OF EVIDENCE FROM THE REPORT OF THE ROYAL COMMISSION, 1882 

The final report of the Commission was a digest of the special studies made by the assistant commissioners on the agriculture of the various parts of England and certain foreign countries and, in addition, the interviews with almost 200 witnesses. Among these latter were farmers, laborers, politicians, publicists, and a host of experts, all who could contribute out of their special knowledge some information on the problem. Often the Commis. sion would devote an entire day to the questioning of only one witness, who might be examined not only on his own special field of competence but also on his personal explanation for the general depression, and the final Report contains footnotes referring the reader back to these bits of evidence out of which the digest had been constructed. 

1. The Testimony of Joseph Arch. Refer ence has already been made to the work of Joseph Arch (1826-1919) in organizing the 

Warwickshire Agricultural Laborers' Union in 1872 and the national Union into which it soon grew. An agricultural laborer, Arch later became a member of Parliament. In the words of the Dictionary of National Biogra phy he "did more than any other man of his time to improve conditions of agricultural workers." (28)

To what part of England do you apply that remark that wages in 1871 were at starvation point? -To almost all the midland and western and southern counties. They were the counties that I was most acquainted with. 

Could you enumerate those counties?-In 

Gloucestershire, Wiltshire, Hampshire, Berkshire, Somersetshire, Dorsetshire, and Warwickshire, the wages were very low. 

Are those all the counties that you could give? -Those are the counties that I am myself ac-

quainted with with regard to the low-wage question. I have been in different counties, in Yorkshire, for instance, to work on railways, and I found that in the northern part of England wages were better than they were in the south and west. 

Do I rightly understand you to say that those counties which you have now enumerated are the only counties in England to which the remark as to wages being at starvation point would apply? -No; since our movement has started I have found that wages were very low in Suffolk and 

Norfolk, and in Essex, Sussex, and Surrey. I have been through those counties. 

What do you consider to be what you call starvation point; I do not quite understand how you gauge that?-When a man's wages for the whole of the week do not leave him more than a penny per meal per head, men, women, and children, I think that is next to starvation.

What are the wages now when they are not at starvation point?-Wages are not quite so good as they were, and even now wages are very low in some parts. In Warwickshire, I believe, wages are about 1s. a week better than they are in Hampshire and parts of Wilts. Of course wages are generally better the nearer you are to a large town, but I am speaking now of the outlying villages in these counties. 

Then you do not apply it to the whole county? -I apply it to the whole county so far as I said before, that wages are generally a little better where they are living nearer to a town, because they can go into the town and get a little more. 

Then the object with which the Association was founded was to increase the wages of the laborers? -Yes. 

What do you consider to be the amount of wages that a laborer ought to get, taking any county?—I am not here to express an opinion upon that. As a laborer I should myself want to get the best wages I could.

But you are here to tell us what is the position of the laborer, and what he ought to get in the way of wages?-No, I am not come here to say what he ought to get. I am not come here to draw the line of the laborer's wages. 

But I understood you to say that you are president of this Association, which has been formed with a view of improving the social condition of the laborer, and you state that one way of improving the social condition of the laborer is to increase his wages. That being the object of the 

Association, I want to know what amount of wages the Association would think that the laborer ought to get in order to improve his condition? As much as he can possibly make of his labor in the market.

But what is there to prevent his doing that now?-The fact is that there is a good deal to prevent it now.

What is there to prevent it now?-A great number of laborers have been driven from the land while their labor ought to have been used upon it, and the consequence is, that where laborers are thrown out like that they are often obliged to take lower wages. I know plenty of cases where farmers have thrown out in a village eight or ten men, and sometimes more, just to suit their convenience; not but what they wanted the labor of those men. . . . ...

You have given us a great deal of insight into the condition of the laborer, and you are not altogether satisfied with his condition at the present time; can you suggest any remedies for it?— 

Yes, I can suggest remedies for improving the condition of the laborer; but before you can permanently improve the condition of the laborer, the condition of the farmer must be made satisfactory.

We have examined a great many farmers already. You can suggest no improvement of the condition of the laborer apart from the improvement in the condition of the farmer?-You must improve the condition of the farmer, as his interest and the interest of the laborer are identical. I have always taught that. There is a mode by which the condition of the laborer would be very materially improved; if our large farms were let in small lots there would be more labor employed. 

And less machinery?—I do not know exactly as to that. I have here the experience of one of the most practical stewards in the midland counties; he quite corroborates my view of the question, and I have held this view for years, that our large farm system of amalgamating farms together has tended to diminish the number of laborers, and in many instances I know that farmers who have had large farms have not had sufficient capital to properly cultivate them.

But when you speak of this amalgamation of small farms into large ones having diminished the amount of labor employed, is not that owing to the fact that on large farms more machinery is employed than on small ones, and that it can be employed with advantage on a large farm where it cannot be employed with equal advantage on a small one?-You asked me my opinion as to the advancement of the laborer; I have shown, I think, very clearly, and I think your experience will go with me too, that the amalgamation of farms has been calculated to diminish the number of laborers. ...

But I want an answer to that question [effect of machinery] first? Of course, without a doubt machinery has had a tendency to lessen the number of laborers on the soil; but here is the fact looking us in the face today, that the laborer's lot in life is not what it ought to be, and you ask me my opinion as to what I think would improve it,

and I say that we have the fact that where this machinery has been extensively employed, and these large farms have been held, the large farmers are the first that are going to grief. Our large farmers are today in a worse plight than our smaller ones. My idea of improving the condition of the laborer would be to let the land in small lots where more labor would be employed, and I have no doubt that there would be quite as much machinery in the aggregate and we should get a larger production.

Your first remedy is to divide some of the larger farms, and let them in small farms?—Yes.

Would that result in more or less machinery being employed?-I do not think the machinery would be lessened in the least, but whether it was or not would make no difference in my view. . .

Do you attach any importance to the argument which is used against laborers keeping pigs, on account of its giving an encouragement to pilfering? The laborers are as honest as any other class. 

I am not saying that that is not so, but do you attach any importance to that argument?-Not at all; it is an indefensible slur upon the honesty of my class. 

2. The Testimony of Sir James Caird. In many ways Caird (1816-92) merits the title of the Arthur Young of the nineteenth century. With some practical experience in farming, he became one of the recognized experts on the subject, reported on Irish, Canadian, and American farming to the newspapers and the government, served on innumerable commissions, did a tour of duty as a member of Parliament, and wrote indefatigably on his favorite subject. (29)

And we all know that you take great interest in the agriculture of the country, and that you have also had opportunities of inspecting the agriculture of America and other countries?-That is so.

To what causes do you attribute the depression in agriculture of the last few years?-Firstly, I should say to a succession of bad seasons, unprecedented in its closeness and long continuance; secondly, to the lower range of prices, partly due to foreign imports and partly to the inferiority of quality of the home production; and thirdly, no doubt, to the rise of rent since 1867. 

I conclude that any inferiority of the quality of the production is to be attributable to the bad seasons?-No doubt it is. . . . Perhaps before we go further, your Grace will permit me to mention the apparent rise in rent since 1867. 

Do you apply this to England, to England and 

Wales, or to Great Britain?-To Great Britain.

Of course the remarks as to wheat apply chiefly to England and Wales, so that these tables are founded, so far as wheat goes, upon England and Wales. The rental I shall give separately for the three countries. The land rent is returned under Schedule A for England, and I think if your Grace will examine the returns under Schedule A of the income tax return, it will be found that a considerable rise in rent began in 1867. 

There was a moderate rise in England up to 1867, but from 1867 forward there was a considerable rise. The rent of land in England as shown under Schedule A in 1867 was £46,492,000; in 1877, which is the highest point that it appears to have reached, it was £51,811,000; showing an increase in ten years of £5,319,000, or 11 percent.

That would include, would it not, any extra land coming into cultivation?—No doubt. The rise began earlier in Scotland, but I am taking the same point. In 1867 the rent of land in Scotland was £6,964,000 and in 1877 the rent of land in Scotland was £6,964,000 and in 1887 it was £7,689,000, the increase in 10 years being £725,000 or 10 percent.

To what do you attribute the rise of rent in England in 1867?—I think to the general impetus of a prosperity that seemed to affect everything; the rise that took place, as the prime minister said "by leaps and bounds," affected rents, as it affected everything else. . . . 

What, in your opinion, have been the causes of the lower range of prices?-No doubt the principal cause has been the great increase of foreign imports, and along with that the inferiority, in many cases, of our own corn. 

Has the cost of transport been high or low?—

The cost of transport has been always falling. If it does not detain the Commission too long I should be glad to offer an observation or two upon that subject. I was in America twenty-three years ago, in 1858. Before that time, as I daresay the noble Duke remembers, the American minister here was Mr. Buchanan. I made his acquaintance when he was in this country, and when I was in America I saw him at the White House, he having become President. I had then just returned from the West, and to show how very little the Americans themselves seemed to know of the wonderfully productive character of the whole of the valley of the Mississippi, and all to the west and northwest of it, I may mention that we were talking about the qualities of the land that I had seen in the West, and he asked me what I thought of the Mississippi valley; I described what I had seen of it, and I told him that I thought very highly of its future prospects. He said to me, "Do you think it would be capable hereafter of ever feeding 20,000,000 of people?" 

I said, "I should think at least 200,000,000.” I am only mentioning this as an indication of how rapidly all this enormous increase has come, not only upon us, but upon the Americans themselves. At that time I traveled through the whole of Illinois

and Minnesota, as far west as I could get, through all those great states which find their outlet on the Mississippi, and at Chicago. It was obvious that there was a great future before that country, but I found that the cost of transport, which I carefully inquired into, was 2d. per ton per mile for corn of any kind. On reckoning what 2d. per ton per mile meant, it simply was this, that in 1000 miles a bushel of wheat exhausted itself, that it could not be carried any further by railroad, because the cost of its transport was equal to its value. In regard to Indian corn, which is only half the price of wheat, corn, bearing the same cost of transport, exhausted its value in 500 miles and could be carried no further. So long as anything like that cost of transport was likely to be maintained (and at that time there was no apparent probability of its being much reduced, for the railways in the West were paying badly), it seemed to me that the prospect of a competition with us by those rich countries was a distant one. 

But that has been all changed in the course of the last twenty years, and now the cost of transport, instead of being 2d. per ton per mile, has been reduced to d. and even d. per ton per mile, and where it can be carried by water, to less than half that rate. So that of course we have in a manner been drawn closer to those enormous regions of production, so near as one could hardly have contemplated to be possible twenty years ago, and unquestionably it has made an immense difference in the prospects of the competition to which we are now exposed. What has also greatly added to the effect of the diminished cost of transport has been the fact that, whilst in western Europe during the last six or eight years we have had an unprecedented run of bad seasons, in America they have had an equally unprecedented run of good seasons. They have had an immense production and splendid crops all concurrent with our unfavorable position. That has stimulated production in America to an extraordinary extent; their production of wheat had risen, I think, to 60,000,000 quarters. Their production of Indian corn is something astonishing. But I notice that this year they have had a change of seasons, they have had a bad harvest, and it is reported that in this last harvest there will be a diminished yield of wheat equal to 12,000,000 quarters, which is equal to our whole production of wheat in this country; and they expect a diminution in the yield of Indian corn equal to 50,000,000 quarters, which is 10,000,000 quarters more than the production of every description of corn that we have in this country; that is to say, they have a falling off in Indian corn alone, from their yield of last year, equivalent to more than all the corn we produce. From what I have myself seen of America I believe that there will be a recurrence of these vicissitudes in the seasons. . . . As time goes on, we shall find that, although they are opening new and very extensive fields, they are increasing their population at the same time, and still increasing the distance from us as they go west, and I think that with all the advantage that we have of being so close to a good market, we ought not to despair of our own agriculture.

Do you think there is any prospect of any permanent change in the cost of transport?—I do not anticipate that there will be any change to higher charges, except by greater distance. I think a change in the other direction is not likely to be sudden or great, because the charges have reached an extremely low point. . . . 

How would you improve the future condition of agriculture?-The two formidable conditions that we have to meet are the American competition, which it is impossible for us to set aside, and the increasing cost of cultivation, because that also is a fact. If we put aside all idea of a return to protective duties on food, I would say that the safety of the landed interest in this country depends upon the continuance of its commercial prosperity. So long as that continues we have the best market in the world; we who are nearest to it possess that great advantage, and we must use it to the utmost of our power, and that proximity, compared with the cost of transport from America, is equal to the average rent of land here. This leads one to consider in what way the country is at present cultivated; and that divides itself into the two capitals of landlord and tenant. Now what is the tenant? He is the instrument by which the owner of the land at the least labor, risk, and cost to himself, turns his land to account. That instrument can only be effective so long as it can work with adequate power and undivided attention, and with full security of capital. There was sent up to me the other day an agreement quite lately drawn up for a great landowner in this country with his tenantry, in which there are some excellent conditions, but among them this one, which is not at all an uncommon condition, and which I will venture to read to the Commission: That the said tenant shall over and above the aforesaid rent pay the land tax, and all other parliamentary and parochial rates and taxes, which now are, or which may at any time hereafter, during the continuance of this tenancy become chargeable upon the said farm and lands." 

Now why should this future risk be taken from the man who has more legislative power to prevent unfair burdens, and be turned over to him who is but a passive instrument? It is quite clear that landowners must recognize their true position, for upon them alone in the end the whole weight of the depression must ultimately fall. A tenant will retire from the business if he finds it 46

ceases to pay, very likely with much loss; but there is no escape for the landowner; he must make it pay, if possible. This leads me to what we see constantly stated with regard to local taxation. It has been stated that the £150,000,000 of income from real property pays the whole of the local taxation which, in equity, it is argued, should be borne by the £500,000,000 of taxable income. Now would this have long been possible if the landowners had had to pay these local burdens directly, instead of through their tenants? 

The landlords themselves would have at once found the great inequality of such a burden as this; but seeing that it is altogether shifted from them, and divided over a vast number of tenants who have really no great voice in the legislation of this country; . . . 

Do you consider that farmers generally have lost much capital as well as income during these times?-Some of the gentlemen here probably know that there is a small club called the "Political Economy Club," which meets once a month in the winter season to discuss economical questions, and I do not think I am revealing any secrets when I say that a very interesting question was introduced by Mr. Giffen a fortnight ago, in the discussion in which several members took part, Mr. Goschen, Lord Frederick Cavendish, Mr. Charles Villiers, Mr. Lefevre, and myself, and some others. The object was to arrive, if possible, at a money estimate of the loss that had been occasioned by the late bad seasons. The principle which was stated by Mr. Giffen, and which we all agreed upon as being a very good measure by which to test it, was this,-that making allowance for the increase of population, and estimating the consumption on an average of each head of the population, the increase of imported food of every description, less the amount required by the increased population would show (supposing the people of this country to eat as much as they did before), what had been the loss sustained by the bad crops in this country; and I may state shortly what was the result I arrived at. 

It was found that in the period from 1867 to 1869 the annual value of the imports into this country of the food which we consume was £79,140,000. In 1877 to 1879, ten years later, it was £129,632,000, making an annual increase of £50,492,000. Now, if we take the increased population, 3,177,000, at the annual consumption per head of £9 5s. 6d., upon which my estimates were based, it gives £29,462,000 to be subtracted from the above £50,492,000 and that would leave £21,030,000 as the annual loss apparently sustained in consequence of the diminished production; and if we multiply that by four years (because we take a higher rate for 1880-81) that would make £84,120,000. But for the two years, 1880 and 1881, the increase of imports was £63,000,000 instead of £50,000,000; and there was also an increase of population to be taken into account; and when we deduct that, we find that for the last two years instead of having £21,000,- 

000 as the loss, we have £27,354,000 as the loss, which for these two years is £54,708,000, thus bringing out an estimated total loss of farmers' capital in the United Kingdom, in the six years, of £138,828,000. . . . 

You have noticed, have you not, a great tendency to lay land down to grass within the last ten years? Yes. 

Do you think that that is a desirable result?—I think that where it is judiciously done it is a very prudent measure. 

Do you expect to see that process continue?—I think it is very likely.

The result of that will be the employment of less labor and less capital upon the land, will it not?—I am not quite sure that that follows. Of course if you laid down the whole countryside into grass, it would decrease the demand for labor; but I noticed many years ago, in going through a part of this country where there is a large proportion of land in grass, and a considerable proportion in arable, that it does not seem to diminish the demand for labor. For instance you will find that in those districts the wages of labor are generally as good as they are in the purely agricultural counties. If the price of labor is a test, one would say that laying down land to grass has not had that effect. I speak rather appealing to my memory at this moment, but I think that the result of my own inquiries in England in 1850 and 1851 was that in the dairy and pastoral counties the rate of wages was higher than in the purely agricultural counties.

But speaking as a practical farmer you would certainly say that the laying down of land to grass lessens the employment of labor on the land?— 

No doubt it would. 

And I suppose that this tendency to lay down land to grass has been fostered by the scarcity and the depreciated quality of English labor of late years, has it not?-I could not venture to offer that as a reason.

But you look upon the laying down of land to grass as a natural result of the lower prices of agricultural produce do you not?-Of the lower prices of corn; but I do not at all agree with you that it is in consequence of the diminished value of labor, for I have no experience to that effect. 

You consider do you not that it is to the disadvantage of the community that the land should be thrown out of cultivation?-No, not if it is thrown into grass. If you mean by "thrown out of cultivation" thrown out of corn into grass, I do not think it is a disadvantage.

But the gross produce of land thrown into grass will be far less than it would be under cultivation would it not?-I have no objection to that if the country can get its corn at a more advantageous rate.

You think it matters not to the country whether the produce of English land is great or small?—

Yes, I think it matters greatly to the country that 

English produce should be great.

But your last answer seems to imply that it does not matter?-I think not. I should say that the producer would endeavor to get that produce which is to him the most remunerative, and if he finds grass the most remunerative, he is quite right to lay his land to grass.

The grassland may be more remunerative to him, in as much as the balance left as profit to him would be greater; but it may be obtained with a much smaller employment of labor, and consequently the community might suffer?-I do not think that the case of the laborer seems to have grown worse in the course of these depressed times. The laborer's wage seems to have been almost the only thing that has remained good. . . .

The recent census shows a great diminution, does it not, in rural labor?-I should expect it. I have not seen the complete recent census, but according to previous census there is no doubt that in purely agricultural districts the agricultural population is diminishing. 

Is not that a disadvantage to the community?—

Not if the agricultural population is better off. 

So that if a farmer by laying down land to grass may grow half the gross produce that he would get if the land were under cultivation, if he gets a larger profit to himself you think it is to the advantage of the community that the process should go on?—I think it to the advantage of the community that the land of this country should leave the largest profit to those engaged in it, by whatever means that profit can be obtained.

But must we not draw a distinction between the profit to the landowner and the farmer, and the gross produce?—The profit to the landowner and the farmer is a matter that must right itself. 

The farmer will not go on unless he gets such a profit as he believes to be necessary to enable him to meet his engagements, and to give a fair remuneration for his capital and labor. The landowner must take his chance. 

3. The Testimony of John Clay, Jr. Clay was one of the most active assistant commissioners, who contributed reports not only on English agriculture but also on conditions in 

America. Clay had himself done some farming in the United States. Sections of his report follow. (30) 

You say, "men living in this country, and more especially those farming in it, have seen within the last two years a great increase in the value of land, equal at least to 20 percent in the middle and western states; in some portions of the West it has been over 100 percent." And then you say, "The rigor of a pioneer life had to be borne by those parties who ventured out to the prairie, and the experiences they had were more hard to bear than is the usual lot of those who engage in a frontier life." And then you say that the “average wheat grower makes but little money." How do you account for the great increase in the value of land which you mention at page 7 of your report, notwithstanding the small profits to be made by farming which you allude to on page 6, and the hard life which you say farming entails? -I may explain that in this way, that most of the wheat that is being produced in America just now is produced upon the basis of the prices of the land that was bought in those cheap times, but I believe that the farmers of America cannot possibly produce wheat so cheaply as they did in those years of depression, or shortly after those years of depression, because the price of land has risen so materially; and I think that the price of wheat has an upward tendency at the present moment, because in the West land has risen more than 20 percent in value; and then labor has risen from 15 to 20 percent in the last three years. 

Even if wheat could have been produced three years ago at 40s. per quarter, I cannot see how it could possibly be produced at anything like that price now; and I have come to the conclusion that the American farmer at the present prices of land, and the present price of labor, cannot at the present moment produce it under 45s. per quarter.

That will allow him a fair profit. I believe, as I have said in this report, that whatever he gets over 45s. will be extra profit to the American farmer. I must, however, say that this year he cannot produce wheat at 45s., because there has been such a short crop in America. 

You say on page 4 that there are signs of changes in the American system of culture, and you say, "Those changes will be gradual, but we shall find the details worked out slowly and surely, and when that period is reached the bad management of present times will cease, necessity will bring it, and the science of agriculture, fostered by education, specially directed to it, will thrive and wax very great." Do you think, that the farmers have found that the fertility of the soil has been decreased by the constant growth of wheat?-Undoubtedly.

To what extent will the change in system affect the future price of wheat in the English market? -It would be very difficult to give that in figures. 

For instance, in the new Northwest, which I have written an appendix about, a road might be

opened up through the Hudson's Bay, which might bring wheat just as cheaply as it is brought now, so that actually the cost of transit from there would be very little more than what it is from 300 miles west of Chicago at the present moment. 

Then you say, "If the American farmer can get no more than 40s. per quarter for his finest wheat in the Liverpool markets it will be a sad day for him, it is his only stronghold." What change of system would he adopt in growing wheat?-If you will allow me to make a slight correction, I should have said the "Western farmers" instead of the "American farmers." In answer to that question I may explain that Illinois was and still is a very large wheat-producing country, but gradually they are coming on to grazing, and the best beeves that come to this country from the States come from Illinois at this moment. As the wheat production goes westward by north it gradually fails. Wheat after wheat so runs out the land that it will not produce wheat to any extent say after 10 or 15 years. The result is that a wave of grazing lands comes after that, so that, probably, after the western farmer has taken so much out of his soil by wheat growing he will put it down to grazing and raise beef. ...

Of course you have not only had experience in America, but you have had great experience at home before going there, and you have thought well to speak of the prospects of home agriculture. On page 2 you say "It is no false feeling or jealousy of the American people, it is the welfare of thousands and thousands of British subjects that you must protect. British agriculture is wasting under some terrible disease, whose direful effects are intensified by disastrous seasons. Providence will provide a cure for the latter, but the former must be seen to by the representatives of the farmers and our legislators, and the Commission is placed in a position to do much that is good, and to it the eyes of the British farmers are turned." Will you kindly tell the Commission what remedies you think desirable for this state of things?—I may say that I only say this as an

Anglo-American farmer. I felt that rents had become so high here that it was impossible for me to live on this side, that I could not get what I considered a fair field for my own efforts; and going to America, I personally find has been very greatly to my own benefit. But I look upon the agriculture of Great Britain just now as suffering more from the seasons than from anything else. 

These bad seasons have unfortunately come at a time when we had great commercial depression throughout Great Britain, and the one has intensified the other; and I think that probably we shall have to have the land laws under which we are living to a certain degree ameliorated; I do not wish to pull down, as I have said, any old established rules; I do not wish to interfere with the rights of property; but I think that this Commission might give the government some ideas which might ameliorate the condition of the farmer at the present moment. 

You consider that the expenses which the British farmer has had to meet of late in rent and rates and taxes have placed him in such a position that he cannot compete with the producers of the great American continent?-If the seasons continue such as we have had, I think it will be impossible. 

But even with better seasons can he with the same amount of outgoing, compete with the American farmer?-I think it depends in a great measure upon the rent which he pays, whether he will be able to compete or not. 

Do you not consider that it would be a sad thing for this country if numbers of our young men and farmers were to leave and settle in Canada or in the States; would you not look upon that as a national evil?-Certainly.

And you think it desirable that every effort should be made by the legislature of this country to prevent any such catastrophe?-I think it is desirable. If you allow the best young men (who will eventually be the old men) of the country to go from it, in a few years it will have a very direful effect upon the agriculture of Great Britain. 

With your knowledge of agriculture in England and Scotland do you think it desirable that there should be a legislative enactment to compensate farmers on leaving a farm for any improvements of which they have not derived the full benefit?-Yes I do. 

And that during the last two years there has been a good flood of prosperity in agriculture in America?-Yes.

There have been four years of extraordinary and exceptionally favorable seasons?—Yes, I grant that, except this last year, 1881. 

And it is mainly in consequence of those, you think, that people prophesied that 40s. per quarter would be the price at which wheat for the future would be landed in England?—Yes, but I cannot see how they could have prophesied that, because practically wheat has not been at that price for the last four years; it has been above that price.

But it is in consequence of this exceptional state of things in America, that we have had to contend with the low prices that wheat has been at for the last few years?—I think that wheat has been selling these last two years in England at a very fair price, but unfortunately the quality has been so bad that the British farmers have not been able to command the price that they should actually have had. 

But do I rightly understand you to mean that this exceptional prosperity in America has had a

tendency to lower the prices in this country?— 

The large crop, of course, has had that effect. 

Now you are speaking of the United States of 

America. We will take that first. The real point, you tell us, is not the cost of production in America, but the cost of the wheat at great centers like 

New York or Chicago?—Yes. 

Then it really becomes a question of freight?- 

In a great measure.

I suppose it is the case that the land in the West of America and particularly in the new districts of the Red River and the Saskatchewan are incomparably more fertile than the generality of the land in England?-Yes, very much richer.

Then, unless it were for the cost of freight, the growers of wheat in those districts must inevitably undersell the growers of wheat in England? -Yes, there is no question of that.

In fact, if the freights were materially lowered, it would have the effect of putting wheat out of cultivation in England?-If you materially lowered them; but, of course, railway companies, as well as steamship companies, must live and make a fair profit, and more especially a railway company in these western states.

If that is the case, the cost of production would become a very serious thing for us to consider in this country, if freights were to fall materially?—

But we have freights as low at the present moment as there is much probability of their ever being.

I suppose it has been the tendency of the freights between America and England to fall ever since America was discovered, and probably we may look forward to further reductions in freight as years go on?—Yes. 

And if that was to be the case, then I am right in supposing that the cost of production there would be a very serious matter for us to consider? -But you must put against that that the wheat production is continually going further from the seaboard, so that you meet it in that way. I have made a calculation which shows that the wheat center of America is going about ten miles west by north every year, so that, supposing that they do bring freights down a little, you will have always to bring the wheat from a point ten or fifteen miles further west every year for a number of years to come. 

But I suppose it would take a vast number of years, even at that rate of progress, to make any material difference in the cost of freight?-I cannot see how that would be, because you have 100 miles in ten years. 

What is the cost of freight every 100 miles?—

That is what it is impossible to tell in present circumstances, because a railway company in America has no conscience, but it has been computed that the freight for bringing wheat from the wheat centers of America is about 55 cents per bushel, and that railway and steamship companies can afford to bring it at that. But what they could afford to do two years ago they cannot afford to do at the present moment, because it takes more to build their road, and it takes more to work them, and the price of coal and everything has gone up, and at the present moment a great railway war is going on. 

Then I gather from you that under no probable circumstances which you can foresee is the cost of production in itself likely to be a very serious matter for us, and that it will always be more a question of freight than a question of the cost of production?—I think so. Allow me to explain that the cost of production will always have a certain effect upon it; but at the present moment it is not a question of production so much, it is the question what the price of wheat is at the great centers. Although I am in America myself, I am unable to calculate what it will take to bring wheat. I give in my report a very notable instance of how a railway company can charge. 

Is that what occurred in your own case?—Yes, it is my own personal case. 

You say that, "The rate on wheat from the point where the writer (that is yourself) resides is sometimes greater than it is at Chicago, 500 miles further from the seaboard"; is that what you refer to?—Yes. Then I give another instance at page 5, where I say, "While the writer saw a contract made to carry 100 lbs. of wheat from Chicago to Liverpool, via rail to New York, a distance of 800 miles, and other 3000 miles by sea, at the above rate of 21 cents per 100 lbs.; he had to pay one of the railway companies who contracted to carry this grain part of the way, and must have got about 1 percent per 100 lbs. for every 100 miles, at the rate of 10 cents per 100 lbs.," or 5d. for 100 lbs., and they carried it only a distance of thirty miles, where actually they carried 100 lbs. 4000 miles for 21 cents. That is an actual circumstance, and those contracts were made upon the same day. I may explain that the 

21 cents was equal to 60 cents the year before; it was, of course, extraordinarily low freight. 

And that is a circumstance which I suppose might and would probably be repeated in every district where you were not adjacent to the main line, or close to the great centers?—Yes.

Talking of the great centers, I observe that you say, "From New York wheat cannot be landed here now at less than 47s. to 48s. per quarter"?—Yes; it is selling at the present moment at about 46s. in New York, and if you add on 4s. for freight, which is the freight quoted, it is 50s., and with a charge of 2s. in Liverpool, that makes 52s. at present.

From Chicago you put it even higher; that is

in consequence, I suppose, of the inland freight; you put it from Chicago at 52s.?-That is what it was costing on the 14th of October 1881. "Wheat was carried from Chicago to Liverpool at 21 cents per 100 pounds. Supposing then the original cost of wheat in Chicago to be 45s., the freight to be 

4s., and the insurance and handling 3s., the wheat would cost at Liverpool 52s." The paying freight is supposed to be about 10s. to 12s. instead of 4s. 

If they had charged other 8s. for freight, which would have paid them, it would have been landed here at 60s. per quarter.

Then what this evidence amounts to is something of this nature, that unless the railroads are to continue to carry the wheat at a loss it cannot be landed here at much less than 60s. per quarter?-In the year 1881, at the then prices. If we are to have wheat at 45s. in Chicago for all time to come, of course they will be splendid times for the farmers, because it will make about 60s. here, but I have no idea that it will keep at the price which it is making just now in America, because we have a very short supply. Instead of having 

480,000,000 bushels, we have this year only 380,- 000,000 bushels, which is a decline of 100,000,000 bushels, but I think that the average price in Chicago will be about 32s. to 34s. per quarter.

Then according to you, if it is to be carried at a remunerative rate, you must add at least 15s. to that? Yes, you must add 15s. to that. If you made it 34s., and gave the companies a remunerative rate for carrying it, and for handling in Liverpool and everything, say 12s., 10s. for carrying and 

2s. for handling, and add it to the 34s., you have 

46s. at Liverpool; but the average of the last few years has been above that. 

Then I understand you that at the present price of wheat in Chicago, if the rates are to be remunerative, the price of wheat in England would be 60s. per quarter; and at the average, or what you expect to be the average future price of wheat in Chicago, if the rates are to be remunerative, it would be 47s. or 48s. per quarter?-Yes, that is the conclusion that I have come to here. . . . 

You speak of America as an inventor; what do you mean by that phrase?-I mean that an American farmer is a man who if he does not himself invent very readily takes hold of any inventions put before him which will lessen his labor bill. 

For instance, in the western prairie nearly all the grain upon these large farms is cut by automatic self-binders, and all the implements are of the very first class. They are, perhaps, not so substantial as the implements of the English farmer, but they are very much more easily handled. 

And this great power of invention has been brought to bear in a singular way on American farming. in a way that has never been practiced in any other country?-That is so. Necessity, in fact, has been the mother of it. We could not get labor, and we had to invent an implement to replace manual labor.

And they have generally mastered a difficulty of that sort?—Yes, I think you may say that it has always been mastered.

But yet at the same time you say that the American farmer is not as good as a farmer in the old country?—No; his general system of agriculture in the working of his land is not so good. 

Do you mean that his knowledge is inferior, that it is due to the necessities of his position?—I think it is due to both causes, to want of knowledge and to the necessities of his position. 

Then you think that personally the American farmer is not equal to the English farmer?—I do not think he is.

Do you think very highly of the standard of the farming knowledge of the English farmer generally?—I do not like to pass a verdict upon the class to which I myself belong.

Do you think that education might do very much for the English farmer?—Yes, I think that agricultural education has been neglected very much in this country. 

Is there any agricultural education at all in America?-We have a most perfect system of agricultural education there. 

Do you think that the system of protection which is so largely adopted in America has any bearing upon the farmer; does it injure the farming? I think it is most injurious, because our western farmers have to pay duty upon everything; every bit of machinery that we have. 

But the machinery does not come from abroad; and if he does not pay it in the shape of a duty in what shape does he pay a protection tax?-Upon every bit of clothing that he puts on to his back he has to pay a protection tax. 

Does he not wear American clothing? We do not produce nearly enough clothing in America to supply the whole of the American people. 

Does not the system of protection make the American farmer pay much more for things made in America, because they cannot be made as cheaply as they would in Europe?-That is so. 

And that really amounts to a tax?-Quite so.

The man who feels this protection most is the western farmer.

Do you find any sentiment growing up amongst the great farming population of America of revolt against this protection?-Undoubtedly; all the western farmers are free traders, and the people in the East are protectionists. 

Which do you find gains ground, free trade or protection?-In the West the population is in creasing so rapidly that the balance of parties will probably be equalized very shortly.

And on the whole you expect an approach to free trade? We are getting nearer to it every day, I think.

What do you think is the effect which that American protection has upon the British farmer here? I think you would need to be more explicit upon the point, because it would lead us into a question of political economy of very wide range to explain that. 

Do you think that the duties which the Americans put upon clothing, and that sort of goods act at all upon the British farmer?—I think they are in favor of the British farmer because it takes the western farmer more to produce his grain, or his produce out there. 

But on the other hand, it diminishes the trade of England, and therefore the English buyers suffer?-All his surplus goods have to come here. 

In reference to a paragraph in this report in which you state that, “British agriculture is wasting under some terrible disease whose direful effects are intensified by disastrous seasons." Mr. 

Chaplin asked you some questions and I understood you to say in answer to him that the disease consisted of two things, one being the absence of compensation for the unexhausted capital, which the farmer puts into the land, and the other being the high rents?—Yes. 

4. The Testimony of Mr. A. G. Robinson. 

The Royal Commission interrogated numerous persons whose occupations gave them an indirect connection with the agricultural crisis. Among them was a steamship agent, Mr. 

Anthony George Robinson. (31)

Would the fact of bringing over this American beef, dead or alive-and killed at Deptford, if that is carried out in any degree-will that not bring down the price of the English mutton and beef? It is inevitable.

Why has not it done so now?-It is only within the last three years since it commenced at all, and they have not fitted out the vessels as I consider properly for it yet, and I think they have not the proper class of vessel for it, and they are gradually getting into it in consequence of finding it pay, and as the steamers increase to an enormous extent there will be so many more vessels put into the trade, and they will be better fitted for the purpose. 

But, then, might I ask one question more. Can you give an estimate as to what price American meat will before long-that is, within any practical time-be brought to sell in the English market, and at what price the English market will have to compete with this American meat?-I think, as I said before, that the English farmer will have to compete with meat at 6d. per lb. wholesale. 

Not the sirloins, but all round?-6d. all round.

My opinion is that the English farmer, if he produces meat, must produce it at 6d. per lb. 

Now, you won't undertake to say what we eaters of the meat have to pay?-No, that is your business.

The House of Lords Crisis, 1909-11

They do not understand, As bright will shine Great Britain's rays

The House of Lords crisis, it has been stated, was "a constitutional conflict more serious than any that had arisen since 1688." (1) In 1911 there was no supposititious Catholic heir, no Dutch invasion, no fugitive king; but contemporaries thought that the political cleavage ran as deep as in the Glorious Revolution. As time lengthens historical perspective, however, men may well see that the significance of the events of 1909-11, profound though it be, lies on a different plane. 

The idea of reforming the House of Lords did not originate in the Edwardian era. As early as 1719 the Whigs had sought to limit the royal prerogative of creating peers following Anne's "packing" the Upper House to secure the passage of the Treaty of Utrecht, but the Peerage Bill was defeated by the Commons. 

After the Great Reform Act some philosophic radicals had mooted a limitation upon the powers of the Lords, and again in 1884 John Morley had raised the cry that the Lords must be "mended or ended." Ten years later Gladstone's last speech in the House of Commons contained a solemn warning that the Upper Chamber must be revised, and in 1895 the Liberals had made reform of the Lords a plank in their election platform. These threats and suggestions came to nothing, but they demonstrate that the crisis of 1909-11 was no sudden cataclysm but had its origins deep in the past. 

The House of Lords which occupied the center of the stage in the crisis was of variegated composition. In 1909 it consisted of 618 members, who were of five different types. First were the 544 hereditary peers, most of whom were of recent origin. Only thirty-two dated their peerages from the seventeenth century, eleven from the sixteenth, four from the fifteenth, five from the fourteenth, and two from the thirteenth. The creations of hereditary peers in recent years, moreover, had enormously increased their number. Whereas there had been only 153 in 1688, there were 174 in 1760, 326 in 1830, 400 in 1865, and finally 544 in 1909. 

The second group were the lords spiritual, the two archbishops and twenty-four senior bishops. Third were the sixteen representative peers of Scotland, elected to each Parliament under the Act of Union of 1707. Fourth were the twenty-eight 

Irish representative peers, elected for life under the Act of Union of 1800. And fifth were the four lords of appeal in ordinary, life-peers first appointed in 1876 to try cases when the Upper House sat as the supreme court of the British Empire. 

This was the body about which the controversy raged. The chief antagonists in the controversy were the two great political parties. On the one hand were the 

Liberals, from 1898 to 1907 under the leadership of Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman and thereafter through the crisis under Herbert Henry Asquith. While they clung to free-trade doctrines, the Liberals in this period adopted a broad program of social reform, and since 1886 Home Rule for Ireland had been a major Liberal cause. Because of their platform Liberals were often termed Radicals, and in the Edwardian era Liberal and Radical were synonymous. On the other hand were the Conservatives, from 1901 to 1911 under the leadership of Arthur James Balfour. Though not averse to social reforms, the Conservatives were more cautious than the Liberals, and they were gradually moving away from free trade to favor a tariff policy of imperial preference. They were unalterably opposed to 

Irish Home Rule, and, having coalesced with a small group of Liberals who had deserted their own party on this issue, the Conservatives were often called Unionists, as being in favor of maintaining the Act of Union with Ireland. 

In addition to the two major parties there were two smaller ones which played a not inconsiderable part in the House of Lords crisis. The Irish Nationalists, who usually numbered about eighty, were a group devoted to the achievement [ 493 ]

of Irish Home Rule. They therefore ordinarily voted with the Liberals. The infant Labor party was really born at the general election of 1906. Numbering forty to fifty, the Laborites favored a program similar to that of the Liberals. 

When Liberals and Conservatives were fairly evenly balanced, these two smaller parties could turn the scales. 

With these facts in mind, the student is to examine the great constitutional conflict of 1909-11. The documents in Part I of the Problem provide an insight into the background of the crisis. In Part II the materials indicate the development and settlement of the conflict itself.

THE BACKGROUND OF THE CRISIS 

To comprehend the nature of the crisis which brought about the reform of the House of Lords in 1911, it is necessary to review a number of factors affecting the position of the Upper Chamber in the preceding period. The documents in this part reveal the relationship of the peers to the Constitution, to English society, and to the political scene in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. A.

THE PEERS AND THE CONSTITUTION 

The Reform Act of 1832, by altering the composition of the House of Commons, inevitably affected the constitutional position of the Lords. The nature of their new position is indicated in the following documents. 

1. Roebuck's Observations, 1835. The Lords came into conflict with the Commons over the Municipal Reform Bill of 1835. In the course of the debate J. A. Roebuck (180279), a radical member, delivered a heated speech on the function of the Lords. Selections from his speech follow. (2) 

Every day brings us fresh evidence that vital changes in our constitution are required for the peace and the welfare of this nation. The result to which we are not arriving is to me no disappointment. They who form their opinions respecting government on an investigation of the principles of human nature, expected and predicted the present state of things. Many of these inquiries into the science of government long since foretold what would be the inevitable result of carrying into practice the theory of the British constitution. Experience is but too fatally verifying the accuracy of their statements. 

The noble lord below me [Lord John Russell] is, I know, a believer in the theory of the English constitution. Every day's experience, I should think, ought to lead him to doubt the correctness of this belief. He, however, acting under that belief, did, under the ministry of Lord Grey, propose to reform this House, and thereby to carry into execution the description so often given of this our mixed constitution: in other words, the noble lord determined to create a House of Commons wholly independent of the Lords; to make two separate and independent legislative bodies; and he hoped that these two bodies, thus independent, could and would carry on the business of government with perfect harmony, and thus work out the happiness of the nation. 

For myself, I had no such expectation; and I found many, for whose opinions I had great reverence, who had formed conclusions directly opposite to those of the noble lord. To us, it appeared that the House of Commons representing the people, and the House of Lords, representing themselves, had hostile and irreconcilable interests: that the interest of the people was one thing, the interest of the Lords another and very different thing; and that we, pursuing the interests of the people, should soon be driven into hostile collision with the House of Lords, who would steadily pursue their own interests. 

The event has justified this expectation. The 

Commons and the Lords are now in opposition. 

We, the Commons, acting in our character of the people's representatives, performing faithfully a sacred and imperative duty, find ourselves violently opposed, insulted, and scoffed at by the irresponsible House of Lords, who represent themselves, and who are steadily pursuing their own private, aye, and pecuniary interest also. From the moment when the first formed Parliament met, this strife commenced. For a time, it was shrouded in some mystery, and its true nature was sedulously hidden from the eyes of the multitude. It has become too plain to be misunderstood. All men see that the two branches of the legislature are in collision, and we all know and feel that the question we have now to determine is, not simply the passing of the Municipal Reform Bill, but whether the wishes of the people or of the Lords are to govern in this country. 

It is idle-it is worse than idle-to attempt to hide this from ourselves. The machine of government has come to a standstill. The noble lord was often told before the passing of the Reform Bill, that he was framing a machine for government that could not work. He clung to his preconceived ideas respecting our constitution; he passed the Reform Bill, called into operation [ 495 ]

Problem XX: The House of Lords Crisis, 1909-11 

hostile elements, and now wonders that strife is the result. Whether the government of this country is hereafter to be an aristocratic or democratic one is now the great point to be determined. 

There is no middle course. One or other party must succumb; and I, as a friend of democratic government, look anxiously to the result. [Cheers]

That I am a friend of democratic government is not wonderful. I am one of the people; I have the same feelings and interests; and while doing my duty as a representative, I pursue my interest as a citizen. Now comes the question, what is to be done? I answer boldly that the evil must be cured in its cause, and that the existence of the House of Lords in its present shape is incompatible with the welfare of England. If we look at their deeds for the last three years, even if we confine ourselves solely to the consideration of their doings of this year, no disinterested and sane person for one instant will assert that the well-being of the country has been forwarded by their conduct. 

2. Bagehot's Observations, 1860. Roebuck's peroration did not produce any legislation reforming the Lords, but the means by which the Upper Chamber was adapted to the revised constitution are indicated in the following selection from The English Constitution, published in 1860 by the essayist and economist, Walter Bagehot (1826-77). (3)

From the Reform Act the function of the 

House of Lords has been altered in English history. Before that Act it was, if not a directing chamber, at least a chamber of directors. The leading nobles, who had most influence in the Commons, and swayed the Commons, sat there. 

Aristocratic influence was so powerful in the House of Commons, that there never was any serious breach of unity. When the Houses quarreled, it was, as in the great Aylesbury case [1704], about their respective privileges, and not about the national policy. The influence of the nobility was then so potent, that it was not necessary to exert it. The English constitution, though then on this point very different from what it now is, did not even then contain the blunder of the Victorian or of the Swiss constitution. It had not two houses of distinct origin, it had two houses of common origin-two houses in which the predominant element was the same. 

The danger of discordance was obviated by a latent unity.

Since the Reform Act the House of Lords has become a revising and suspending House. It can alter bills; it can reject bills on which the House of Commons is not yet thoroughly in earnestupon which the nation is not yet determined. 

Their veto is a sort of hypothetical veto. They say, we reject your bill for this once, or these twice, or even these thrice; but if you keep on sending it up, at last we won't reject it. The 

House has ceased to be one of latent directors and has become one of temporary rejectors and palpable alterers.

It is the sole claim of the Duke of Wellington to the name of a statesman that he presided over this change. He wished to guide the Lords to their true position, and he did guide them. In 

1846, in the crisis of the Corn-Law struggle, and when it was a question whether the House of Lords should resist or yield, he wrote a very curious letter to the late Lord Derby: "For many years, indeed from the year 1830, when I retired from office, I have endeavored to manage the House of Lords upon the principle on which I conceive that the institution exists in the constitution of the country, that of conservatism. I have invariably objected to all violent and extreme measures, which is not exactly the mode of acquiring influence in a political party in England, particularly one in opposition to government. I have invariably supported government in Parliament upon important occasions, and have always exercised my personal influence to prevent the mischief of anything like a difference or division between the two Houses-of which there are some remarkable instances, to which I will advert here, as they will tend to show you the nature of my management, and possibly, in some degree, account for the extraordinary power which I have for so many years exercised, without any apparent claim to it. "Upon finding the difficulties in which the late King William was involved by a promise made to create peers [1832], the number, I believe, indefi nite, I determined myself, and I prevailed upon others, the number very large, to be absent from the House in the discussion of the last stages of the Reform Bill, after the negotiations had failed for the formation of a new administration. This course gave at the time great dissatisfaction to the party; notwithstanding that I believe it saved the existence of the House of Lords at the time and the constitution of the country. "Subsequently, throughout the period from 1835 to 1841, I prevailed upon the House of Lords to depart from many principles and systems which they as well as I had adopted and voted, on Irish tithes, Irish corporations, and other measures, much to the vexation and annoyance of many. But I recollect one particular measure, the union of the provinces of upper and lower Canada, in the early stages of which I had spoken in opposition to the measure, and had protested against it; and in the last stages of it 

I prevailed upon the House to agree to, and pass it, in order to avoid the injury to the public in-

terests of a dispute between the Houses upon a question of such importance. Then I supported the measures of the government. . . "I am the servant of the Crown and people.
